teile.einleitung: Countless chunks of rock orbit the sun between the planets Mars and Jupiter. This area is called the **asteroid belt**. Unlike in many films, though, the chunks there are very far apart.
wichtigste: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids are chunks of rock that orbit the sun.
There are around a million larger asteroids there.
All of them together are much lighter than our moon.
Vesta is the brightest asteroid.
The space probe Dawn visited first Vesta and then Ceres.

abschnitte.text: **Asteroids** are chunks of rock and metal that orbit the sun. Most of them are in the **asteroid belt** between **Mars and Jupiter**. The largest are hundreds of kilometres across, but most are much smaller. There are around **a million larger** asteroids and many more small ones. Most small asteroids have an **irregular shape**, rather like potatoes.

The first asteroid was discovered in 1801: **Ceres**. At almost 1,000 kilometres across, it is the largest object in the belt and is now considered a **dwarf planet**. **Vesta** is smaller, but it is the **brightest asteroid**. In good conditions you can sometimes even see it **without a telescope**. The space probe **Dawn** visited first Vesta and then Ceres and sent many pictures back to the Earth.

abschnitte.titel: Less mass than you might think
abschnitte.text: Although there are so many asteroids, **together they are much lighter than our moon**. Their mass is estimated at only a few per cent of the moon's mass. A large part of it is in the four largest asteroids. Researchers think that the strong gravity of **Jupiter** stopped the chunks from joining together to form a planet.

In films spacecraft often have to fly through dense fields of rock. In reality the asteroids are **very widely spread out**, often hundreds of thousands of kilometres apart. That is why flying through the belt is **usually not dangerous** for a space probe. Several probes have already flown through it without hitting an asteroid.

gewusst: Ceres probably contains a lot of water in the form of ice.
From the surface of an asteroid in the belt you would usually not see the other asteroids at all, because they are so far away.

teile.einleitung: At the centre of almost every large galaxy sits a huge **black hole**. When it swallows a lot of gas and dust, its surroundings shine more brightly than the whole galaxy. This is then called an **active galactic nucleus**, AGN for short.
wichtigste: An active galactic nucleus is powered by a supermassive black hole.
Falling matter forms a hot, glowing disc around the black hole.
Seyfert galaxies, quasars, blazars and radio galaxies are different types.
The unified model says that many types differ mainly in the angle from which we see them.
Some nuclei hurl out jets of particles at almost the speed of light.
Active nuclei can slow down the formation of stars in their galaxy.

abschnitte.text: A **supermassive black hole** can be millions to billions of times heavier than the sun. When gas falls towards it, it first circles in a flat **accretion disc**. As it does so, it rubs against itself, becomes extremely hot and shines very brightly. But there is an upper limit: at the **Eddington luminosity** the radiation pushes outwards so strongly that it holds back the falling matter.

Astronomers have found various kinds of active nuclei. A **Seyfert galaxy** is usually a spiral galaxy with a bright, active nucleus. **Quasars** are particularly luminous nuclei, often very far away. **Radio galaxies** have huge **radio lobes**, which are fed by jets from the nucleus. In a **blazar** a jet points almost exactly at the Earth, which is why it looks particularly bright and changes quickly.

The **unified model** explains why the nuclei look so different. According to it, many of them have a similar structure, and we only see them from different **angles**. Around the inner region lies a thick ring of dust, the **dust torus**, rather like a doughnut. If we look from the side, it hides the bright interior. If we look from above, we see straight in.

Some active nuclei hurl out two focused beams of particles at almost the **speed of light**, called **jets**. They can reach far beyond the galaxy. The radiation and the jets heat up the gas in the galaxy or blow it away. Then fewer new stars can form. This effect is called **AGN feedback**.

gewusst: At the centre of our Milky Way there is also a black hole, Sagittarius A*. But at the moment it is fairly quiet.
The brightest quasars shine more brightly than hundreds of ordinary galaxies together.

teile.einleitung: Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy that drives the universe apart faster and faster. So far nobody knows exactly what it is. Even so, according to current knowledge it makes up about 68 per cent of the total energy content of the universe.
wichtigste: Dark energy causes the universe to expand faster and faster.
It makes up about 68 per cent of the energy density of the universe.
The accelerating expansion was discovered in 1998 through observations of distant supernovae.
Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
The simplest explanation is Einstein's cosmological constant of 1917.
The ESA space telescope Euclid has been studying dark energy since 2023.
What dark energy really is remains one of the greatest puzzles in physics.

abschnitte.text: Since Edwin Hubble, we have known that the universe is expanding. For a long time people believed that gravity must slow this **expansion** down. But the measurements show the opposite: the expansion is getting faster. The unknown cause of this is called **dark energy**, because it can be neither seen nor measured directly.

Two research teams observed distant exploding stars, so-called **type Ia supernovae**. These always shine with about the same brightness and are therefore suited as cosmic measuring sticks. The supernovae were fainter than expected, so further away than they should have been in a universe that is slowing down. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

In 1917, Albert Einstein introduced the **cosmological constant** Λ (lambda) into his field equations. He wanted to use it to describe an unchanging universe, but later rejected the idea. Today it is the simplest explanation for dark energy: an energy that is contained in empty space itself. For it, the equation-of-state parameter w, that is, pressure divided by energy density, has the value minus 1.

Physicists have tried to calculate the energy of empty space, the **vacuum energy**, from quantum physics. The result is greater than the measured value by an unimaginable number of powers of ten. This huge discrepancy is called the **vacuum catastrophe**. Other theories suspect that dark energy changes over time, and more recent measurements give first hints of this.

The expansion has been accelerating for about 5 to 6 billion years; before that, the gravity of matter slowed it down. The ESA space telescope **Euclid** launched in 2023 and is mapping billions of galaxies in order to study dark energy and dark matter. Swiss universities such as the University of Geneva and ETH Zurich also work on Euclid. Together with dark matter, they make up about 95 per cent of the universe; only about 5 per cent is ordinary matter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stretching out of the universe.
The enormous explosion of a star, which shines very brightly.
A number in Einstein's equations that describes an energy of empty space.
Energy that is supposed to be present even in completely empty space.

gewusst: Einstein is said to have later called the cosmological constant his greatest blunder; today it is very much back in the spotlight.
The more the universe expands, the more dark energy there is in total, because every new bit of space brings it along.
Everything we can see, that is, stars, planets and gas, makes up only about 5 per cent of the universe.

teile.einleitung: Is there life anywhere in the universe? **Astrobiology** deals with this big question. It combines astronomy, biology, chemistry and geology and also studies how life on the Earth began.
wichtigste: Astrobiology studies the origin, development and spread of life in the universe.
Extremophiles are living things that thrive in extreme conditions.
In 2007 water bears survived several days unprotected in space.
The Miller-Urey experiment showed that amino acids can form from simple gases.
Oxygen and methane together in an atmosphere are considered a strong biosignature.
NASA's drone Dragonfly is meant to land on Saturn's moon Titan.

abschnitte.text: An important part of astrobiology is the question of how life on the Earth began. In **1953** Stanley Miller and Harold Urey carried out a famous experiment. They filled a glass flask with simple gases like those that may have existed on the young Earth and sent electric sparks through it. This produced **amino acids**, which are important building blocks of life. The **Miller-Urey experiment** showed that building blocks of life can form from simple substances and energy.

On the Earth there are living things that live in astonishing places: in boiling hot springs, in very acidic water or deep in the ice. They are called **extremophiles**, meaning “lovers of the extreme”. The tiny **water bears** are particularly tough. In **2007**, in an experiment on a satellite, they survived **several days unprotected in space**. Such findings show that life might also be possible in harsh places in space.

Researchers are looking on **Mars** for traces of past life. Moons with water under the ice, such as Europa and Enceladus, are also exciting. On Saturn's moon **Titan** there are lakes of liquid **methane**. NASA's drone **Dragonfly** is meant to land there and fly around. In **1996** researchers claimed to have found possible traces of **microfossils** in the Martian meteorite **ALH84001**. But today most experts do not consider these traces to be proof.

You cannot fly to planets around other stars. But you can study their light and work out from it which gases are in their atmosphere. Some gases can be signs of life, and they are called **biosignatures**. If **oxygen and methane are found together**, this would be a strong sign, because the two gases destroy each other and would have to be constantly renewed. Another idea is **panspermia**: life or its seeds could travel through space from planet to planet.

gewusst: So far life has not been found for certain anywhere outside the Earth.
Water bears are usually smaller than a millimetre and can dry out almost completely and later come back to life.

teile.einleitung: Organelles are the small parts inside a cell. Like organs in the body, each organelle has its own task.
wichtigste: **Organelles** are parts of the cell with their own tasks.
Membranes divide the cell into **compartments**.
**Chloroplasts** are found in plant cells, not in animal cells.
The **nuclear envelope** separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm.
**Peroxisomes** break down hydrogen peroxide with catalase.
Bacteria have **no nucleus** with a nuclear envelope.
**Plasmodesmata** connect neighbouring plant cells.

abschnitte.text: Eukaryotic cells are divided by membranes into many **compartments**, that is separate reaction spaces. This allows opposite processes such as the **building up** and **breaking down** of substances to take place at the same time without disturbing each other. The **nucleus** is surrounded by the **nuclear envelope** made of two membranes. Nuclear pores allow exchange with the cytoplasm. Bacteria lack such a nucleus, and their DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm.

The **mitochondria** obtain energy from nutrients and are often called the power stations of the cell. Proteins are built at the **ribosomes**. The **endoplasmic reticulum** and the **Golgi apparatus** process and package substances. **Lysosomes** break down waste. The small **peroxisomes** break down long-chain fatty acids and split poisonous **hydrogen peroxide** into water and oxygen with the enzyme **catalase**.

Plant cells have **plastids**, which animal cells lack. **Chloroplasts** contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. **Chromoplasts** contain pigments such as lycopene or beta-carotene. They colour ripe tomatoes red and carrots orange. **Amyloplasts** are colourless and store starch, for example in potato tubers.

Many plant cells have a large **central vacuole** with cell sap. It is surrounded by a membrane, the **tonoplast**. This controls the exchange of substances with the cytoplasm. Neighbouring plant cells are connected by fine channels in the cell wall, the **plasmodesmata**. Through them the cytoplasm of the cells is linked.

gewusst: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small DNA. It is thought that a very long time ago they were free-living bacteria.
A liver cell can contain over a thousand mitochondria.

teile.einleitung: A brown dwarf is an object between a planet and a star. It is too heavy to be a planet, but too light to fuse hydrogen for good like a true star.
wichtigste: Brown dwarfs lie in mass between large planets and small stars.
From about 75 Jupiter masses, an object starts burning hydrogen permanently and becomes a star.
Above about 13 Jupiter masses, brown dwarfs can fuse deuterium for a while.
They are hardly bigger than Jupiter and keep cooling down.
The term was coined by Jill Tarter in 1975.
The nearest known brown dwarfs form the Luhman 16 system.

abschnitte.text: A star shines because **hydrogen** fuses into helium in its core. This needs great heat and a lot of pressure. Below about 0.075 solar masses, which is roughly **75 to 80 Jupiter masses**, the core never gets hot enough. Such objects are called **brown dwarfs**. From about 13 Jupiter masses, however, they can fuse **deuterium** for a while. This is a heavy form of hydrogen that fuses at lower temperatures. But the supply is small and is soon used up.

Brown dwarfs have no lasting source of energy. They give off the heat that was released when they formed and **steadily cool down**. That is why they shine only faintly, mainly in infrared light. Although they can have up to about 80 times the mass of Jupiter, they are hardly bigger than it. The reason is the **degeneracy pressure** of the electrons: the particles cannot be squeezed together as tightly as you like.

The astronomer **Shiv Kumar** predicted such objects as early as 1962. The name “brown dwarf” was suggested by **Jill Tarter** in her doctoral thesis in 1975. For a long time none could be found. In 1995 **Gliese 229B** was detected as a companion of a red dwarf. Its light clearly showed **methane**, a gas that survives only at low temperatures. This made it clear that the object is much cooler than any star.

Young brown dwarfs look similar to small red dwarf stars. One clue is the element **lithium**. True stars destroy lithium quickly in their hot interiors. Brown dwarfs with a low mass never get hot enough for that, so lithium can still be found in their light. This check is called the **lithium test**.

The nearest known brown dwarfs form the **Luhman 16** system. It is a pair of two brown dwarfs that orbit each other. It lies about **6.5 light years** away. It was discovered in 2013 with data from the infrared satellite **WISE**. Because brown dwarfs shine so faintly, researchers suspect that there are still many undiscovered ones.

gewusst: To our eyes, a brown dwarf does not shine brown but rather dark red.
The coolest known brown dwarfs are colder than boiling water.

teile.einleitung: ClearSpace is a Swiss company from Lausanne that wants to collect space debris. Its satellite ClearSpace-1 is meant to remove a defunct object from orbit on behalf of ESA.
wichtigste: ClearSpace was founded in 2018 as a spin-off of EPFL in Lausanne.
The company wants to remove space debris from orbit.
In 2020, ESA ordered the mission ClearSpace-1.
The satellite is meant to catch an object with four grabbing arms.
Afterwards, both are meant to burn up in the atmosphere.
Since 2024, the old ESA satellite PROBA-1 has been the target.

abschnitte.text: Many defunct satellites, rocket parts and fragments orbit Earth. They are called **space debris**. They are very fast and can damage working satellites. If two pieces collide, even more fragments are created. That is why experts are looking for ways to clean up the orbits.

**ClearSpace** was founded in **2018** as a **spin-off** of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (**EPFL**). A spin-off is a company that grows out of a university. Its aim: to build satellites that catch defunct objects in space and dispose of them. In **2020**, the European Space Agency **ESA** ordered the mission **ClearSpace-1** for about 86 million euros. It is meant to be the first mission of its kind.

ClearSpace-1 has **four grabbing arms** that work like a claw. The satellite approaches the piece of debris, wraps around it and holds it tight. At the end it steers the pair into the **atmosphere**, where **both burn up**. This is difficult, because a dead satellite does not help: it **sends no signal** and may be **tumbling**. The catcher therefore has to navigate very precisely using cameras and sensors.

The first target was a rocket adapter called **Vespa**. In 2023, however, it was probably hit by other fragments and broke into several pieces. So in **2024**, ClearSpace-1 was given a new target: **PROBA-1**, a small ESA satellite that was launched in **2001**. The incident with Vespa shows how big the problem of space debris already is.

gewusst: Space debris often flies at several kilometres per second, faster than a bullet.
Even small fragments can punch holes in satellites.

teile.einleitung: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It was discovered as a planet, then counted as an asteroid, and since 2006 it has been classed as a dwarf planet.
wichtigste: Ceres has a diameter of about 940 km.
It contains about 25 to 40 per cent of the mass of the whole asteroid belt.
Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it in Palermo on New Year's night 1801.
One turn on its own axis takes only about 9 hours.
Ahuna Mons is an ice volcano, and the bright spots in the crater Occator are salt.
It is named after the Roman goddess of agriculture.

abschnitte.text: The Italian priest and astronomer **Giuseppe Piazzi** observed Ceres on New Year's night 1801 at the **Palermo Observatory**. At first he took it for a comet. Then it was counted as a new **planet**. When more and more similar bodies were found between Mars and Jupiter, Ceres was long regarded as an **asteroid**. Since 2006 it has counted as one of the **dwarf planets**, like Pluto.

Ceres measures about **940 km** across. For comparison: Earth is about 12,700 km across, and Switzerland is about 350 km wide from west to east. Ceres is by far the **most massive body** between Mars and Jupiter. Depending on the estimate, it makes up about **25 to 40 per cent** of the mass of the whole asteroid belt. It is heavy enough that its own gravity has made it almost **perfectly round**.

Ceres turns once on its own axis in about **9 hours**. A day on Ceres is therefore much shorter than a day on Earth. For one trip around the Sun, however, it needs several years, because it is much further from the Sun than Earth is.

The NASA probe **Dawn** studied Ceres up close from 2015. It discovered **Ahuna Mons**, a single mountain about 4 km high. It is an **ice volcano**: it probably formed when salty ice and mud rose up from the interior. In the crater **Occator**, bright spots shine. They consist mainly of **salts** such as sodium carbonate. These probably come from salty water from the interior that evaporated at the surface.

In Roman myth, Ceres was the **goddess of agriculture** and grain. The English word **“cereal”** for breakfast flakes comes from her name. The chemical element **cerium** was also named after the object shortly after its discovery.

gewusst: Ceres was the first body in the asteroid belt ever to be discovered.
Dawn was the first space probe to orbit two different bodies one after the other: first the asteroid Vesta, then Ceres.

teile.einleitung: The fibula is the thin bone on the outer side of the lower leg. It carries little weight, but it is very important for the ankle joint and many muscles.
wichtigste: The fibula lies on the outside next to the thicker shinbone.
Its Latin name is fibula, which means clasp or brooch pin.
The fibula is not part of the knee joint, and its head lies below the knee.
At the bottom it forms the outer ankle bone and stabilises the ankle joint.
Many muscles of the lower leg are attached to the fibula.
Because it carries little weight, a piece of it can be used as a replacement bone.

abschnitte.text: The lower leg has two long bones: the strong **shinbone** on the inside and the slender **fibula** on the outside. The two lie almost parallel next to each other. At the top, the **head of the fibula** is joined to the shinbone at the side below the knee. However, the fibula does not take part in the knee joint itself. At the bottom it ends in the **outer ankle bone**, which you can easily feel at the foot.

The Latin name of this bone is **fibula**. In ancient times a fibula was a pin or clasp used to hold clothes together. The shinbone and fibula together recall such a clasp. That is why the nerve of the fibula is also called the **fibular nerve** in medical language. Many parts of the body still have Latin names today.

The fibula carries only a little body weight, and the shinbone takes most of it. Even so, it is important. With the outer ankle bone, together with the shinbone, it grips the **talus** like a fork. This keeps the upper **ankle joint** stable at the sides. The fibula also serves as an attachment area for many muscles, for example the **fibular muscles**, which lift the outer edge of the foot.

A fracture of the outer ankle bone is a common sports injury. Doctors classify such fractures after the Swiss surgeon **Bernhard Georg Weber**: Weber A, B and C, depending on the height at which the bone breaks. At the head of the fibula the **fibular nerve** runs just under the skin. If it is squashed there, you can no longer lift your foot properly. Because the fibula carries little weight, surgeons sometimes remove a piece of it, for example to rebuild a jawbone.

gewusst: You can usually walk well with a piece of fibula missing, because the shinbone carries the load.
The Weber classification of outer ankle fractures comes from a Swiss doctor and is used worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Asteroids are small bodies of rock and metal that orbit the sun. Most of them are in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Some are as small as a house, others hundreds of kilometres across.
wichtigste: Asteroids consist mainly of rock and metal.
Most asteroids orbit in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
The largest object in the asteroid belt is Ceres, which is now considered a dwarf planet.
Around 66 million years ago an asteroid impact caused most of the dinosaurs to die out.
In 2022 the NASA mission DART deflected an asteroid by crashing into it.
In 2023 the probe OSIRIS-REx brought rock samples from the asteroid Bennu to the Earth.
Astronomers watch near-Earth asteroids to spot possible dangers early.

abschnitte.text: Asteroids are leftovers from the time when the solar system formed around 4.6 billion years ago. They are also called **minor planets**. They are usually irregularly shaped like potatoes, because their gravity is too weak to make them round. So far over a million asteroids are known (as of about 2024).

The **asteroid belt** lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. The gravity of giant Jupiter prevented a planet from forming there. The largest object is **Ceres**, almost 1,000 kilometres across, which has been considered a dwarf planet since 2006. Other well-known asteroids are Vesta and Pallas, and despite the many chunks the belt is so empty that space probes fly through it without any problem.

Sometimes asteroids cross the Earth's orbit. Around 66 million years ago an asteroid about 10 kilometres across struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. The **Chicxulub crater** still bears witness to this today, and the effects led to most of the dinosaurs dying out. Small pieces that fall to the Earth are called **meteorites**.

Many space probes have visited asteroids. In 2020 the Japanese probe Hayabusa2 brought samples from the asteroid Ryugu to the Earth. In 2023 the NASA probe **OSIRIS-REx** delivered rock from the asteroid Bennu. In 2022 the mission **DART** successfully tested whether an asteroid can be deflected by a probe crashing into it on purpose.

Telescopes all over the world search the sky for **near-Earth asteroids**. Their orbits are calculated precisely so that possible collisions can be spotted decades in advance. At present no large asteroid is known that will hit the Earth in the next hundred years. With the Hera mission, the European Space Agency ESA, of which Switzerland is also a member, is sending a probe to the asteroid that DART hit.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ring of many asteroids between Mars and Jupiter.
A round body that is smaller than a planet and has not cleared its orbit.
A piece of rock from space that lands on the Earth.
An asteroid whose orbit comes close to the Earth's orbit.

gewusst: All the asteroids in the asteroid belt together have less mass than our moon.
Some asteroids have their own small moons.
International Asteroid Day is celebrated every year on 30 June.

teile.einleitung: During the change of teeth the milk teeth fall out one by one and the permanent teeth grow in. In most children this begins at about the age of 6.
wichtigste: A child's first teeth are called **milk teeth**.
A child has 20 milk teeth.
The change of teeth usually begins at about **6 years** of age.
A loose milk tooth is called a **wobbly tooth**.
The permanent tooth underneath pushes the milk tooth out.
At about the age of 6 the first large molars grow at the back, the **six-year molars**.
In many stories the **tooth fairy** collects the milk tooth.

abschnitte.text: Babies usually get their first teeth in their first year of life. By about their third birthday all **20 milk teeth** are there. They are smaller and whiter than the later teeth. Although they fall out again, they are important: they keep the **space** free for the permanent teeth. Diseased milk teeth can also harm the new teeth, so you brush them well.

Under each milk tooth the **permanent tooth** is already growing. It pushes upwards. As it does, the body gradually breaks down the root of the milk tooth. The milk tooth becomes loose and wobbles, and it is called a **wobbly tooth**. Finally it falls out and the new tooth appears.

The change of teeth takes several years. During this time milk teeth and permanent teeth are in the mouth at the same time. This set of teeth is called the **mixed dentition**. Usually the lower front teeth fall out first. In some children the change begins a little earlier, in others later. This is completely normal.

abschnitte.titel: New teeth at the very back
abschnitte.text: At about the age of 6 the first **large molars** grow behind the milk teeth. No milk tooth falls out for them. Because they come at this age, they are also called **six-year molars**. Many people do not even notice them, so you should not forget them when brushing. A complete set of permanent teeth has 32 teeth, including the wisdom teeth.

In many families the milk tooth that has fallen out is put under the pillow. During the night the **tooth fairy** collects it and brings a little surprise. In other countries there are other customs, for example a mouse that fetches the tooth.

gewusst: Permanent teeth grow only once. They have to last a whole lifetime.
In Spain and Latin America it is often a little mouse that collects the milk teeth in the stories.

teile.einleitung: Our body consists of many different types of cell, such as nerve cells, muscle cells or blood cells. The way little-specialised cells turn into such specialists is called cell differentiation.
wichtigste: **Cell differentiation** is the specialisation of a cell for a particular task.
Almost all body cells carry the same genetic material.
Depending on the cell type, **different genes are active**.
**Transcription factors** switch genes on or off.
**DNA methylation** can switch genes off permanently.
**Pluripotent** cells can form almost any type of cell.
Shinya Yamanaka received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2012 with John Gurdon.

abschnitte.text: A liver cell and a nerve cell from the same person look completely different. Even so, they basically carry the same **DNA**. The difference lies in which **genes are active**. Each cell switches on only the genes it needs for its task. This produces a particular type of cell with its own shape and function.

**Transcription factors** are proteins that bind to control sections of the DNA. They decide which genes are read. Certain combinations determine which type of cell develops. In addition there are **epigenetic marks**. One example is **DNA methylation**: small methyl groups on the DNA prevent genes from being read. Such marks are passed on to the daughter cells when the cell divides.

**Stem cells** are little-specialised cells that can divide and turn into other types of cell. **Pluripotent** cells can form cells of all the major tissue types. **Multipotent** cells are limited to a few types of cell. One example is the blood stem cells in the **bone marrow**: red and white blood cells and platelets develop from them.

In 1957 the British biologist **Conrad Waddington** described a well-known image, the **epigenetic landscape**. A ball rolls down a slope with branching valleys. At the start it can still go in many directions. The further down it is, the more fixed its path is, that is the type of cell. Specialised cells do not normally roll back up.

In 2006 the Japanese researcher **Shinya Yamanaka** showed that a few genes are enough to put skin cells back into a stem-cell-like state. These cells are called **induced pluripotent stem cells**. For reprogramming specialised cells, he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2012 together with **John Gurdon**. Researchers hope one day to use this to replace diseased tissue.

gewusst: A human being has more than 200 different types of cell, although almost all carry the same genetic material.
Yamanaka's method needed only four genes to reprogramme a skin cell.

teile.einleitung: Toothpaste, also called tooth cream in German, is part of brushing your teeth every day. It helps to remove plaque and protects the teeth from tooth decay with fluoride.
wichtigste: In German, “Zahnpasta” and “Zahncreme” mean the same thing.
The most important protective substance in toothpaste is **fluoride**.
Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and protects it from acid.
For schoolchildren a pea-sized amount is enough.
Children's toothpaste contains less fluoride, because small children often swallow some.
After brushing you spit out the foam and rinse only a little.

abschnitte.text: Toothpaste is made of several ingredients. Very fine **cleaning particles** help to rub plaque off the teeth. **Fluoride** strengthens tooth enamel. There is also water, substances that keep the paste moist and smooth, and foaming agents. Flavours such as peppermint give a fresh taste.

Bacteria in plaque make acid from sugar. This acid attacks **tooth enamel**, and **tooth decay** can develop, in other words a hole in the tooth. Fluoride makes enamel harder and more resistant to acid. It also helps to repair small damage on the surface. That is why dentists recommend toothpaste with fluoride.

A lot of toothpaste does not clean better. For schoolchildren a **pea-sized amount** on the toothbrush is enough. For small children there is special **children's toothpaste** with less fluoride, because they often swallow some while brushing. Older children and adults use toothpaste with more fluoride. The important thing is to brush thoroughly twice a day.

Toothpaste is for cleaning, not for eating. After brushing you spit out the foam. Many experts advise rinsing only a little with water afterwards, or not at all. This way more fluoride stays on the teeth and can work for longer.

Toothpaste usually comes in a soft **tube**. When you squeeze it, the paste comes out at the front. In the past people often cleaned their teeth with tooth powder. Paste in a tube only really caught on in the 20th century.

gewusst: In Switzerland, table salt with fluoride has been on sale for many decades. This gives the teeth extra protection.
Toothpaste without cleaning particles would remove plaque much less well. But the particles are so fine that you can hardly feel them.

teile.einleitung: On 28 January 1986, the American space shuttle Challenger broke apart shortly after launch. All seven people on board were killed. The accident changed space travel and its safety rules.
wichtigste: Challenger broke apart on 28 January 1986, about 73 seconds after launch in Florida.
There were seven crew members on board, and nobody survived.
On board was the teacher Christa McAuliffe.
The cause was a sealing ring on one of the solid rocket boosters at the side.
The great cold on the day of the launch made the rubber seals hard.
It was not until September 1988 that a space shuttle flew into space again.

abschnitte.text: On **28 January 1986**, the space shuttle **Challenger** launched in Florida. About **73 seconds** after lift-off it broke apart in the air. On board were **seven crew members**, and none of them survived. Because many schools were following the launch live, millions of people saw the accident on television. It was one of the worst setbacks in the history of space travel.

On board was **Christa McAuliffe**, a teacher from the USA. She had been chosen for the **“Teacher in Space”** programme. From space she wanted to teach lessons to school classes and show children how space travel works. That is why especially many children were watching that day.

The space shuttle had two **solid rocket boosters** at its sides. Their sections were joined with rubber seals called **O-rings**. On one of the boosters, such a ring no longer sealed properly. Hot gases escaped and damaged the large **external tank** holding the fuel. This caused the shuttle to break apart. The weather played an important part: the night before the launch it was **unusually cold** in Florida, and the rubber seals became hard.

A commission investigated the accident. One of its members was the famous physicist **Richard Feynman**. He showed the cause with a simple experiment: he put a piece of sealing rubber into a glass of **ice water**. Afterwards it lost its elasticity and no longer sprang back. That way everyone could see why the seal had failed in the cold. The commission also criticised the fact that warnings from engineers had not been taken seriously enough.

After the accident, no American space shuttle flew into space for about **two and a half years**. During this time the solid rocket boosters were redesigned and the safety procedures were improved. It was not until **September 1988** that a space shuttle, **Discovery**, launched again. The accident showed how important it is to speak openly about safety concerns.

gewusst: Many schools, streets and even craters on the Moon now carry the names of the Challenger crew.
Before the accident, Challenger had already been into space successfully nine times.

teile.einleitung: Many stars do not travel alone, but have one or more companions. Two stars that are joined by gravity and orbit each other are called a binary star.
wichtigste: In a true binary star, two stars orbit a common centre of mass.
An optical double star only happens to lie in almost the same direction.
Mizar and Alcor in the Plough were regarded as an eyesight test.
Albireo in Cygnus shows an orange and a blue star in a telescope.
Algol regularly becomes dimmer because a companion passes in front of it.
Some binary stars give themselves away only through their light spectrum.

abschnitte.text: In a **true binary star**, two stars are joined by **gravity**. They orbit a **common centre of mass**. Besides these there are **optical double stars**: two stars that, seen from Earth, only happen to lie in almost the same direction. In reality they are far apart and have nothing to do with each other. There are also systems of three or more stars. They are called **multiple systems**, and with three stars a **triple system**.

In the **Plough**, the bright star **Mizar** stands in the middle of the handle. Right next to it shines the fainter little star **Alcor**. Anyone who can see the two separately has good eyes. That is why the pair used to be called the **eyesight test**. With a telescope it turns out that Mizar itself also consists of several stars.

A popular target for small telescopes is **Albireo** in the constellation **Cygnus** (the Swan). A golden-orange and a blue star stand close together. The colour reveals the temperature: blue stars are hotter, orange ones cooler. In summer, Cygnus is also high in the sky over Switzerland.

The star **Algol** in the constellation **Perseus** becomes dimmer for a few hours about every **3 days**. The reason: its two stars orbit each other in such a way that the darker one regularly passes in front of the brighter one. Such stars are called **eclipsing variables**. Other pairs are so close together that even the best telescope shows only one point. They give themselves away through their **light spectrum**: the lines shift regularly back and forth, because the stars move around each other.

Planets can also orbit binary stars. The space telescope **Kepler** discovered the planet **Kepler-16b** in 2011, which orbits a pair of two stars. Kepler looked for planets that pass in front of their star and briefly dim it. So a sky with two suns is not just imagination from films.

gewusst: A large share of the stars in the Milky Way belong to binary or multiple systems.
The name Algol comes from Arabic and means roughly “head of the demon”.

teile.einleitung: A bandage protects a wound from dirt and germs, stops bleeding or supports an injured part of the body. With a little practice you can put on a simple bandage yourself in first aid.
wichtigste: A clean, sterile dressing goes straight onto the wound first.
Over it you wrap a bandage of soft cloth.
A bandage should sit firmly but must not be too tight.
If the fingers turn blue or cold or tingle, the bandage is too tight.
For heavy bleeding a pressure bandage helps, and at the same time you call the emergency number 144.
With a triangular bandage you can tie up an injured arm.
Disposable gloves protect helpers and the injured from germs.

abschnitte.text: A bandage usually has two parts. Straight onto the wound you lay a **sterile dressing**, that is, a germ-free piece of cloth. Over it you wrap a **bandage** that holds everything in place. Bandages are made of soft cloth such as **gauze** or of stretchy fabric. For small wounds a plaster is often enough, which already combines both.

Before bandaging you put on **disposable gloves**. They protect against blood and germs. You wrap the bandage evenly, so that the layers overlap a little. The bandage should sit **firmly but not too tight**. If it is too loose, it slips off, and if it is too tight, it cuts off the blood. If fingers or toes turn blue or cold or tingle, you have to loosen the bandage.

If a wound bleeds heavily, for example on the leg, a **pressure bandage** helps. You lay on a dressing and wrap a few layers of bandage over it. Then you place a firm pad, such as a bandage that is still in its packaging, on the wound and keep wrapping. This way the bandage presses on the wound and slows the bleeding. At the same time someone calls the **emergency number 144**.

The **triangular bandage** is a large cloth in the shape of a triangle. With it you can make an **arm sling** and tie up an injured arm. This way the arm stays still and hurts less. You can also fold the cloth up and use it as a bandage or pad. There should be one in every first aid kit.

In Switzerland you often find a **first aid kit** in the car, at school and in gyms. It contains plasters, bandages, dressings, gloves, scissors and a triangular bandage. It is worth checking the contents now and then and replacing what has been used. Anyone who wants to get a driving licence in Switzerland has to attend an **emergency aid course**. There you also practise bandaging.

gewusst: A bandage is not only for wounds: an elastic bandage can also support a sprained joint.
In many communities in Switzerland, Samaritan associations offer courses in which you practise first aid.

teile.einleitung: The **Andromeda Galaxy** is the nearest large neighbouring galaxy to our Milky Way. It is around **2.5 million light years** away and yet can be seen with the naked eye as a small, blurry patch. This makes it one of the most distant things you can see without a telescope.
wichtigste: The Andromeda Galaxy is a large spiral galaxy, similar to the Milky Way.
It is around 2.5 million light years away from us.
In Switzerland it is best seen in the evening sky in autumn.
In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that it lies outside the Milky Way.
According to estimates it contains around a trillion stars.
It is moving towards the Milky Way.

abschnitte.text: As early as the **10th century** the Persian astronomer **Al-Sufi** described the Andromeda Galaxy as a “small cloud”. In Switzerland it can be seen well in the evening in **autumn**, best of all far from city lights. With the naked eye you see only the bright core. But on long-exposure photos it appears as big as **several full moons** side by side. In Charles Messier's catalogue it has the number **M31**.

For a long time astronomers argued about whether this “nebula” belonged to the Milky Way. In the 1920s **Edwin Hubble** found special stars in the Andromeda Galaxy, the **Cepheids**. Their brightness changes in a particular rhythm, and from this their distance can be calculated. In this way Hubble showed that Andromeda lies far **outside the Milky Way**. This was a big step: the universe is much larger than people had thought.

The Andromeda Galaxy is the largest galaxy in our neighbourhood, the **Local Group**. According to estimates it contains around **a trillion stars**, that is a thousand billion. Like the Milky Way, it has spiral arms. It is orbited by several small **satellite galaxies**. Two bright ones are **M32** and **M110**.

The Andromeda Galaxy is **coming closer to us** at about **110 kilometres per second**. If it always stayed at the same speed, it would need around **7 billion years** for the 2.5 million light years. But because gravity pulls the two galaxies together more and more strongly, it could happen faster. Experts expect that in a few billion years they could collide or pass close by each other. The stars themselves would hardly crash into each other, because the distances between them are huge.

gewusst: The light we see from the Andromeda Galaxy today has been travelling for around 2.5 million years.
In the sky the Andromeda Galaxy is much bigger than the full moon, but it is so faint that you do not notice this with the naked eye.

teile.einleitung: Wisdom teeth are the back molars. They are the last teeth to appear and often cause problems because there is too little room in the jaw.
wichtigste: The wisdom tooth is the third large molar.
A complete set of teeth has four wisdom teeth.
They often come through between about 16 and 25 years of age.
In the dental numbering system it has the number 8, which is why it is also called the eight.
Many people are missing some or all of their wisdom teeth.
If there is too little room, they often have to be removed.

abschnitte.titel: The tooth at the very back
abschnitte.text: The **wisdom tooth** is the tooth at the very back of each row of teeth. Experts call it the **third molar**, that is the third large back tooth. A complete set of permanent teeth has **32 teeth**. In each of the four quarters of the jaw, a wisdom tooth sits at the back. So altogether there are **four**.

Dentists count the teeth in each **quarter of the jaw** from the middle outwards from 1 to 8. The front teeth have the numbers 1 and 2. The wisdom tooth is the **eighth** and last. That is why it is also simply called the **eight**. This way every professional knows at once which tooth is meant.

Wisdom teeth are the last teeth to come through, usually in the late teenage years or as a young adult. This often happens between about **16 and 25 years** of age. Because you are already older then and supposedly wiser, it was called the **wisdom tooth**. But it has nothing to do with cleverness. In some people the wisdom teeth never come through, and in others they are **not formed** at all. This is harmless.

abschnitte.titel: When there is not enough room
abschnitte.text: Often there is too little room in the **jaw**. Then the wisdom tooth tilts and stays completely or partly stuck in the bone. This is called an **impacted** or **retained** tooth. It can press on the neighbouring teeth or become inflamed. Then it is often removed, usually under a local anaesthetic.

gewusst: An X-ray often shows wisdom teeth years before they come through.
The large molars have no milk teeth before them, and they grow straight in as permanent teeth.

teile.einleitung: Astronauts have to eat and drink in space too. But in weightlessness everything that is not held down floats around. That is why **space food** is specially packed and prepared.
wichtigste: Astronauts' food is often packed in pouches and tins.
Dried food has water added before it is eaten.
Instead of bread astronauts often eat tortillas, because they make hardly any crumbs.
Salt comes dissolved in liquid.
Drinks are taken from a pouch with a straw.
Fresh fruit comes to the space station on supply flights.

abschnitte.text: On the **International Space Station** there is no kitchen with a cooker and fridge like at home. The food is mostly packed in **pouches** and **tins** so that it keeps for a long time and does not float around. Many dishes are **dried**. Before eating them, you add **water**. There is a **small heating device** for warming food up. The astronauts can choose from many different dishes.

On the Earth crumbs simply fall to the floor. But in weightlessness they **float** through the space station. They can fly into people's **eyes** or get into **equipment** and damage it. That is why astronauts often eat **tortillas** instead of bread, thin, soft flatbreads that make hardly any crumbs. For the same reason there is **salt dissolved in liquid** and pepper in oil. Sprinkling would not work.

You cannot use a glass of water in weightlessness. The water would float out of the glass as a ball. That is why astronauts drink from a closed **pouch with a straw**. A large part of the water on board is treated and reused, for example from the moisture in the air.

To many astronauts the food in space tastes **less strong** than on the Earth. In weightlessness more fluid rises into the head, and the nose feels blocked, a bit like with a cold. That is why many like spicy food. **Fresh fruit** is particularly popular. It comes to the space station on a **supply flight** and has to be eaten quickly, because it does not keep for long.

gewusst: Astronauts often fix their food pouches with Velcro or clips so that they do not float away.
Lettuce has even been grown and eaten on the space station.

teile.einleitung: Claudius Ptolemy was a scholar of antiquity who lived in Alexandria in Egypt. His picture of the universe with Earth at the centre shaped thinking in Europe and the Arab world for about 1,400 years.
wichtigste: Ptolemy lived from about 100 to 170 AD in Alexandria.
His main astronomical work is known as the “Almagest”.
The name “Almagest” comes from Arabic.
He explained the loops of the planets with small circles on large circles.
His star catalogue describes 48 constellations.
In the “Geographike” he collected the coordinates of about 8,000 places.

abschnitte.text: Claudius Ptolemy lived in the **2nd century AD**, from about 100 to 170. He worked in **Alexandria** in Egypt, one of the great centres of knowledge of antiquity. At that time Egypt belonged to the Roman Empire, but scholars mostly wrote in Greek. Ptolemy worked on astronomy, mathematics, geography and music.

His main astronomical work was actually called **“Mathematike Syntaxis”**. It became known under the name **Almagest**. The work reached Europe through **Arabic translations**. The name goes back to the Arabic “Al-Majisti”, which means roughly “the greatest”. The Almagest also contains a **star catalogue** with a good 1,000 stars in **48 constellations**. Many of them are still among the 88 official constellations today.

Ptolemy imagined that **Earth stands at the centre** and that the Sun, Moon and planets circle around it. One problem was the **looping movements** of the planets: sometimes they seem to run backwards across the sky. Ptolemy explained this with **small circles on large circles**. Each planet moved on a small circle, the **epicycle**, whose centre travelled along a large circle around Earth. This let him predict the positions of the planets surprisingly well.

In **geography**, too, Ptolemy wrote a famous work, the **“Geographike”**. In it he collected the coordinates of about **8,000 places**. With this information, maps of the then known world could be drawn. The work shaped mapmaking right into modern times.

abschnitte.titel: A world view with a long influence
abschnitte.text: The **Ptolemaic world view** was regarded as the authority for about **1,400 years**. It was only in the 16th and 17th centuries that the idea won through that Earth orbits the Sun. **Nicolaus Copernicus** and **Johannes Kepler** contributed most to this. Even though his world view was wrong, Ptolemy is regarded as one of the most important scientists of antiquity.

gewusst: Almost nothing is known about the life of Ptolemy, only his works survive.
A crater on the Moon and a crater on Mars carry his name.

teile.einleitung: Astronauts are people who fly into space in a spacecraft. They do research in space stations, repair satellites and have even walked on the moon. The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
wichtigste: The first person in space was the Russian Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
The first woman in space was Valentina Tereshkova in 1963.
The first Swiss person in space was Claude Nicollier.
Outside in space a spacesuit protects the astronauts.
In the space station astronauts float because they are weightless.
In 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to walk on the moon.
Training to become an astronaut takes several years and is very demanding.

abschnitte.text: The word astronaut means roughly star sailor. In Russia people say **cosmonaut**, and in China taikonaut. Astronauts fly into space on rockets and often work there for months. Today they usually live on the **International Space Station** ISS around 400 kilometres above the Earth.

On 12 April 1961 the Soviet citizen **Yuri Gagarin** circled the Earth once in the spacecraft Vostok 1, and the flight lasted about 108 minutes. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to fly into space. In 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk. On 21 July 1969 Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the moon as part of the **Apollo 11 mission**.

**Claude Nicollier** from the canton of Vaud became the first Swiss person in space in 1992. Altogether he was in space four times with the American space shuttle. On two flights he helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope, and in 1999 he made a spacewalk. In 2022 ESA chose the Swiss Marco Sieber for its new astronaut corps.

For work outside the station astronauts need a **spacesuit**, which supplies them with oxygen and protects them from cold, heat and radiation. In the station they float because they are **weightless**, since together with the station they are constantly falling around the Earth. That is why they sleep in sleeping bags that are tied down and eat out of pouches. Every day they exercise for about two hours so that their muscles and bones do not become weak.

Anyone who wants to become an astronaut usually needs a degree in science, engineering or medicine, or training as a pilot. You also have to be very healthy, speak good English and be able to work in a team. In the ESA selection of 2021 and 2022 over 22,000 people applied, and only a few were chosen. The **training** that follows includes training under water, survival training and Russian lessons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Russian name for an astronaut.
A state in which you feel none of your weight and float.
A protective suit with its own air supply for work in space.
Work done by an astronaut outside the spacecraft.

gewusst: In space astronauts become a few centimetres taller, because their spine stretches.
On the ISS astronauts see about 16 sunrises every day.
So far only twelve people altogether have walked on the moon.

teile.einleitung: Cepheids are stars that become brighter and dimmer in a fixed rhythm. Because their rhythm reveals their true luminosity, astronomers use them as measuring sticks for huge distances.
wichtigste: Cepheids pulsate: they expand and contract again at regular intervals.
The longer the period, the greater the luminosity.
Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered this relationship and published it in 1912.
Edwin Hubble used Cepheids to show that the Andromeda Nebula is a galaxy of its own.
The Pole Star is a Cepheid.
The class is named after the star Delta Cephei.

abschnitte.text: A Cepheid is a star that **expands and contracts** in a regular beat. As it does so, its brightness changes. Such stars lie in a narrow band in the **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**, an overview of all stars by colour and luminosity. It is called the **instability strip**. Stars that cross this region begin to pulsate.

What drives the pulsation is called the **kappa mechanism**. In one layer of the star, helium is partly ionised. When this layer is squeezed together, it lets less radiation through, so it becomes more opaque. As a result, heat builds up, and the layer expands, cools and falls back again. Then everything starts over, like a valve that keeps opening and closing.

The American astronomer **Henrietta Swan Leavitt** found out at Harvard: the longer a Cepheid takes for one beat, the more **luminous** it is. She published this **period-luminosity relation** in 1912. If you measure the period, you therefore know the true luminosity. If you compare it with the brightness we see, you can calculate the **distance**. An example: if two Cepheids look equally bright, and one actually shines 100 times more strongly, then it is 10 times as far away, because brightness falls with the square of the distance.

In the 1920s, **Edwin Hubble** found Cepheids in the **Andromeda Nebula**. He worked out their distance and got a value far outside the Milky Way. This made it clear that Andromeda is a **galaxy of its own**. In 1952, **Walter Baade** realised that there are two types of Cepheids and that the measuring stick had been based on the wrong kind. After the correction, the distances to other galaxies were about **twice as large**.

The name comes from the star **Delta Cephei** in the constellation Cepheus. The young English astronomer **John Goodricke** discovered its changes in brightness with the naked eye in 1784. The **Pole Star** is also a classical Cepheid. It pulsates with a period of about 4 days, but its brightness varies only very slightly, so you cannot notice it without instruments.

gewusst: Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked as a so-called “computer” and analysed thousands of photographic plates of stars.
With the Hubble Space Telescope, Cepheids can even be found in galaxies that are tens of millions of light years away.

teile.einleitung: The root is the part of the tooth that you cannot see. It sits in the jawbone and holds the tooth firmly so that it does not wobble when you chew.
wichtigste: The **root of the tooth** sits in the jawbone.
It is covered with **root cement**, not with enamel.
Each root sits in a **tooth socket**, the alveolus.
Fine fibres of the **periodontal ligament** hold the tooth in the bone.
Upper large molars usually have three roots, lower ones usually two.
Nerves and blood vessels enter the tooth at the tip of the root.
Dental implants are usually made of **titanium**.

abschnitte.text: Every tooth consists of the visible **crown** and the **root**. The root is often longer than the crown. It sits out of sight in the **jawbone**. On the outside it is covered not with enamel but with a thin, bone-like layer, the **root cement**.

abschnitte.titel: How the tooth stays in place
abschnitte.text: Each root sits in a hollow in the jawbone, the **tooth socket**. Experts call it the **alveolus**. Between the root and the bone lies the **periodontal ligament** with thousands of fine fibres. These fibres are anchored in the root cement and in the bone. They cushion the pressure of chewing, which is why a healthy tooth can be moved just a tiny bit.

Not every tooth has the same number of roots. Front teeth and canines usually have only one. **Upper large molars** usually have **three**, lower ones usually **two**. Several roots spread the great pressure of chewing over the bone. At the **tip of the root** there is a tiny opening through which nerves and blood vessels reach the root canal.

abschnitte.titel: The root of the milk tooth
abschnitte.text: When a permanent tooth moves up, the body gradually breaks down the root of the milk tooth. In the end only a little tissue holds the milk tooth. It wobbles and falls out. That is why a milk tooth that has fallen out has almost no root left.

If a tooth is missing, a **dental implant** can replace it. This is an artificial root that is placed in the jawbone. Most implants are made of **titanium**. This metal is very well tolerated by the body and grows firmly together with the bone. Later an artificial crown is fixed on top of it.

gewusst: The canine usually has the longest root of all the teeth.
Root cement is similar to bone, but it has no blood vessels of its own.

teile.einleitung: Warts are small, rough lumps on the skin. They are caused by viruses and are harmless, but sometimes annoying.
wichtigste: Common warts are caused by papillomaviruses.
Warts are catching, through contact or via objects.
Verrucas on the sole of the foot hurt when walking.
The black dots in a wart are tiny blood vessels, not roots.
In children many warts disappear by themselves over time.
The idea that toads give you warts is an old mistaken belief.

abschnitte.text: Common warts are caused by **papillomaviruses**. The viruses infect cells of the **outer layer of the skin** and make them grow strongly. This produces a hardened, rough bump. Warts do not have real **roots**. The small black dots in them are tiny **blood vessels** in which the blood has clotted.

Warts are **catching**. The viruses are passed on through direct contact or via objects such as towels. Small injuries to the skin make it easier to catch them. The viruses survive well on damp floors in **swimming pools** and **changing rooms**. That is why **flip-flops** help to protect you from warts on your feet.

**Verrucas** grow on the **sole of the foot**. Because the body's weight presses on them with every step, they grow inwards. That is why they hurt when walking, as if you had a thorn in your foot. You should not cut or scratch at them yourself. This could spread the viruses further.

In children many warts disappear **by themselves** after months or a few years, because the **immune system** fights the viruses. The chemist's sells products that soften the hardened skin. Stubborn warts can be **frozen** by a dermatologist. For this she uses **liquid nitrogen**, which is about minus 196 degrees Celsius cold. The wart tissue dies and later falls off.

gewusst: Toads do have warty-looking skin, but they do not pass on warts.
Liquid nitrogen is so cold that it starts to steam immediately in the air.

teile.einleitung: When the sun goes down, the sky often turns a beautiful red, orange and pink. In German this is called **“Abendrot”**, the evening red. It happens because in the evening sunlight travels a particularly long way through the air.
wichtigste: The evening red is a red sky in the evening at sunset.
In the morning the red colouring is called the morning red.
During the day the sky is blue in fine weather.
In the evening the light has to travel far through the air, and the blue is lost on the way.
When mountain peaks glow reddish, this is called alpenglow.
An old weather saying goes: “Abendrot, Schönwetterbot”, meaning a red evening sky brings fine weather.

abschnitte.text: The light of the sun looks white, but it contains all the colours of the rainbow. As it passes through the air, it meets tiny particles of the air. These deflect **blue light** to the side much more strongly than red light. Experts call this **scattering**. That is why during the day blue light reaches us from all directions, and the sky looks **blue**.

In the evening the sun is low on the horizon. Its light now has to travel a much **longer way through the air** before it reaches us. On the way, almost all the blue light is scattered to the side. What remains is mainly **red** and **orange**. Dust and fine water droplets in the air can make the colours even stronger. Then clouds often glow red, orange and pink as well.

In the mountains there is a particularly beautiful spectacle: **alpenglow**. When the sun goes down, the mountain peaks glow with a reddish or pink light while the valleys are already in shadow. In Switzerland you can see this well, for example, on snow-covered peaks. It can also happen in the morning.

In the past people watched the sky closely to forecast the weather. A well-known German saying goes: “**Abendrot, Schönwetterbot**. Morgenrot, schlecht Wetter droht.” It is like the English saying “Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning.” In our part of the world the weather often comes from the west. If the sky in the west is clear in the evening, the sun can colour the clouds red, and the fine weather is on its way. With a **red morning sky** it is often the other way round: it can mean that clouds and rain are coming soon. But such rules are not completely reliable.

gewusst: On Mars it is the other way round: there the sky around the sun looks bluish at sunset.
After large volcanic eruptions, red evening skies can glow particularly strongly because of the fine particles in the air.

teile.einleitung: A cotton bud is a small stick with soft cotton wool at the ends. It is handy for crafts and personal care, but it does not belong deep inside the ear.
wichtigste: The head of a cotton bud is made of cotton wool.
On the ear you may only use it on the outside of the outer ear.
In the ear canal it can injure the eardrum.
The outer ear is cleaned well with a damp flannel.
If your ears are blocked, you go to the doctor.
Used cotton buds belong in the bin, not in the toilet.

abschnitte.text: A **cotton bud** consists of a thin stick with soft **cotton wool** wound around its ends. That is where the name comes from. You can use it to clean small spots carefully. Cotton buds are popular for crafts and painting, for example for putting **dabs of paint** on paper. This makes lovely dot pictures.

Deep inside the ear lies the **eardrum**, a thin membrane that vibrates when we hear. A cotton bud in the **ear canal** can injure it. It also often pushes **earwax** further in. That is why you use a cotton bud only **on the outside of the outer ear**. It is even better to clean the outer ear and the skin behind the ear with a damp **flannel** and dry it well.

**Earwax** is a soft, wax-like substance. It is usually **yellowish to brownish**. Earwax is useful: it traps dust and dirt and protects the skin in the ear canal. Normally it moves outwards by itself. If an ear is blocked, you go to the **doctor**, who can remove the wax safely.

Used cotton buds belong in the **bin**. In the toilet they block pipes and cause problems at **sewage treatment plants**. If they get into rivers and seas, they pollute nature. That is why there are now many cotton buds with sticks made of paper or wood instead of plastic.

gewusst: Many packets state clearly that the buds should not be put into the ear canal.
The ear cleans itself: the earwax is slowly pushed outwards.

teile.einleitung: Wernicke's area is a region of the brain that is important for understanding language. It is named after the German neurologist Carl Wernicke.
wichtigste: Carl Wernicke described the area in 1874.
It usually lies on the left in the rear part of the superior temporal gyrus.
It corresponds mainly to Brodmann area 22.
If it is damaged, Wernicke's aphasia develops, a disorder of understanding language.
The arcuate fasciculus connects it with Broca's area.

abschnitte.text: **Wernicke's area** usually lies in the **left half of the brain**. More precisely, it lies in the rear part of the **superior temporal gyrus**, in the temporal lobe. It is close to the **auditory cortex**, which processes sounds. In Brodmann's classification it corresponds mainly to the rear part of **area 22**. It helps us to understand words we hear.

In 1874 the German neurologist **Carl Wernicke** described patients with a striking disorder. They spoke fluently but hardly understood language. Wernicke linked this disorder to a region in the **temporal lobe**. Before that, the French doctor Paul Broca had described an area in the frontal lobe that is important for speaking. This led to the idea of different **language centres**.

**Aphasia** is a language disorder after brain damage, for example after a stroke. In **Wernicke's aphasia** it is mainly understanding that is disturbed. That is why it is also called **sensory aphasia**. The people affected speak fluently but often without meaning, with wrong or made-up words. Also typical is **paragrammatism**: parts of sentences are wrongly tangled together. The people affected often do not notice their mistakes.

A bundle of fibres, the **arcuate fasciculus** or **arcuate bundle**, connects Wernicke's area with **Broca's area**. It runs from the temporal lobe to the frontal lobe. In this way it connects understanding language with speaking. If this connection is interrupted, **conduction aphasia** develops. Then it is mainly **repeating** what someone has said that is disturbed, although understanding is relatively good.

gewusst: Carl Wernicke was only in his mid-twenties when he published his famous description.
In most people the most important language areas lie in the left half of the brain.

teile.einleitung: **51 Pegasi b** is a famous planet: it was the first to be discovered around a sun-like star outside our solar system. It was found in 1995 by the Geneva astronomers **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz**. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
wichtigste: 51 Pegasi b orbits the star 51 Pegasi in the constellation of Pegasus.
The system is around 50 light years from Earth.
The planet is a “hot Jupiter”: a gas giant very close to its star.
One orbit takes only about 4.2 days.
Since 2015 the planet has officially been called Dimidium and the star Helvetios.
The measurements came from the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in France.

abschnitte.text: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from the **University of Geneva** observed the star 51 Pegasi with a telescope at the **Observatoire de Haute-Provence** in the south of France. They did not see the planet directly. Instead they measured that the star regularly wobbles a little back and forth. This wobble happens because the planet pulls on the star with its gravity. This is called the **radial velocity method**. In October 1995 they announced their discovery.

Many experts were surprised at first, because nobody had expected a planet like this. Only a few days after the announcement, the Americans **Geoffrey Marcy** and **Paul Butler** confirmed the discovery with their own measurements. This started the search for **exoplanets**, that is planets around other stars. Today thousands of them are known.

51 Pegasi b is a **gas giant** with about half the mass of Jupiter. But it orbits very close to its star: its distance is only about **one twentieth** of the distance between the Earth and the Sun. That is why a year on this planet lasts only about **4.2 days**. According to calculations it is around **1,000 °C** hot. Such planets are called **hot Jupiters**.

In 2015 the public was allowed to suggest names to the **International Astronomical Union**. Since then the planet has been called **Dimidium**, which is Latin for “half”, because it is about half as heavy as Jupiter. The star was given the name **Helvetios**, after the Helvetii. This recalls Switzerland, where the discoverers come from.

gewusst: The star 51 Pegasi is quite similar to our Sun and can just about be seen with the naked eye under a very dark sky.
Before 1995 many researchers believed that gas giants could only exist far out from their star, like Jupiter in our solar system.

teile.einleitung: Cassini-Huygens was one of the biggest space missions to the planet Saturn. The Cassini probe orbited Saturn for over 13 years, and the Huygens lander touched down on Saturn's moon Titan.
wichtigste: NASA, ESA and the Italian space agency ASI ran the mission together.
Cassini launched in 1997 and reached Saturn's orbit on 1 July 2004.
With swing-by manoeuvres at Venus, Earth and Jupiter it gained speed.
Three radioisotope batteries supplied the power.
Huygens landed on Titan and sent data from the surface for about 72 minutes.
On 15 September 2017, Cassini was deliberately steered into Saturn's atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: The mission was a joint effort of three space organisations. The American **NASA** built the main probe Cassini. The European **ESA** built the lander **Huygens**. The Italian space agency **ASI** supplied, among other things, the large antenna for the radio link to Earth. The mission is named after the astronomers Giovanni Domenico Cassini and Christiaan Huygens, who studied Saturn in the 17th century.

Cassini launched in October 1997. For a direct flight to Saturn the probe would have needed huge amounts of fuel. So it flew past Venus twice, past Earth once and past Jupiter once, gaining momentum each time. This method is called a **swing-by** or **gravity assist**. On **1 July 2004**, Cassini swung into orbit around Saturn. Because sunlight there is about a hundred times weaker, three **radioisotope batteries** supplied the power: they turned the heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity.

In January 2005, **Huygens** landed on the large moon **Titan**. The probe ran on batteries and sent its data to Earth via Cassini. After about **72 minutes**, Cassini disappeared behind the horizon and no more surface data arrived. Using radar, Cassini later found **lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane** in Titan's polar regions. This makes Titan, besides Earth, the only known body with stable liquids on its surface.

The small moon **Enceladus** also came as a surprise. Cassini measured a slight wobble called **libration**. In 2015 it turned out to be too large for an ice shell that is firmly attached to the core. From this, researchers concluded that there is a **global ocean** of water under the ice crust. Enceladus is therefore seen as a place where conditions might be friendly to life.

From April 2017, the final phase began, the **Grand Finale**. Cassini flew 22 times through the narrow gap between the innermost ring and Saturn's atmosphere. In doing so, the gravity field and the mass of the rings were measured precisely. Because the fuel was running low, the probe was deliberately steered into the atmosphere on **15 September 2017**, where it burned up. That way it could never crash onto Titan or Enceladus and contaminate these moons with **germs from Earth**. This is called **planetary protection**.

gewusst: To this day, Huygens is the landing of a space probe that is the furthest from Earth.
During its mission, Cassini delivered hundreds of thousands of pictures of Saturn, its rings and moons.

teile.einleitung: The tongue is a movable muscle in our mouth and our most important organ for tasting. With it we can tell whether something is sweet like honey, sour like a lemon, salty or bitter. It also helps with chewing, swallowing and speaking.
wichtigste: The tongue consists mainly of muscles.
With the tongue we recognise tastes such as sweet or salty.
On the tongue there are taste buds, which help with tasting.
There are five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
A lemon tastes sour, and honey tastes sweet.
Besides tasting, the tongue helps with speaking.
For the full experience of flavour, the nose is needed too.

abschnitte.text: The **tongue** consists of many muscles running in different directions. That is why it can stretch, roll, twist and make itself completely flat. At the back it is attached to the floor of the mouth and to the hyoid bone. Its surface is covered with a moist mucous membrane. Many small bumps, the **papillae**, make it rough.

Many papillae contain **taste buds**, and a person has several thousand of them. Each bud contains sensory cells that recognise dissolved substances from food. They report this to the brain along nerves. The sensory cells live only about ten days and are then replaced. That is why your sense of taste recovers quickly after you burn your tongue.

The tongue distinguishes **sweet**, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Honey tastes sweet, a lemon sour, crisps salty and coffee or chicory, for example, bitter. **Umami** means roughly delicious in Japanese and stands for the savoury taste of meat stock, tomatoes or mature cheese. It was discovered in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda. People used to believe that each taste had its own zone on the tongue, but that is not true.

abschnitte.titel: Tongue and nose as a team
abschnitte.text: Much of what we call taste actually comes from the **nose**. When we chew, scents rise from the back into the nose. That is why food tastes bland when the nose is blocked with a cold. With your nose held shut you can hardly tell an apple from a raw potato.

Without a tongue we could not make many sounds, such as L, T, D or N. When eating, the tongue pushes the food between the teeth and forms it into a mouthful. Then it presses it back into the throat for **swallowing**. It also feels the teeth and food and can even sense the tiniest fish bones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small sense organ on the tongue that recognises tastes.
Small bumps on the surface of the tongue.
A savoury basic taste, for example of stock or cheese.
A small bone in the neck to which the tongue is attached.

gewusst: The tongue is so sensitive that it notices a hair in the mouth immediately.
Children have more taste buds than adults and so often find bitter things stronger.
A chameleon can stick its tongue out further than its body is long.

teile.einleitung: The toothbrush is the most important tool for healthy teeth. Anyone who brushes properly and for long enough protects their teeth from tooth decay.
wichtigste: You brush your teeth for about 2 to 3 minutes each time.
Soft bristles are best for children's teeth.
The KAI method means: chewing surfaces, outer surfaces, inner surfaces.
You replace a toothbrush about every 2 to 3 months.
After brushing, the brush should dry standing upright.
With small children, the parents brush again afterwards.

abschnitte.text: **Soft bristles** are best for children's teeth. They clean thoroughly and are gentle on the **gums**. Hard bristles can injure the gums. There are also **electric toothbrushes** with a motor and a rechargeable battery. Their brush head rotates or vibrates.

So that you do not forget any side, the **KAI method** helps. KAI stands for the German words for **chewing surfaces** (“Kauflächen”), **outer surfaces** (“Aussenflächen”) and **inner surfaces** (“Innenflächen”). So you start with the chewing surfaces on top of the back teeth. Then come the outer and the inner sides. A lot of plaque collects along the **gum line**, so you hold the bristles there at a slight **angle**.

For clean teeth you need about **2 to 3 minutes**. An egg timer or a song can help with counting. Small children do not yet brush quite thoroughly. That is why the **parents brush again afterwards** until school age. This way even difficult spots get clean.

After brushing you rinse the brush and stand it up to dry with the **head at the top**. In a damp, closed container germs multiply more easily. Worn-out bristles clean badly. That is why you replace the brush about **every 2 to 3 months**, or sooner if the bristles are splaying apart.

gewusst: The abbreviation KAI is a well-known memory aid for brushing teeth in Swiss schools.
A very long time ago people already cleaned their teeth with chewed twigs.

teile.einleitung: Charon is the largest moon of the dwarf planet Pluto. Compared with Pluto it is so big that the two are often described as a double system.
wichtigste: Charon is about half the size of Pluto: roughly 1,210 km against roughly 2,380 km.
James Christy discovered Charon in 1978.
Pluto and Charon always show each other the same side.
Their common centre of mass lies outside Pluto.
One orbit takes about 6.4 days.
The probe New Horizons flew past Charon in July 2015.

abschnitte.text: The American astronomer **James Christy** discovered Charon in **1978**. On photographic plates, Pluto showed a small **bump** at its edge. This bump moved around regularly. Christy realised that it was a moon. Since then, four more, much smaller moons have been found around Pluto.

Charon measures about **1,210 kilometres**, Pluto about **2,380 kilometres**. So Charon is about **half the size** of Pluto. No other moon is so large compared with its main body. That is why the **common centre of mass** of the two lies not inside Pluto, but in the empty space between them. Both circle around this point, and Pluto visibly wobbles as it does so. This is why people often speak of a **double system**.

Our Moon always shows the same side to Earth. With Pluto and Charon this is true of **both**: they always show each other the same side. Charon circles Pluto in about **6.4 days**, and a day on Pluto lasts exactly as long. From one side of Pluto, Charon is therefore always seen in the same place in the sky, and from the other side never.

The NASA probe **New Horizons** flew past Pluto and Charon on **14 July 2015**. It had been travelling for about nine and a half years. It delivered the first close-up pictures of Charon. They showed large canyons and a strikingly **reddish north pole**. This colouring probably comes from **methane gas**, which Pluto keeps losing. Some of it reaches Charon and freezes at the cold pole. There, sunlight turns it into reddish-brown substances.
