In Greek myth, **Charon** is the **ferryman** who carries the souls of the dead across the river Styx into the underworld. **Pluto** is the Roman name of the ruler of the underworld. That is why the name suits the companion of the dwarf planet.

gewusst: The red polar region of Charon was given the unofficial name “Mordor”, after a place in the books “The Lord of the Rings”.
Charon consists to a large extent of water ice.

teile.einleitung: The cell is the smallest building block of life. All living things consist of cells: bacteria of a single one, humans of trillions of them.
wichtigste: The **cell** is the smallest unit that shows all the features of life.
**Robert Hooke** coined the term “cell” in 1665.
A human being consists of about **30 trillion** cells.
**Bacteria** are single-celled organisms.
Plant cells have **chloroplasts** for photosynthesis.
Cells without a true nucleus are called **prokaryotes**.
**Viruses** do not consist of cells.

abschnitte.text: In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at a thin piece of **cork** under the microscope. He saw many small chambers. They reminded him of the little rooms of monks, so he called them “cells”. In the 19th century researchers such as **Matthias Schleiden** and **Theodor Schwann** realised that all plants and animals consist of cells.

A cell can **feed**, **grow**, **react to stimuli** and **reproduce**. That is why it is the smallest living unit. Atoms and molecules are not alive. Organs such as the heart or liver consist of many cells. **Viruses**, on the other hand, have no cells and no metabolism of their own. They can only multiply in other cells and so are usually not counted as living things.

Every cell is surrounded by a **cell membrane**. Inside it is filled with **cytoplasm**, a jelly-like liquid. In it lie the **organelles**, small parts with their own tasks. Plant cells also have a solid **cell wall** and green **chloroplasts**. These contain chlorophyll and use photosynthesis to turn light energy into sugar.

In **prokaryotes** such as bacteria the genetic information lies freely in the cytoplasm, and there is no true nucleus. Plants, animals, fungi and humans are **eukaryotes**. Their cells have a nucleus surrounded by an envelope. **Bacteria** consist of only one cell, while earthworms, ferns and jellyfish are multicellular.

Most human body cells measure about **10 to 30 micrometres**. That is around one to three hundredths of a millimetre. That is why you need a microscope to see them. According to estimates, an adult human consists of about **30 to 40 trillion** cells. Most of them are **red blood cells**.

gewusst: In the 19th century the doctor Rudolf Virchow realised: every cell comes from another cell.
Some nerve cells have extensions that are over a metre long, for example from the back to the foot.

teile.einleitung: The digestive system includes all the organs that take in food, break it down and bring the nutrients into the blood. It includes the digestive tract from the mouth to the anus and helper organs such as the liver and pancreas. Every organ has its own particular job in this long production line.
wichtigste: The digestive system consists of the digestive tract and the digestive glands.
Already in the mouth, saliva splits starch.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid.
In the small intestine most nutrients are taken into the blood.
The main job of the large intestine is to take water from the chyme.
Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Enzymes break the nutrients down into small building blocks.

abschnitte.text: The **digestive tract** leads from the mouth through the throat, gullet, stomach, small intestine and large intestine to the anus. Together it is several metres long in adults. In addition there are glands that make digestive juices: salivary glands, the **liver** and the **pancreas**. The juices contain **enzymes** that break large nutrients down into small building blocks. This turns starch into sugar, proteins into amino acids and fat into fatty acids.

In the mouth the enzyme **amylase** in saliva already splits starch. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time. In the stomach glands in the stomach wall produce **hydrochloric acid**, which kills bacteria. The enzyme pepsin begins there to break down proteins. A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from the strong acid.

The **liver** is the largest inner organ and makes **bile**. The bile is collected in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine. There it helps to break fat into tiny droplets. The pancreas supplies enzymes for carbohydrates, proteins and fats. It also makes the hormone insulin, which regulates blood sugar.

In the **small intestine** the food is fully digested. Its inner wall is covered with millions of tiny bulges, the **villi**. They enlarge the surface enormously, so that most nutrients are taken into the blood here. The blood brings them first to the liver and then into the whole body. The small intestine is divided into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

The **large intestine** is shorter but wider than the small intestine. Its main job is to take **water** and salts from the chyme. This makes the rest firmer and forms it into faeces. In the large intestine live especially many bacteria, which break down indigestible fibres and make some vitamins. At the start of the large intestine hangs the **appendix**, which can become inflamed in appendicitis.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protein substance that speeds up chemical processes such as the breaking down of food.
Liquid from the liver that helps with the digestion of fat.
Tiny bulges in the small intestine that take up nutrients.
A strong acid in the stomach that kills germs.
An enzyme in saliva that splits starch.

gewusst: If you spread out the inner surface of the small intestine, it would be much larger than the skin surface of the body.
The lining of the stomach renews itself every few days, so that the acid does not harm it.
The brown colour of faeces comes from substances broken down from the bile.

teile.einleitung: Water is the most important substance in our body, and without water we survive only a few days. The body needs it to work properly: it carries nutrients, cools us and flushes out waste. That is why you should drink enough every day.
wichtigste: An adult's body consists of about 60 per cent water.
In babies the proportion of water is even higher, at around 70 per cent.
The body needs water to work properly.
Every day we lose water through urine, sweat and our breath.
Children should drink about 1 to 1.5 litres a day, adults about 1.5 to 2 litres.
Thirst is a warning signal that the body needs water.
In Switzerland tap water is of very good quality.

abschnitte.text: Water is found in almost every part of the body. Blood consists mostly of water, and muscles and the **brain** also contain a lot of it. Only bones and fatty tissue are drier. So a child weighing 30 kilograms carries around 18 litres of water inside them.

Water is a **means of transport**: in the blood it carries nutrients and oxygen to the cells. Through the **kidneys** it flushes waste out with the urine. When we sweat, water evaporates on the skin and so cools the body. Water also keeps joints supple and helps with digestion.

Anyone who drinks too little gets **thirsty**, and often also gets headaches and feels tired. You find it harder to concentrate, which is noticeable at school, for example. Dark yellow urine shows that the body needs more water. A severe lack of water is called **dehydration** and can become dangerous. That is why you need particularly large amounts of fluid in hot weather, during sport or with a fever.

Around 80 per cent of Swiss **drinking water** comes from groundwater and springs, and the rest mainly from lakes. It is strictly checked and can be drunk straight from the tap almost everywhere. Many towns have public fountains with drinking water, and in Zurich alone there are over 1,000. Tap water is much cheaper than bottled water and creates no rubbish.

It is best to drink water or unsweetened tea spread over the day. Sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar and harm the teeth. Fruit and vegetables such as watermelon, cucumbers or tomatoes also provide fluid. Your own water bottle in your school bag helps you to drink regularly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dangerous lack of water in the body.
Two organs that clean the blood and make urine.
Water that collects in the soil under the ground.
A feeling by which the body tells us that it needs water.

gewusst: We also lose water when we breathe out, and on cold days you can see it as a cloud of breath.
Without food a person can survive several weeks, but without water usually only about three days.
In Basel and other towns, fresh drinking water flows from many old fountains.

teile.einleitung: Are we alone in the universe? People have been asking this question for thousands of years. So far **no life has been found outside the Earth**, but researchers are looking for it in many places.
wichtigste: So far no life has been found outside the Earth (as of 2025).
For life as we know it, liquid water is particularly important.
On Mars robot vehicles are searching for traces of past life.
Planets around other stars are called exoplanets.
In 1995 the Swiss Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first planet around a sun-like star.
The Voyager probes carry a golden record as a greeting.

abschnitte.text: All life on the Earth needs **liquid water**. That is why researchers look mainly where there is water or used to be. Life also needs a source of energy, for example sunlight or heat from inside a planet or moon. Certain chemical substances are also important, above all **carbon**. Whether there could also be completely different forms of life, nobody knows.

On **Mars** there used to be rivers and lakes. Today **robot vehicles** are searching there for traces of past life. Moons with ice are also exciting. Under the ice of Jupiter's moon **Europa** there is probably a large **ocean**. Saturn's moon **Enceladus** even sprays **fountains of water** into space. Researchers wonder whether simple living things could exist in such oceans.

Planets that orbit stars other than the sun are called **exoplanets**. The first one around a sun-like star was found in **1995** by the Swiss **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz** from the University of Geneva. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. Today over 5,000 exoplanets are known. Some of them orbit at a distance at which there could be liquid water.

Some researchers **listen** with large **radio telescopes** to see whether radio signals from aliens are arriving from anywhere. So far no such signal has been received for certain. People have also sent greetings into space themselves. The two space probes **Voyager** carry a **golden record**. On it are pictures, music, sounds of the Earth and greetings in many languages.

gewusst: The Voyager probes were launched in 1977 and have now left our solar system far behind.
According to estimates, in our Milky Way alone there are more planets than stars.

teile.einleitung: The spine is the flexible axis of our skeleton and reaches from the head to the pelvis. It consists of about 33 vertebrae, carries the upper body and protects the delicate spinal cord. Thanks to it we can bend down, turn and walk upright.
wichtigste: The human spine has about 33 vertebrae.
It is divided into the cervical spine, the thoracic spine, the lumbar spine, the sacrum and the tailbone.
Seen from the side, the spine has the shape of a double S.
Between the vertebrae lie intervertebral discs, which act like shock absorbers.
The spinal cord runs protected inside the spine.
Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae, even the giraffe.
Exercise and good posture keep the back healthy.

abschnitte.text: The spine consists of about 33 single bones, the **vertebrae**. At the top there are 7 neck vertebrae, below them 12 thoracic vertebrae and 5 lumbar vertebrae. Further down, 5 vertebrae have fused to form the **sacrum**, and at the very bottom 3 to 5 small vertebrae form the tailbone. Because the number varies a little at the lower end, people speak of about 33 vertebrae. The top neck vertebra is called the atlas, after the giant from Greek legend who holds up the sky.

Seen from the side, the spine is not straight but curved like a double S. This shape absorbs jolts when walking, running and jumping. Between the vertebrae lie 23 **intervertebral discs** made of cartilage with a soft core. They act like shock absorbers and make the spine flexible. Many ligaments and muscles hold the whole thing together.

Each vertebra has a hole in the middle. One above the other, these holes form the **spinal canal**. In it lies the spinal cord, a thick bundle of nerves that connects the brain with the body. If the spinal cord is badly injured in an accident, paralysis can be the result. That is why the bony casing is so important.

All animals with a backbone are called **vertebrates**, and they include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Almost all mammals have exactly seven neck vertebrae. In the giraffe, however, each of them is very long. Snakes even have several hundred vertebrae.

A strong back needs exercise, for example swimming, cycling or climbing. Sitting for a long time with a bent back puts strain on the intervertebral discs. A school rucksack should be carried on both shoulders and should not be too heavy. Heavy things are best lifted with a straight back, using your knees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single bone of the spine.
An elastic disc between two vertebrae that absorbs jolts.
A bundle of nerves in the spinal canal that connects the brain and the body.
An animal with a backbone.

gewusst: A giraffe has the same number of neck vertebrae as you, namely seven.
In space astronauts become a few centimetres taller, because the spine stretches without gravity.
The word atlas for the top neck vertebra comes from a giant in Greek legend.

teile.einleitung: The growth plate is a thin disc of cartilage in the long bones of children and teenagers. At it the bones grow in length until growth is finished at the end of adolescence.
wichtigste: The growth plate consists of cartilage.
In technical language it is called the epiphyseal plate.
It lies between the end of the bone and the shaft of the bone.
At the growth plates the long bones become longer.
The plates usually close between about 15 and 20 years.
With an X-ray of the hand the bone age can be determined.
Injuries to the growth plate have to be treated especially carefully.

abschnitte.text: A long bone such as the thigh bone has a long middle part, the **shaft**, and two thickened ends. Between the end at the joint and the shaft lies, in children, the **growth plate**. In technical language it is called the **epiphyseal plate**, because the end of the bone is called the epiphysis. Such plates are found near both ends of a long bone. On X-rays of children you see them as a narrow gap.

The growth plate is a disc of **cartilage**. Its **cartilage cells** keep multiplying. On the side of the shaft the new cartilage is gradually converted into **bone**. This way the bone becomes longer bit by bit. This growth is stimulated especially by the **growth hormone**, which is made in the pituitary gland.

At the end of growth the cartilage discs **turn completely to bone**. This usually happens between about **15 and 20 years**. After that the bones no longer grow in length. On the X-ray the gap has then disappeared. How far the plates have closed is shown by an **X-ray of the hand**: from it the doctor determines the **bone age** and estimates how much a child will still grow.

The growth plate is softer than the finished bone. That is why it can be injured in an accident. If it is damaged, the bone can go on growing **too short** or **crooked**. That is why such fractures in children are treated and checked especially carefully. Often a follow-up X-ray is taken months later.

gewusst: Not all growth plates close at the same time. Some turn to bone earlier, others only later.
Broken bones usually heal much faster in children than in adults.

teile.einleitung: The index finger is the second finger of the hand, right next to the thumb. Its German name, “Zeigefinger”, comes from pointing, and we use it every day for many things.
wichtigste: The **index finger** lies right next to the thumb.
Its German name comes from **pointing**.
It has **three finger bones**.
In English it is called the **index finger**.
In front of the lips it means “Be quiet!”.
A raised index finger is a **warning**.

abschnitte.text: The hand has five fingers: the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger. The **index finger** is the second, right next to the thumb. It has **three sections**, just like the middle finger, ring finger and little finger. The thumb has only two. Together with the thumb, the index finger can grip very finely, for example a thread or a needle.

We use the index finger to point at things or directions. That is where its German name comes from. Because it is nimble and easy to control, we usually use it to press **lift buttons**, doorbells or screens. When **learning to read**, many children run their index finger along under the line so that they do not lose their place.

The index finger can say a lot. If you hold it in front of your lips, it means “Shh” or **“Be quiet!”**. A **raised index finger** while talking is a warning: be careful or listen! At school many children put their index finger up when they want to **answer**. This way the teacher sees who wants to say something.

In English this finger is called the **“index finger”**. The word “index” comes from Latin and means something like pointer. In German, too, people know the word index, for example for a list at the end of a book that points to the right pages.

In Switzerland, when swearing an **oath** or making a solemn promise, people raise three fingers: the thumb, index finger and middle finger. This **oath hand** can also be seen in many pictures of the Rütli oath.

gewusst: The fingertips are among the most sensitive parts of the skin. That is why blind people often read Braille with their index finger.
Many people also tap on their mobile phone or tablet with their index finger when they are not typing with their thumb.

teile.einleitung: In **astrophotography** you take photos of the sky: the moon, planets, stars and distant galaxies. Because most objects in the sky are very faint, special tricks are needed. Today even amateur photographers can take astonishing pictures.
wichtigste: In 1840 John William Draper took one of the first successful photographs of the moon.
In 1850 a star, Vega, was photographed for the first time.
With long exposures stars turn into lines, because the Earth turns.
A motorised tracking mount turns the camera to follow the turning of the sky.
In stacking, many pictures are laid on top of each other to reduce noise.
Light pollution is the biggest problem for astrophotos.

abschnitte.titel: The first photos of the sky
abschnitte.text: Photography was invented in the 1830s. As early as **1840** the American **John William Draper** took one of the first successful photographs of the **moon**. Stars are much fainter, so it took longer. Only in **1850** was a star photographed for the very first time: **Vega**. Later photography became very important for research, because a photographic plate records far more faint stars than the eye.

The Earth turns, which is why the sky seems to turn, by around **15 degrees per hour**. If you make a long exposure with a fixed camera, the stars turn into **lines**, known as **star trails**. With a **4-hour** exposure each arc becomes around **60 degrees** long. If you want stars as points, the **500 rule** helps: you divide 500 by the focal length in millimetres. So with a focal length of 25 mm you can expose for about **20 seconds**.

For long exposures people use a **motorised tracking mount**. It **turns the camera to follow the turning of the sky**, so that the stars always stay in the same place in the picture. Another trick is **stacking**. You take **many single exposures** and lay them on top of each other on the computer. This reduces the annoying **noise**, the fine grains in the picture, and faint details become visible.

Near **towns and cities** the sky is never really dark at night. Street lamps, advertising and lit-up buildings brighten the sky. This **light pollution** is the biggest problem for astrophotos, because faint stars and galaxies are lost in the bright background. That is why many astrophotographers go to the mountains or the countryside. In Switzerland, remote Alpine valleys or the Jura, for example, are suitable.

gewusst: Many famous pictures of galaxies are made from hundreds of single exposures that together add up to many hours of exposure.
With a camera on a tripod you can already photograph the Milky Way if the sky is dark enough.

teile.einleitung: Twice a year the clocks are changed: in spring one hour forward, in autumn one hour back. So in summer summer time applies and in winter standard time.
wichtigste: Switzerland has had **summer time since 1981**.
In 1980 Switzerland was a **time island** without summer time.
Summer time begins on the **last Sunday in March**.
Then the clock is **put forward** from 2 am to 3 am.
In winter **Central European Time** (CET) applies.
Originally the idea was to make better use of daylight and **save energy**.

abschnitte.text: On the **last Sunday in March** summer time begins. At 2 am the clock jumps straight to 3 am. Anyone who gets up at their usual time has slept **an hour less**. On the last Sunday in October summer time ends again. Then the clock is put back from 3 am to 2 am, and you gain an hour. A well-known way to remember it: in spring you put the garden furniture **out in front** of the house, and in autumn you put it **back** in the shed.

In winter Switzerland uses **Central European Time**, CET for short. It is one hour ahead of the world time **UTC**. In summer **Central European Summer Time**, CEST for short, applies, two hours ahead. Switzerland follows the European Union's rules on the dates so that the clocks in neighbouring countries show the same time.

The **German Empire** and Austria-Hungary introduced summer time on 30 April **1916**, in the middle of the First World War. The aim was to save **energy** for lighting. When the clock is put forward, it stays light longer in the evening. This was meant to reduce the need for artificial light. How much energy is really saved today, however, is disputed.

In Switzerland the voters rejected a time law with summer time in **1978**. In the summer of **1980** all the neighbouring countries then had summer time, but Switzerland did not. That is why it was called a **time island**. This caused problems, for example with railway timetables and in trade. So the federal government did introduce summer time in **1981** after all.

Some people feel tired for a few days after the change, because the **body clock** first has to adjust. Others enjoy the long, light summer evenings. In Europe there has been debate for years about whether to abolish the clock change. So far there has been no agreement.

gewusst: On the night of the change in autumn, the time between 2 am and 3 am happens twice.
Radio-controlled clocks and mobile phones change by themselves when the clocks go forward or back.

teile.einleitung: Growth hormone makes children and teenagers grow. It is made in the pituitary gland and is still important in adults for muscles, bones and metabolism.
wichtigste: The technical term for growth hormone is somatotropin, abbreviated to GH.
It is made in the pituitary gland, also called the hypophysis.
Too much growth hormone in childhood leads to gigantism, and too little to short stature.
In adults too much growth hormone leads to acromegaly.
Adults no longer grow taller because their growth plates have closed.
Today growth hormone for medicines is made with genetically modified bacteria.

abschnitte.text: Growth hormone is made in the **pituitary gland**, in technical language the **hypophysis**. It is about the size of a pea and lies under the brain. The technical term for the hormone is **somatotropin**, from Greek “soma” for body. It is often abbreviated to **GH**, for “growth hormone”. A particularly large amount of it is released during **sleep**.

In children and teenagers the hormone stimulates the **growth plates** of the bones. There cartilage cells multiply and the bones become longer. **Adults** still make growth hormone too, though less. It supports **metabolism** and helps to maintain muscles and bones. But adults no longer grow taller, because their growth plates have turned to bone and are **closed**.

If a child makes **far too much** growth hormone, the bones grow excessively long. This is called **giant growth** or gigantism. If growth hormone is lacking, the bones grow too slowly and the child stays much smaller than others of the same age: this is **short stature**. If adults make too much of it, **acromegaly** develops. Then the ends of the body such as the hands, feet, nose and chin become larger: Greek “akros” means tip and “megas” means large.

Children who grow too slowly because of a **lack of hormone** can be treated. They usually receive the missing hormone every day as a small **injection under the skin**. This way they can catch up on their growth. In the past the hormone was obtained with great effort from the pituitary glands of people who had died. Since the 1980s **genetically modified bacteria** have been making human growth hormone from a blueprint that has been inserted into them.

gewusst: Many children grow particularly well at night, because a lot of growth hormone is released in deep sleep.
Growth hormone partly works not directly but through a messenger substance that is made mainly by the liver.

teile.einleitung: A growth chart shows how tall or how heavy a child is at a particular age. Children's doctors add a point at every check-up and so can see how a child develops over the years.
wichtigste: On a growth chart, height or weight is plotted against age.
Final adult height depends strongly on the height of the parents.
In the first year of life a baby grows about 25 centimetres.
Weight roughly triples in the first year of life.
At primary school age you grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year.
Growing taller usually ends at about 16 to 20 years of age.

abschnitte.text: On a **growth chart**, age is shown along the bottom and height or weight up the side. At every check-up a **measurement point** is added. If you join up the points, you can see how a child is developing. Lines for other children of the same age, called **percentiles**, are also drawn on the sheet. If a child is on the 50th percentile, half of the children of the same age are taller and half are shorter.

In Switzerland a newborn baby weighs on average about **3.3 kilograms**. Most babies weigh between 2.5 and 4.5 kilograms at birth. In the first year of life you grow faster than in any later year, about **25 centimetres**. Weight also rises a lot: on its first birthday a baby usually weighs about **three times** as much as at birth.

Between the toddler years and adolescence you grow quite **steadily**. Usually about **5 to 6 centimetres** are added each year. With the growth spurt of adolescence, things then go faster for a while. In girls this growth usually begins and ends somewhat earlier than in boys. By about the age of 20 at the latest, most people have stopped growing taller.

Final **adult height** is largely **inherited**. That is why an approximate target height can be estimated from the height of the parents. A healthy diet, enough sleep and exercise also play a part. Growth stops when the **growth plates** in the bones close. After that, growing taller is no longer possible.

gewusst: More important than a single measurement is the overall course: a child usually grows along their own percentile line.
Girls and boys have their own growth charts, because they grow differently.

teile.einleitung: Viruses are tiny germs that cause illness and are much smaller than bacteria. They cause many well-known illnesses, for example colds, flu, chickenpox or Covid-19.
wichtigste: Viruses are so small that you can usually see them only with an electron microscope.
A virus can multiply only in the cells of a living thing.
The common cold is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses.
True flu is caused by the influenza virus.
Chickenpox is caused by the varicella zoster virus.
Flu viruses keep changing, which is why you can catch flu again and again.

abschnitte.text: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria. An ordinary light microscope is usually not enough to see them. You need an **electron microscope**, which magnifies much more strongly. A virus consists essentially of **genetic information** and a protective coat of protein. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and are therefore not counted as real living things.

A virus cannot multiply on its own. It gets into a **cell**, for example a cell of the lining of the nose. There it makes the cell produce many new viruses. These leave the cell and attack more cells. The body defends itself with its **immune system**, and this often causes fever, a runny nose or tiredness.

The **cold**, with a runny nose, sore throat and cough, is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. After about a week it is usually over. True **flu** is caused by the **influenza virus** and is often more serious. **Chickenpox** is caused by the varicella zoster virus, and typical are itchy blisters all over the body. Tooth decay, by contrast, is caused not by viruses but by bacteria in the mouth.

From the beginning of 2020 a new **coronavirus** spread all over the world. The illness that it causes is called **Covid-19**. Many countries, including Switzerland, took special protective measures at that time. These included keeping your distance, masks and, for a time, closed shops and schools. In a short time researchers developed vaccines against the illness.

Many viruses are passed on through small droplets when coughing and sneezing or through the hands. That is why thorough **handwashing** with soap helps. It is best to cough and sneeze into the crook of your arm. **Vaccinations** train the defences so that they recognise a virus more quickly. Flu viruses, however, keep changing a little, which is why the flu vaccine is adjusted every year.

gewusst: Antibiotics work against bacteria, but not against viruses.
There are also viruses that attack only bacteria. They are called bacteriophages.

teile.einleitung: **Aristarchus of Samos** was a Greek astronomer and mathematician. He lived in the **3rd century BC** and had a bold idea: the sun does not go around the Earth, but the Earth goes around the sun. With this he was almost 1,800 years ahead of his time.
wichtigste: Aristarchus came from the Greek island of Samos.
He lived in the 3rd century BC.
He suggested that the Earth goes around the sun.
He concluded that the sun is much larger than the Earth.
We know about his model of the world mainly through Archimedes.

abschnitte.text: Most scholars of ancient times thought that the Earth stood still at the centre of the world. Aristarchus, by contrast, suggested that the **Earth goes around the sun** and spins on its own axis as it does so. Such a picture of the world is called **heliocentric**, after the Greek word “helios” for sun. His writing about this idea is lost. We know about it mainly through the famous mathematician **Archimedes**, who mentioned it in one of his works.

A work of his on the **sizes and distances of the sun and moon** has survived. In it Aristarchus observed the moon at **half moon**. At that moment the Earth, moon and sun form a triangle with a right angle. He measured the angle between the moon and the sun and calculated from it that the sun is **about 20 times** further away than the moon. In reality it is around 400 times as far, but his method was right. The problem was that the angle could not be measured precisely enough at that time.

abschnitte.titel: How big are the sun and moon?
abschnitte.text: To estimate the size of the moon, Aristarchus used a **lunar eclipse**. During it the moon moves through the Earth's shadow, and from the size of the shadow you can work out the size of the moon. Because the sun is much further away than the moon but looks the same size in the sky, he came to an important conclusion: the **sun is much larger than the Earth**. Perhaps it was exactly this that gave him the idea of putting the sun in the middle.

Many scholars rejected the model. One important reason: if the Earth goes around the sun, the stars ought to **shift** slightly in the sky over the course of a year. But this shift could not be seen. It really does exist, but it is so tiny that it could only be measured in the 19th century. Only in the 16th century did **Nicolaus Copernicus** make the heliocentric picture of the world widely known.

gewusst: On the moon there is a bright crater named after Aristarchus.
The stars are so far away that their yearly shift was only measured in 1838.

teile.einleitung: Coeliac disease is an illness in which the body cannot tolerate the cereal protein gluten. Gluten then damages the lining of the small intestine. With a gluten-free diet you can still live well.
wichtigste: Coeliac disease is triggered by the protein gluten.
Gluten is found in wheat, spelt, rye and barley.
It is mainly the small intestine that is damaged.
Coeliac disease is considered an autoimmune disease.
The treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
About 1 in 100 people has coeliac disease.

abschnitte.text: **Gluten** is a protein found in many kinds of cereal. In German it is also called “Klebereiweiss”, sticky protein, because it makes dough elastic. Gluten is found in **wheat**, **spelt**, rye and barley. Spelt is closely related to wheat. **Rice**, **maize** and **millet**, on the other hand, are naturally gluten-free. **Buckwheat** also contains no gluten despite its name, because it is not wheat at all.

In coeliac disease the immune system reacts wrongly to gluten. The lining of the **small intestine** becomes inflamed. Normally it has many tiny projections, the **intestinal villi**, which take in nutrients. In coeliac disease they become flatter. Then the body cannot take in nutrients so well. Because the immune system also turns against the body's own tissue, coeliac disease is counted among the **autoimmune diseases** and not among the classic allergies.

The symptoms vary a great deal. Some people have stomach ache, diarrhoea or a bloated stomach. Others are often tired or grow more slowly as children. Some notice almost nothing. It is estimated that about **1 in 100 people** has coeliac disease. Many do not know it. A doctor can diagnose the illness with blood tests and an examination of the intestine.

There is no medicine that cures coeliac disease. The treatment is a **lifelong gluten-free diet**. Anyone who sticks to it strictly usually has no more symptoms, and the intestine recovers. **Potatoes**, rice, vegetables, meat and fruit are gluten-free. Spaghetti, couscous and bulgur, on the other hand, are made from wheat. When shopping, the symbol of the **crossed-out ear of grain** on gluten-free products helps.

gewusst: Even small breadcrumbs can irritate the intestine of people with coeliac disease, which is why special care is needed in the kitchen.
There is gluten-free bread and gluten-free pasta made from rice, maize or buckwheat.

teile.einleitung: Cytotoxic T cells are white blood cells and are part of the body's defence. They track down diseased body cells and kill them in a targeted way. That is why they are also called killer cells.
wichtigste: Cytotoxic T cells carry the co-receptor CD8.
They mainly kill cells infected with viruses and tumour cells.
With perforin they punch holes in the target cell.
Granzymes trigger self-destruction in the target cell.
When attacking, they form an immunological synapse.
Modern cancer medicines release the brake PD-1.

abschnitte.text: Every body cell shows small pieces of its proteins on its surface. For this it uses molecules called **MHC class I**. Cytotoxic T cells carry the co-receptor **CD8**, which binds to these molecules. That is why they are also called **CD8-positive T cells**. If a cell shows foreign pieces of protein, for example from a virus, the T cell recognises this. This is how it finds **cells infected with viruses** and **tumour cells**.

Once the T cell has found a diseased cell, it attaches itself closely to it. A limited contact zone forms, the **immunological synapse**. The T cell releases its sacs of poison precisely into this zone. This way healthy neighbouring cells are spared.

The protein **perforin** inserts itself into the membrane of the target cell and forms **pores**. Through these pores **granzymes** get inside. These are enzymes that split proteins. They activate the **caspases** in the cell and so start programmed cell death, **apoptosis**. The cell breaks itself down in an orderly way.

Cytotoxic T cells have another option too. On their surface sits the **Fas ligand**. It binds to the receptor **Fas** on the target cell, also called CD95. The signal sets off a chain of reactions there, at the end of which the cell dies. This way works without perforin.

T cells have built-in brakes, for example the molecule **PD-1**. Many tumours exploit this brake and switch the T cells off. Medicines such as **pembrolizumab** block PD-1 and release the brake again. They are called **checkpoint inhibitors**. In **CAR T-cell therapy** a patient's own T cells are given an artificial receptor in the laboratory. It is used mainly against certain **blood cancers** such as leukaemias and lymphomas.

gewusst: A single cytotoxic T cell can kill several diseased cells one after another.
The T in the name comes from the thymus, an organ behind the breastbone in which these cells mature.

teile.einleitung: **Ariane** is a family of European rockets. They mainly carry satellites into space and launch from Kourou in South America. Several versions have flown since 1979, and Switzerland also helps to build them.
wichtigste: Ariane rockets are built for the European Space Agency ESA.
They launch from Kourou in French Guiana.
The very first Ariane was launched in 1979.
The Ariane 5 flew from 1996 to 2023 and took the James Webb Telescope into space in 2021.
The Ariane 6 flew for the first time in 2024.
Specialists in Switzerland build the casing of the rocket's nose.

abschnitte.text: Europe wanted to be independent and to be able to put its own satellites into space without relying on the USA or Russia. That is why several countries developed the Ariane together for the **European Space Agency ESA**. **Switzerland** is also a member of ESA. The rocket is named after **Ariadne** from a Greek legend, who is called “Ariane” in French.

Ariane rockets launch from **Kourou** in **French Guiana**, which lies on the north coast of South America and belongs to France. The place is close to the **equator**. There the Earth spins particularly fast, and the rocket gets extra momentum at launch. It can also fly out over the open sea, which is safer.

The very first Ariane was launched in **1979**. After that larger and larger versions were built. The **Ariane 5** flew from **1996 to 2023** and was very reliable. In December **2021** it took the **James Webb Space Telescope** into space. Its successor, the **Ariane 6**, flew for the first time in **2024**. Ariane rockets mostly carry **satellites**, for example for television, weather or navigation.

Right at the top of the rocket sits a protective casing, the **payload fairing**. It protects the satellites from the air and heat during launch and is thrown off as soon as the rocket is high enough. This **casing of the nose** is built by specialists in Switzerland, in Emmen in the canton of Lucerne. So many Ariane launches also contain Swiss technology.

gewusst: Because Kourou is so close to the equator, a rocket from there can carry heavier loads into space than from further north.
The James Webb Telescope was launched on Christmas Day 2021.

teile.einleitung: Sugar tastes sweet and gives energy. But many foods contain more sugar than you might think. Too much of it harms above all the teeth.
wichtigste: Drinks such as **iced tea** and **cordial** contain a lot of sugar.
**Ketchup** also contains a lot of added sugar.
**Fruit juice** contains a lot of natural fruit sugar.
**Plain yoghurt** and unsweetened **oat flakes** contain little sugar.
Sticky **dried fruit** stays on the teeth for a long time.
The **little tooth man with an umbrella** marks sweets that are kind to teeth.
Sweet things do the least harm to the teeth straight after a meal.

abschnitte.text: Sugar is one of the **carbohydrates**. It gives the body **energy** quickly. In Switzerland household sugar is obtained mainly from **sugar beet**, and in other countries also from sugar cane. Fruit contains natural **fruit sugar**. The body needs energy, but too much sugar can harm the teeth and contribute to being overweight.

A lot of sugar is found where you would not immediately expect it. **Iced tea** tastes refreshing but contains a lot of sugar. **Cordial** consists to a large extent of sugar. **Ketchup** tastes not only of tomatoes but also sweet. **Orange juice**, even without anything added, contains a lot of fruit sugar and acid. Colourful breakfast cereals and fruit yoghurt are often heavily sweetened. A look at the list of ingredients helps.

**Plain yoghurt** has no added sugar. You can mix it yourself with fresh fruit. Unsweetened **oat flakes** have hardly any sugar. **Water** and unsweetened tea are best for quenching your thirst, because they contain no sugar at all.

Bacteria in plaque make **acid** from sugar. This attacks tooth enamel and can cause **tooth decay**. Sticky **dried fruit** such as raisins is particularly bad, because it stays stuck to the teeth for a long time. Frequent snacking throughout the day is also bad. If you eat sweet things all at once **straight after a meal**, your teeth then get a long break, and saliva can protect them.

The **little tooth man with the umbrella** comes from Switzerland. Sweets with this symbol are **kind to teeth**. They are usually sweetened with sugar substitutes that bacteria do not turn into acid. Today the symbol is also found in other countries.

gewusst: The World Health Organization recommends that added sugar should make up less than a tenth of daily energy.
Sugar beet also grows in many fields in the Swiss Plateau.

teile.einleitung: An **asteroid impact** happens when a chunk of rock from space hits a planet. Small chunks usually burn up in the air, but large ones can make huge craters. Luckily, large impacts on the Earth are very rare.
wichtigste: In an asteroid impact a chunk of rock from space hits a planet.
Small asteroids usually burn up in the air.
In 1908 an explosion at Tunguska in Siberia flattened huge forests.
Large impacts are very rare.
Researchers watch asteroids close to the Earth to spot dangerous chunks early.
In 2022 the space probe DART deliberately nudged an asteroid.

abschnitte.text: **Asteroids** are chunks of rock or metal that orbit the sun. Every day many tiny particles fall from space onto the Earth. Most of them **burn up** in the air, because they get very hot there due to their high speed. Then you see a **shooting star**. If a piece reaches the ground, it is called a **meteorite**. Large asteroids, on the other hand, hit the Earth **very rarely**.

On 30 June **1908** there was a huge explosion over **Tunguska** in **Siberia**. A chunk from space burst apart high in the air. The shock wave knocked down millions of trees over a huge area. Because the region was hardly inhabited, there were almost no victims. In memory of this, **30 June** is **International Asteroid Day** every year.

How strong an impact is depends on the size and speed of the chunk. A large asteroid can make a **crater** and fling a lot of dust into the air. If it hits the **sea**, it could set off a **huge wave**, a tsunami. About 66 million years ago a very large asteroid hit the Earth. It probably contributed to the dinosaurs dying out.

Experts all over the world search the sky with telescopes for asteroids that come close to the Earth. In this way they want to **spot dangerous chunks early** and calculate their orbit precisely. In **2022** NASA tested with the space probe **DART** whether an asteroid can be **deliberately nudged**. The probe crashed into the small asteroid Dimorphos and really did change its orbit. The asteroid was never a danger, and it was only a test.

gewusst: In 2013 a meteor exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk, and its flash of light was brighter than the sun.
You can see far more craters on the moon than on the Earth, because there is neither weather nor plants there to wear them away.

teile.einleitung: Wound healing is the name for the process by which the body repairs an injury to the skin. After a fall, a scab first forms on the wound so that it can heal. Underneath, the body works hard to build new tissue.
wichtigste: With an injury, the body first stops the bleeding.
A scab forms on the wound so that it can heal.
White blood cells fight germs that have got into the wound.
New tissue grows back under the scab.
Larger wounds often leave a scar.
You should not pick off a scab, because otherwise the wound takes longer.
Deep, heavily bleeding or dirty wounds need medical treatment.

abschnitte.text: When the skin is injured, the blood vessels contract immediately. **Blood platelets** stick together at the injured spot and close the hole. Then a net of the protein **fibrin** forms, in which blood cells get caught. This process is called **blood clotting** and usually takes only a few minutes. The scab then forms from the dried blood.

abschnitte.titel: The scab as a protective layer
abschnitte.text: The **scab** is a hard, brown crust on the wound. It acts like a natural plaster and keeps dirt and germs away. Underneath, the skin can grow back in peace. When the wound has healed, the scab falls off by itself. If you pick it off earlier, the wound opens up again.

In the first few days the wound is often a little red, warm and swollen. This is a normal **inflammation**, because the body sends many white blood cells to the spot. These defence cells eat up bacteria and dead cells. But if the redness keeps getting worse, the wound produces pus or you get a fever, you should see a doctor.

After a few days the body forms new tissue with a good blood supply. New **skin cells** grow over the wound from the edges until it is closed. With small grazes the injury usually disappears completely. With deeper wounds a **scar** remains, which is paler and less elastic than normal skin. It can take months until a scar has fully matured.

It is best to rinse a small graze with clean water. After that you can disinfect it and protect it with a **plaster**. On heavily bleeding wounds you press a clean cloth. The vaccination against **lockjaw**, also called tetanus, is also important, because this disease can get into wounds from soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard crust of dried blood that protects a wound.
The process in which the blood becomes solid and stops bleeding.
New, firmer tissue that remains after a deep wound.
A dangerous disease caused by bacteria from soil, against which you can be vaccinated.

gewusst: Wounds in the mouth heal particularly quickly, because there are many blood vessels there and saliva helps.
In children wounds usually heal faster than in older people.
A healing wound itches because new nerve fibres and skin cells are growing back.

teile.einleitung: Tartar is hard, calcified plaque. It forms when soft plaque stays on the teeth for too long, and it can no longer be removed with a toothbrush.
wichtigste: **Tartar** is hardened, calcified plaque.
The minerals for it come from **saliva**.
It forms particularly often on the inside of the lower front teeth.
Hard tartar is removed by a professional, often the **dental hygienist**.
An **ultrasonic device** is often used for this.
New plaque sticks particularly well to its rough surface.

abschnitte.text: A soft layer called **plaque** constantly forms on the teeth. It consists of bacteria and remains of food. If it stays there for longer, **calcium** and **phosphate** from saliva are deposited in it. The plaque hardens and becomes solid tartar. Thorough brushing stops it from getting that far.

Large **salivary glands** open under the tongue. There is a particularly large amount of saliva with minerals there. That is why a lot of tartar is often deposited on the **inside of the lower front teeth**. It is also often found on the upper back teeth facing the cheek.

Tartar itself does not make a hole in the tooth. But it is rough and **porous**. New plaque keeps settling on it, and this inflames the **gums**. Tartar below the gum line is usually darker and sticks very firmly. It can encourage **periodontitis**, an inflammation of the tissues that hold the teeth.

The porous surface easily takes up colouring. In people who smoke or drink a lot of tea or coffee, tartar therefore often becomes yellowish to brown. Tartar under the gums takes up blood pigments and looks dark.

You cannot brush off hard tartar yourself. In Switzerland it is often removed during regular professional cleaning by **dental hygienists**, both **women and men**. They use special instruments and often an **ultrasonic device**, whose fine tip vibrates very fast. The vibrations loosen the hard deposit without damaging the tooth.

gewusst: Dogs and cats can also get tartar. Vets then remove it too.
In the tartar of very old skeletons researchers find traces of what people used to eat.

teile.einleitung: BepiColombo is a space probe on its way to Mercury, the smallest planet and the one closest to the sun. The mission is a cooperation between Europe and Japan, and Switzerland is also taking part with an important measuring instrument.
wichtigste: BepiColombo is a joint mission of the European ESA and the Japanese JAXA.
The probe was launched on 20 October 2018 on an Ariane 5 from Kourou.
It consists of two orbiters and a transfer module with ion engines.
On the way it flies past planets nine times: once past the Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury.
The laser altimeter BELA was developed largely at the University of Bern.
According to plans (as of 2025), BepiColombo is to enter orbit around Mercury in November 2026.

abschnitte.text: BepiColombo consists of two probes that travel together. ESA built the **Mercury Planetary Orbiter**, which studies the surface and the interior of Mercury. JAXA supplied the **magnetospheric orbiter Mio**, which investigates the magnetic field and the surroundings of the planet. A third part, the transfer module, takes both to their destination. At Mercury the probes separate and work in their own orbits.

The mission honours the Italian mathematician **Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo**. He explained why Mercury turns exactly three times on its axis while it goes twice around the sun. This relationship is called a **3:2 resonance**. Colombo also suggested letting the American probe Mariner 10 fly past Mercury several times. This is how his name became linked with the exploration of Mercury.

The **Mercury Transfer Module** produces electricity with large solar panels. With it, **ion engines** accelerate electrically charged particles of the gas xenon. The thrust is very small, but it acts over months and years. From April 2024 the engines no longer delivered full power. ESA replanned the route, and the arrival was put back by eleven months from December 2025 to November 2026.

abschnitte.titel: Why the journey is so long
abschnitte.text: Anything flying towards the sun gets faster and faster, like a ball rolling down a slope. To be captured by little Mercury, a probe therefore has to **brake** very hard. That would need huge amounts of fuel. BepiColombo therefore uses **flybys**: every close flight past a planet changes the path and slows the probe down relative to the sun. There are nine such flybys altogether.

On board is the laser altimeter **BELA**. It sends laser pulses to the surface and measures how long the light takes to go there and back. From this the height of mountains, plains and craters can be calculated. BELA was built by the **University of Bern** together with the German Aerospace Center (DLR). In this way a precise map of Mercury's surface relief is being made.

gewusst: Mercury turns so slowly that a day there lasts longer than a Mercury year.
At Mercury the probe has to withstand great heat, because the sun shines much more strongly there than near the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The diaphragm is a flat, dome-shaped muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen. It is our most important breathing muscle and works day and night without us thinking about it. When it suddenly twitches, we get hiccups.
wichtigste: The diaphragm separates the chest from the abdomen.
It is the most important muscle for breathing.
When breathing in, it contracts and becomes flatter.
As a result the lungs expand and draw in air.
When breathing out, the diaphragm relaxes and curves upwards again.
Hiccups are caused by sudden twitches of the diaphragm.
Only mammals have a true diaphragm.

abschnitte.text: The **diaphragm** lies below the lungs and heart and above the liver, stomach and spleen. It has the shape of a **dome** curving upwards, rather like a parachute. At its edges it is attached to the lower ribs, the breastbone and the spine. The oesophagus, the main artery and a large vein pass through three larger openings. Its German name, “Zwerchfell”, comes from the old word “zwerch”, which means across.

When we breathe in, the diaphragm contracts and flattens. This makes the chest larger and the **lungs** expand. Low pressure develops, and air flows in through the nose or mouth. When we breathe out, the muscle relaxes, curves upwards again and pushes the air out. At rest adults breathe about 12 to 18 times a minute.

Because the diaphragm presses downwards when we breathe in, the belly bulges slightly forwards. This is called **belly breathing**. Singers and musicians who play wind instruments practise it on purpose so that they have plenty of air. Alphorn players also need good diaphragm breathing. Calm, deep breathing into the belly can help you to relax.

With **hiccups** the diaphragm suddenly contracts without you wanting it to. At the same time the vocal folds in the larynx close, which is why the typical “hic” sound is made. Triggers can be eating too fast, fizzy drinks or excitement. Hiccups usually stop by themselves after a few minutes. When laughing or coughing hard, the diaphragm also works hard.

The diaphragm is controlled by the **phrenic nerve**, which comes from the neck section of the spinal cord. Breathing happens automatically, and the breathing centre in the brainstem sets the rhythm. Even so, we can also influence our breathing consciously, for example when holding our breath under water. Many experts think that a stitch when running is also connected with the diaphragm, but this has not been fully explained.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dome-shaped muscle between the chest and the abdomen.
The space in the upper body in which the heart and lungs lie.
Breathing in which it is mainly the diaphragm that moves.
A sudden twitching of the diaphragm with a “hic” sound.

gewusst: With every deep breath the diaphragm moves up and down by several centimetres.
From 1922 an American had hiccups for around 68 years, which is considered a record.
The ancient Greeks believed the diaphragm was the seat of feelings and of reason.

teile.einleitung: Viruses are tiny germs that cause illness. They are much smaller than bacteria and become visible only under an electron microscope. They cannot multiply by themselves, only inside the cells of other living things. Viruses cause many well-known illnesses such as colds, flu and measles.
wichtigste: Viruses can multiply only in other cells, which is why they are not counted as independent living things.
They are usually much smaller than bacteria.
An ordinary cold is usually caused by viruses.
Flu, measles and chickenpox are also viral illnesses.
Antibiotics do not help against viruses, only against bacteria.
Vaccinations protect against many dangerous viral illnesses.
Washing your hands and sneezing into the crook of your arm slow down the spread.

abschnitte.text: At its core a **virus** consists of genetic information, that is DNA or RNA. It is surrounded by a coat of protein, and some viruses also have a coat of fat. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and cannot gain energy. That is why they can multiply only in other cells. For this reason they are usually not counted as independent **living things**.

Viruses are usually much smaller than bacteria, often only 20 to 300 nanometres in size. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. With an ordinary light microscope you therefore cannot see them, and only the **electron microscope** makes them visible. This first succeeded in the 1930s. There are, however, also giant viruses that are almost as big as small bacteria.

A virus attaches itself to a suitable **host cell** and slips its genetic information inside. The cell is thereby reprogrammed and now builds new viruses instead of its own building blocks. Often hundreds or thousands of new viruses arise this way. When they are released, the cell often dies. The new viruses attack more cells or other people.

The ordinary **cold** is usually set off by viruses, especially rhinoviruses. Other viral illnesses are flu, measles, mumps, chickenpox and Covid-19. Viruses also attack animals and plants, and there are even viruses that attack bacteria, the **bacteriophages**. **Antibiotics** work only against bacteria, so they do not help with flu. Against some viruses there are special medicines, which are called antiviral drugs.

The best protection is offered by **vaccinations**, which prepare the immune system for a particular germ. Thanks to vaccinations smallpox was wiped out worldwide by 1980. Many viruses are passed on through droplets when coughing and sneezing. Washing your hands regularly with soap, sneezing into the crook of your arm and airing rooms help to avoid infections. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health recommends vaccinations against measles, mumps and rubella, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cell that a virus attacks in order to multiply inside it.
A very powerful microscope with which you can make viruses visible.
Prevention that prepares the immune system for a germ.
A virus that attacks bacteria.

gewusst: The word virus comes from Latin and means poison or slime.
Parts of our own DNA come from ancient viruses that built themselves into the genetic material of our ancestors a very long time ago.
There are more than a hundred different rhinoviruses, which is why you can get a cold again and again.

teile.einleitung: Betelgeuse is a bright, reddish star in the constellation of Orion, which you can easily see with the naked eye in winter. It is one of the largest stars we know, and it is at the end of its life.
wichtigste: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in the constellation of Orion.
Its diameter is about 800 times that of the sun.
About half a billion suns would fit into its volume.
In the winter of 2019/2020 it became noticeably darker.
It will probably end its life as a supernova.
Afterwards a neutron star will probably be left.

abschnitte.text: Betelgeuse is a **red supergiant**: a huge, rather cool star that has almost used up its fuel. Because its surface is cooler than the sun's, it shines reddish. Its diameter is around **800 times** the diameter of the sun. If it stood where the sun is, it would reach far beyond the Earth's orbit. However, its diameter varies, because the star **pulsates**, that is it swells up and shrinks again.

About **half a billion suns** would fit into the volume of Betelgeuse. But its mass is only around twenty times that of the sun. This means that the outer layers are very thinly spread. A star with so much mass lives much less long than the sun, because it uses up its fuel faster.

In the winter of 2019/2020 astronomers noticed something strange: Betelgeuse became noticeably **darker**. Its brightness fell to less than half. Some wondered whether the explosion was about to happen. Today the main cause is thought to be a **cloud of dust** that the star had thrown out and that hid part of its light. After that it became brighter again.

Betelgeuse is so massive that in the end it will explode as a **supernova**. When this will happen nobody knows exactly, perhaps only in many thousands of years. Seen from the Earth, the explosion would be so bright that the star could be seen for weeks even in the **daytime sky**. It is not dangerous for us, because Betelgeuse is too far away. What will probably remain is a **neutron star**, an extremely dense remnant only around 20 kilometres across.

The name comes from **Arabic**. It goes back to an expression that means roughly “hand of the giantess”. When old writings were copied, there was a **reading mistake**, and this is how today's form of the name came about. Many bright stars have Arabic names, because scholars in the Arab world greatly developed astronomy in the Middle Ages.

gewusst: From Switzerland you can see Betelgeuse in winter at the top left of the constellation of Orion.
A neutron star is so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh hundreds of millions of tonnes on the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The **Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer**, AMS-02 for short, is a large measuring instrument on the International Space Station ISS. It catches particles of **cosmic radiation** and studies them. Researchers want to use it to solve mysteries about antimatter and dark matter.
wichtigste: AMS-02 has been in use on the International Space Station since 2011.
The space shuttle Endeavour took it into space in May 2011.
The project is led by the Nobel Prize winner Samuel Ting.
Among other things, the instrument searches for nuclei of antihelium.
It is operated from a control centre at CERN near Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Tiny, very fast particles are constantly raining down on the Earth from space. They are called **cosmic radiation**. The Earth's atmosphere slows many of them down. That is why they are best measured high up, outside the atmosphere. So AMS-02 sits on the outside of the **ISS**. A **magnet** deflects the particles, and measuring instruments determine which particles they are and how much energy they have.

abschnitte.titel: The journey to the space station
abschnitte.text: A smaller predecessor, AMS-01, flew in 1998 on a test flight with a space shuttle. The large **AMS-02** was taken to the ISS in **May 2011** with the space shuttle **Endeavour**. Originally a superconducting magnet was planned, which has to be cooled all the time. But in the end a **permanent magnet** was fitted so that the instrument could work much longer. The international project is led by the physicist **Samuel Ting**, who received the Nobel Prize in 1976.

abschnitte.titel: What the AMS is looking for
abschnitte.text: One important aim is the search for **antimatter**. This is a kind of mirror image of normal matter. If nuclei of **antihelium** were found, this would be a sign of antimatter somewhere in space. In its first results in **2013**, AMS-02 confirmed an **excess of high-energy positrons**, which are the antiparticles of electrons. Where they come from has not yet been explained. One possible explanation is **dark matter**, another is pulsars.

After a few years, pumps in the cooling system failed. The AMS had not really been built to be repaired in space. Even so, in several **spacewalks** in **2019 and 2020** a new cooling system was successfully fitted. They were led by the ESA astronaut **Luca Parmitano** from Italy. The AMS is controlled from a control centre at **CERN** near Geneva, where the data is also analysed.

gewusst: AMS-02 weighs several tonnes and has now counted billions of particles.
The repair of 2019 and 2020 is considered one of the most difficult jobs ever carried out outside the ISS.

teile.einleitung: The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine. It joins directly onto the stomach. Here the food pulp is mixed with important digestive juices.
wichtigste: The duodenum follows directly after the stomach.
It is around 25 to 30 centimetres long, about the width of twelve fingers.
Bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum.
The pancreatic juice neutralises the acid from the stomach.
The duodenum curves like a C around the head of the pancreas.
After it come the jejunum and the ileum.

abschnitte.text: The duodenum gets its name because it is about as long as twelve fingers laid side by side are wide. In German it is called “Zwölffingerdarm”, the “twelve-finger intestine”. That is around **25 to 30 centimetres**. It lies in the upper abdomen just behind the stomach. In a **C-shaped curve** it wraps around the head of the **pancreas**.

At the exit of the stomach there is a ring muscle, the **pylorus**. It keeps opening briefly. In this way the food pulp gets into the duodenum **a portion at a time**. This is important, because the intestine can only process small amounts well at once.

The **bile duct** and the duct of the pancreas open into the duodenum. They end together at a small bump in the wall of the intestine. **Bile** from the liver helps to digest fats. **Pancreatic juice** contains enzymes that split fats, proteins and carbohydrates. It also contains **hydrogen carbonate**, which neutralises stomach acid. Only then can the digestive enzymes work properly.

The food pulp from the stomach is very acidic. That is why there are special glands in the wall of the duodenum, **Brunner's glands**. They make an **alkaline mucus**, which protects the lining. Even so, the lining can sometimes be damaged. Then an **ulcer** develops, a kind of open wound in the lining.

A common cause of ulcers in the stomach and duodenum is the bacterium **Helicobacter pylori**. It can survive in the lining and damage it. For a long time people believed that stress in particular caused ulcers. Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed the part played by the bacterium and received the **Nobel Prize in 2005** for it. Today such ulcers can often be healed with medicines.

gewusst: The jejunum, which follows the duodenum, gets its name from the Latin for “empty”, because it was often found empty in people who had died.
For his research Barry Marshall drank a solution containing Helicobacter bacteria himself, to prove their effect.

teile.einleitung: NASA's **Apollo programme** took twelve people to the moon between 1969 and 1972. It was one of the largest technical projects in history. To this day it is the only one in which people have walked on the moon.
wichtigste: With the Apollo programme the USA wanted to take people to the moon.
The astronauts flew with the Saturn V rocket.
There were six crewed moon landings and twelve people on the moon.
At Christmas 1968 Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to orbit the moon.
In December 1972 Gene Cernan was the last person to leave the surface of the moon.
Only the command capsule returned to Earth with the crew.

abschnitte.text: In 1961 the American President **John F. Kennedy** set the goal of taking people to the moon and safely back during the 1960s. At that time the USA was in a race with the Soviet Union to conquer space. Hundreds of thousands of people worked on the programme. The astronauts flew with the **Saturn V**, a rocket over 100 metres tall.

In **1967** a terrible accident happened: during a test of the capsule **Apollo 1** on the ground, a **fire** broke out and the **three astronauts** died. After that the spacecraft was made safer. At Christmas **1968**, **Apollo 8** was the first crewed mission to orbit the moon. It was then that the famous photo **“Earthrise”** was taken, which shows the Earth above the moon's horizon.

**Apollo 11** was the first mission to land on the moon, in July 1969. After that came Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17, so **six landings** in all. Apollo 13 had to turn back because of a breakdown. On Apollo 15, 16 and 17 the astronauts drove an **electric moon car**, the Lunar Roving Vehicle. On **Apollo 17** in 1972, for the first and only time, a scientist went along: **Harrison Schmitt**, a geologist. In December 1972 **Gene Cernan** was the last person to leave the surface of the moon.

An Apollo spacecraft consisted of several parts. The **command capsule** was where the crew sat. Behind it was the **service module** with fuel, oxygen and power. The **lunar module** took two astronauts to the moon and back into orbit. In the end **only the command capsule** came back to the Earth, landing in the sea with parachutes.

gewusst: Altogether the Apollo astronauts brought several hundred kilograms of moon rock back to the Earth.
The moon cars from Apollo 15, 16 and 17 are still on the moon today.

teile.einleitung: Wholemeal bread is baked from flour for which the whole grain of cereal has been ground. That is why it is usually brown and contains more dietary fibre than white bread.
wichtigste: For wholemeal flour the whole grain is ground, with husk and germ.
In white flour the husk and germ are missing.
Wholemeal bread contains more dietary fibre, also called roughage.
Because the dark husk is ground with it, wholemeal bread is usually brown.
In Switzerland wheat is the most important bread cereal, and spelt is also popular.
At least half of the cereal products should be wholegrain.

abschnitte.text: A grain of cereal consists of three parts. On the outside lies the **husk**, inside the pale **endosperm**, and at one end sits the small **germ**. For **wholemeal flour** the whole grain with all its parts is ground. For **white flour** only the pale inside is ground, and husk and germ are removed. Because the dark husk stays in wholemeal flour, wholemeal bread is usually **brown**.

Wholemeal bread contains a lot of **dietary fibre**, also called **roughage**. It is good for digestion and keeps you full for a long time. In the husk and in the germ there are also many **vitamins** and **minerals**. In white flour a large part of these is lost. That is why wholemeal bread counts as an especially valuable food.

In Switzerland **wheat** is the most important bread cereal. From wheat flour people bake, for example, the plaited loaf “Zopf” and the bread roll “Weggli”. **Spelt**, an old kind of wheat, is also very popular. It has been grown in Switzerland for a long time and baked into bread. Wholemeal bread is made from wheat, spelt or rye.

In the **food pyramid** wholemeal bread belongs to the group of **cereal products**, together with potatoes and pulses. These foods supply the body with a lot of energy. The **Swiss nutrition recommendations** advise eating at least **half** of the cereal products as wholegrain. A wholemeal bread for breakfast is a good start for this.

gewusst: In “Ruchbrot”, a typical Swiss bread, more parts of the husk stay in the flour than in white flour. That is why it is darker.
The germ is the part of the grain from which a new cereal plant can grow.

teile.einleitung: The central nervous system is the control centre of your body. It consists of two parts, the brain and the spinal cord. Here sense impressions are processed, thoughts are formed and commands are sent to the muscles.
wichtigste: The central nervous system consists of the brain and the spinal cord.
It is often abbreviated to CNS.
The brain lies protected in the skull, and the spinal cord in the spinal canal.
The nerves in the rest of the body form the peripheral nervous system.
The human brain contains around 86 billion nerve cells.
Simple reflexes are switched directly in the spinal cord.
Injuries to the CNS heal badly, which is why protection, for example with a helmet, is important.

abschnitte.text: In adults the **brain** weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms. The cerebrum is responsible for thinking, speaking, remembering and conscious movement. The cerebellum takes care of balance and finely coordinated movements. The **brainstem** controls vital processes such as breathing and the heartbeat. Although it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight, the brain uses around a fifth of the energy.

The **spinal cord** is a bundle of nerve tissue as thick as a finger and in adults about 45 centimetres long. It runs in the spinal canal of the spine. Like a data motorway, it carries signals back and forth between the brain and the body. 31 pairs of spinal nerves branch off from the spinal cord. These lead to the arms, legs and trunk.

Some reactions happen without the brain. If you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand back in a flash. This **reflex** is switched directly in the spinal cord and so is particularly fast. Only afterwards does the brain notice that it hurts. Another well-known reflex is the knee-jerk reflex, which doctors test with a small hammer.

The CNS is very delicate and so has several layers of protection. On the outside are the bones of the **skull** and the spine. Underneath, three membranes wrap around the brain and spinal cord. Between them flows the cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions jolts like a water cushion. A cycle helmet or ski helmet gives extra protection in a fall.

Besides the CNS there is the **peripheral nervous system**. It consists of all the nerves that run from the brain and spinal cord into the body. Sensory nerves report, for example, warmth, pressure or pain to the CNS. Motor nerves carry the commands to the muscles. Together they make it possible for us to feel, think and act.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for central nervous system, that is the brain and spinal cord.
A cell that passes on electrical signals, also called a neuron.
A lightning-fast, unconscious reaction of the body.
All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.

gewusst: Signals can race along nerves at over 100 metres per second, faster than a car on the motorway.
The brain itself feels no pain, because it has no pain sensors.
The spinal cord is shorter than the spine and ends at about the level of the upper lumbar vertebrae.

teile.einleitung: Vitamins are substances vital for life that the body needs in small amounts but usually cannot make itself. That is why we have to take them in with food, especially with fruit and vegetables. If a vitamin is missing for a long time, you can become ill.
wichtigste: The body needs vitamins for growth, defence and many metabolic processes.
Fruit and vegetables are healthy because they supply vitamins that the body needs.
Humans need 13 different vitamins.
A distinction is made between water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins.
The skin can make vitamin D itself with the help of sunlight.
A lack of vitamins can cause illnesses such as scurvy.
With a varied diet you usually need no vitamin tablets.

abschnitte.text: **Vitamins** are substances that the body needs for many jobs, for example for fighting illnesses, healthy bones and good eyes. They supply no energy, but help to make use of nutrients. Humans need **13 vitamins**, which are named with letters, for example A, C, D, E and K. In addition there is a whole group of B vitamins. Even small amounts are enough, often only millionths of a gram a day.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are **fat-soluble**. The body can store them, and they are taken up better if you eat a little fat with them. That is why people like to add a little oil to carrots. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are **water-soluble**. The body usually gets rid of any surplus in the urine, so you need them regularly.

Vitamin C is found in peppers, kiwis, oranges and cabbage. Carrots contain a lot of **beta-carotene**, from which the body makes vitamin A, which is important for the eyes. Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and milk. Vitamin K is found in green leafy vegetables such as spinach. People who live on a **vegan** diet have to add vitamin B12.

**Vitamin D** is a special case, because the skin can make it itself with the help of sunlight. It helps the body to take in calcium for strong bones. In Switzerland the sun in winter is often too weak for this. That is why vitamin D drops are recommended, above all for babies. Oily fish such as salmon also supplies vitamin D.

In the past sailors on long voyages suffered from **scurvy**: the gums bled, and wounds did not heal. The Scottish doctor **James Lind** showed in 1747 that citrus fruits help, and today we know that vitamin C was missing. The name vitamin was coined in 1912 by the biochemist **Casimir Funk**. A lack of vitamin D leads in children to rickets, with soft, bent bones. Too much of a fat-soluble vitamin from tablets can, however, also do harm.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dissolves in fat and can be stored in the body.
Dissolves in water, and any surplus is got rid of.
An illness caused by a lack of vitamin C.
The orange pigment in carrots, from which the body makes vitamin A.

gewusst: Most animals can make vitamin C themselves, but humans, apes and guinea pigs cannot.
The word vitamin is made up of the Latin vita for life and the word amine.
A pepper often contains more vitamin C than an orange of the same weight.

teile.einleitung: The Chandrasekhar limit is the greatest mass a white dwarf can have. It is about 1.4 solar masses. If a white dwarf becomes heavier, it can no longer hold itself up against its own gravity.
wichtigste: A white dwarf is the burnt-out core of a star.
It is held up by the degeneracy pressure of the electrons.
The limiting mass is about 1.4 solar masses.
Chandrasekhar calculated it in 1930 on a ship journey to England.
Arthur Eddington publicly rejected the result in 1935.
In 1983, Chandrasekhar received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

abschnitte.text: When a star like the Sun has used up its fuel, a small, very dense remnant is left: a **white dwarf**. It mostly consists of **carbon and oxygen**, because the star had earlier fused helium into these elements. It was too light for any further fusion. In the white dwarf, no more nuclear fusion takes place. It is about as big as Earth, but has roughly as much mass as the Sun.

Without fusion, the heat that puffs a star up from inside is missing. Something else holds the white dwarf up: the **degeneracy pressure of the electrons**. According to the **Pauli principle**, electrons cannot move as close together as you like. They resist being squeezed together. Strangely, the **more mass** a white dwarf has, the **smaller** it becomes, because the stronger gravity packs the electrons more tightly.

At very high density, the electrons move at almost the **speed of light**. They are said to become **relativistic**. Then their pressure no longer grows fast enough to hold back gravity. Above about **1.4 solar masses**, the white dwarf therefore collapses. The exact value depends on how many nuclear particles, that is, **nucleons**, there are per electron. For carbon and oxygen it is 2.
