The young Indian student **Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar** travelled by ship from India to England in 1930 to study there. During the crossing he combined the **theory of relativity** with quantum physics and so found the upper limit for the mass of white dwarfs. In 1935 the famous astrophysicist **Arthur Eddington** sharply criticised the idea at a meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society. With time, however, Chandrasekhar's result won through.

In **1983**, Chandrasekhar received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for his work on the structure and evolution of stars. He shared the prize with **William Fowler**. Today the Chandrasekhar limit is important for understanding why some stellar remnants explode or turn into neutron stars.

gewusst: A spoonful of material from a white dwarf would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
An X-ray telescope of NASA was called “Chandra” in honour of the researcher.

teile.einleitung: Tooth enamel is the hard, shiny layer that protects your teeth from the outside. It is the hardest substance in the whole human body. But it has a weakness: once it is damaged, it does not grow back.
wichtigste: Tooth enamel protects the teeth from the outside.
It is the hardest substance in the human body.
Tooth enamel consists of about 95 per cent minerals.
It contains no living cells and so cannot repair itself.
Acids from bacteria and drinks attack tooth enamel.
Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant.
Tooth enamel is slightly translucent, and the yellowish colour comes from the dentine underneath.

abschnitte.text: **Tooth enamel** covers the crown of each tooth, that is the part you can see in the mouth. It consists almost entirely of the mineral **hydroxyapatite**, a compound containing calcium and phosphate. This makes it harder than bone. On the chewing surfaces of the back teeth it is up to about 2.5 millimetres thick. Without this armour the teeth would quickly wear down when chewing.

Tooth enamel is formed before a tooth comes through the jaw. Special cells, the **ameloblasts**, deposit minerals. When the tooth comes through, these cells die. That is why the body cannot make new tooth enamel later. So a hole in the enamel stays until a dentist fills it.

Bacteria in **plaque** turn sugar into acid, which dissolves minerals out of the enamel. This is how **tooth decay** begins. Acidic drinks such as lemonade, fruit juice or iced tea also attack the enamel directly. This is called dental erosion. That is why after acidic food you should wait about half an hour before brushing your teeth.

**Fluoride** from toothpaste and fluoridated table salt is built into the tooth enamel. This makes it more resistant to acid. **Saliva** also helps, because it washes away acid and brings minerals back to the surface of the tooth. Little sugar, thorough brushing and regular check-ups are the best protection.

Many animals also have teeth with enamel. In rodents such as beavers the enamel of the gnawing teeth is only present at the front and is often coloured orange, because it contains iron. Because the back wears away faster, the teeth always stay as sharp as a chisel. Elephants' tusks, on the other hand, consist almost entirely of dentine, which is ivory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard mineral made of calcium and phosphate, of which tooth enamel consists.
The wearing away of tooth enamel by acid, for example from drinks.
Cells that form tooth enamel while the tooth is still in the jaw.
A mineral that makes tooth enamel harder.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is so hard that researchers still find traces in it in fossils millions of years old.
Tooth enamel contains neither nerves nor blood vessels, which is why you often do not feel a small defect in it at all.
Beaver teeth are orange because their enamel contains iron.

teile.einleitung: Veins are blood vessels that bring the blood from the whole body back to the heart. You can even see some of them as bluish lines under the skin, for example at the wrist.
wichtigste: Veins carry the blood back to the heart.
Through the skin veins look bluish, but the blood in them is dark red.
Veins have a thinner wall than arteries, because there is little pressure in them.
In the veins of the legs, vein valves stop the blood from flowing back.
Working leg muscles press on the veins and push the blood upwards.
When blood is taken, it is usually taken from a vein in the crook of the arm.

abschnitte.titel: The way back to the heart
abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through the **arteries** into the whole body. In the organs the blood gives up oxygen and nutrients. After that the **veins** collect the blood again. Small veins flow together into ever larger ones. The largest veins, the **venae cavae**, finally open into the heart.

At the wrist or on the back of the hand you can see veins as **bluish** lines. The blood in them is not blue, however, but **dark red**. It has less oxygen than the bright red blood in the arteries. That the veins look blue is due to the skin: it lets red light through differently from blue. That is why you see a bluish shimmer from outside.

In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against gravity. The **vein valves** help with this. Like small doors they open in only one direction, namely towards the heart. When you walk or run, the **leg muscles** press on the veins. This pushes the blood upwards bit by bit.

In the veins the blood flows at low pressure. That is why their wall is **thinner** than the wall of the arteries. Veins, however, are stretchy and can hold a lot of blood. If you let your hand hang down, the blood flows back more slowly. The veins on the back of the hand then fill up and stand out clearly.

If a doctor needs a blood sample, she usually takes the blood from a vein in the **crook of the arm**. There the veins lie just under the skin. Beforehand a band is put around the upper arm, so that the vein fills well. Then she puts a fine needle in. In the laboratory you can measure, for example, sugar or iron in the blood.

gewusst: The largest part of the blood in the body is in the veins.
The pulmonary veins are an exception: they bring oxygen-rich, bright red blood from the lungs to the heart.

teile.einleitung: William Harvey was an English doctor. In 1628 he was the first to describe exactly how the heart pumps blood around the body in a circuit.
wichtigste: William Harvey came from England.
In 1628 his work “De motu cordis” on the circulation of the blood was published.
He disproved Galen's old teaching that the liver constantly makes new blood.
Using the valves in the veins, he showed that blood in the veins flows towards the heart.
He could not yet see the capillaries, and Marcello Malpighi managed this in 1661.
Harvey was personal physician to King James I and King Charles I.

abschnitte.titel: A doctor at the royal court
abschnitte.text: **William Harvey** lived from 1578 to 1657. He was an **English doctor** who worked in **London** after studying in Italy. He became **personal physician** to King **James I** and then to King **Charles I** of England. Alongside his work as a doctor, he did research on the heart and blood for many years. In 1628 he published his famous work **“De motu cordis”**, which means roughly “On the motion of the heart”.

For many centuries doctors followed the teaching of the ancient doctor **Galen**. He believed that the **liver** constantly made new blood from food. This blood was then used up in the organs. Harvey doubted this. He estimated how much blood the heart pumps out with each beat and multiplied it up. In a short time this gave far more blood than a person could take in with their food.

Harvey concluded from this: the blood is not used up but flows in a **circuit**. The **heart** pumps it through the arteries into the body, and it comes back through the veins. With experiments in which he blocked the blood flow in the arm, he showed how the **valves in the veins** work. They let blood through only in the direction of the heart. This made it clear which way the blood flows.

There was one question Harvey could not answer: how does the blood get from the arteries into the veins? He had to assume that there was an invisible path. Only with the **microscope** did the fine **capillaries** become visible, which are also called hair vessels. In 1661 the Italian **Marcello Malpighi** observed in a frog's lung how arteries and veins are connected. With that, Harvey's circulation was complete.

gewusst: Harvey proved the circulation of the blood without a microscope, just by observing and calculating.
The capillaries are so fine that the blood cells can only pass through them one at a time, one behind the other.

teile.einleitung: A calf compress is an old home remedy against high fever. Damp cloths are wrapped around the lower legs and gently cool the body.
wichtigste: Calf compresses are wrapped around the lower legs.
They can bring down a high fever a little.
The water should be lukewarm to cool, not ice-cold.
The wet cloth is wrung out well, and a dry cloth goes over it.
With cold feet or shivering, you do not use calf compresses.

abschnitte.titel: What a calf compress is for
abschnitte.text: With a **fever** the body temperature rises above its normal level. Fever helps the body to fight germs. But if it gets very high and unpleasant, a **calf compress** can help. It brings the fever down a little and gives relief. With a high or long-lasting fever, especially in small children, you ask a doctor.

You need **cloths** and a bowl of **water**. The water should be lukewarm to cool, that is a little cooler than the body. Ice-cold water would be too unpleasant. You dip a cloth in, **wring it out** and wrap it around the calf. It should be damp but not dripping wet. A **dry cloth** goes over it so that the bed stays dry.

The damp cloth takes up **heat** from the skin. The water also slowly **evaporates**. To evaporate, water needs heat, which it takes from the body. This cools the body down. After a few minutes the cloth gets warm, and then you take the compress off again or renew it.

Calf compresses are only suitable when the body feels warm. If someone has **cold feet** or is shivering, the body is trying to keep its heat. Then you should not cool it further. You also take the compress off if the sick person feels uncomfortable. With a fever, rest and drinking enough are important too.

gewusst: Calf compresses have been used as a home remedy in many families for generations.
The cooling effect is based on evaporation, in the same way that sweating cools us in summer.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin D is important for strong bones. The body makes it mainly itself in the skin when sunlight falls on it. In the Swiss winter the sun is often not enough for this, and a deficiency can arise.
wichtigste: The skin makes vitamin D with the help of UVB radiation.
In winter the sun in Switzerland stands too low, so hardly any UVB arrives.
Vitamin D3 is called cholecalciferol.
The liver makes calcidiol from it, and the kidney makes the active calcitriol.
Vitamin D encourages the uptake of calcium in the gut.
The vitamin D status is measured through the blood value 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Infants in Switzerland receive vitamin D drops from birth.

abschnitte.text: Unlike most vitamins, the body can make vitamin D itself. For this the skin needs **UVB radiation** from sunlight. In the skin it converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into a precursor of **vitamin D3**. Vitamin D3 is chemically called **cholecalciferol** and is also often used in supplements. Besides it there is vitamin D2, ergocalciferol from mushrooms.

abschnitte.titel: Why a deficiency threatens in winter
abschnitte.text: In winter the sun in Switzerland stands **low**. Its light then has a long way through the atmosphere. The **ozone layer** filters the UVB largely out. So in the winter months the skin hardly makes any vitamin D. People who are also outdoors little have a higher risk of **vitamin D deficiency**.

Vitamin D is converted in the body in two steps. First the **liver** makes **calcidiol** from it, which is the storage form in the blood. Then the **kidney** converts it into the active hormone form **calcitriol**. Calcitriol encourages the uptake of **calcium** in the gut. It increases the production of transport proteins that bring calcium into the blood, and the body needs calcium for firm bones.

To check the supply, you measure **25-hydroxyvitamin D** in the blood, that is calcidiol. It shows the supply over the last weeks. Good natural sources are rare, and one of them is **oily fish** such as herring, salmon or mackerel. That is why you take supplements when needed. The amount is given in micrograms or in **international units**: 1 microgram corresponds to 40 IU, so 20 micrograms to 800 IU.

In Switzerland **infants** routinely receive **vitamin D drops** from birth. Babies should not be in the blazing sun, and from food they get too little vitamin D. The daily dose protects their growing bones. In a severe deficiency in children the bones can become soft and deformed. This illness is called **rickets**.

gewusst: Rickets used to be widespread in industrial cities with a lot of smoke and little sun. It was also called the “English disease”.
Cod liver oil, an oil from the liver of cod, used to be given to children by the spoonful against vitamin D deficiency.

teile.einleitung: The crown is the part of the tooth that you can see in the mouth. It is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
wichtigste: The crown sticks out visibly from the gums.
It is covered with enamel.
Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
It consists mostly of the mineral hydroxyapatite.
The body cannot replace lost enamel.
Tooth decay easily develops in the fissures of the back teeth.

abschnitte.text: The **crown** is the part of the tooth that you can see in the mouth and that you chew with. The **root** and the tooth socket lie hidden in the jawbone. On the outside the crown is covered with a hard, shiny layer of **enamel**. It protects the more sensitive inside of the tooth. Underneath lies the **dentine**.

Enamel is the **hardest substance** in the human body. About **95 per cent** of it consists of minerals, mainly **hydroxyapatite**. This mineral contains calcium and phosphate. That is why enamel withstands chewing for decades. But the cells that build it die as soon as the tooth has come through. That is why the body **cannot replace** lost enamel.

**Back teeth** have a broad **chewing surface** with several **cusps**. With them, food is ground as if between two millstones. Between the cusps lie fine grooves, the **fissures**. Food remains and bacteria easily get stuck there. That is why **tooth decay** develops particularly easily in the fissures.

In **fissure sealing** the dentist fills the deep grooves with a runny **plastic**. This stops bacteria from settling there. If a tooth is badly damaged, it is capped with an artificial **crown**. It replaces the lost crown of the tooth. A **bridge**, on the other hand, spans a gap between teeth.

gewusst: Enamel is harder than any bone in the body.
A hole in the enamel never heals by itself, and it has to be filled by the dentist.

teile.einleitung: The large dinosaurs ruled the Earth for over 150 million years. About **66 million years ago** they suddenly died out. Most researchers agree: a large **asteroid** hit the Earth.
wichtigste: The large dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.
Most researchers think that a large asteroid hit the Earth.
The asteroid was about 10 kilometres across.
The impact crater lies in Mexico.
About three quarters of the animal species of that time died out.
Birds are descended from dinosaurs.

abschnitte.text: About **66 million years ago** an asteroid about **10 kilometres** across hit the Earth. It struck the Yucatán Peninsula in what is now **Mexico**. A huge crater formed there, the **Chicxulub crater**. Today it is hidden under rock and sea. The impact caused fires, earthquakes and enormous tidal waves.

The impact flung huge amounts of **dust** and **soot** into the air. They spread around the whole Earth and **darkened** the sky for a long time. It became colder, and many plants got too little light. As a result many animals had no food. About **three quarters** of the animal species of that time died out. Some researchers think that large volcanic eruptions in India at the same time also played a part.

In 1980 researchers led by Luis and Walter Alvarez discovered a lot of **iridium** in rock layers from this time. This metal is rare on the Earth's surface but more common in asteroids. The layer is found in many places in the world. Later the matching crater was found in Mexico. Today most experts consider the asteroid impact the most important cause of the extinction.

Not all animals died out. **Small mammals** survived and afterwards became more and more common and varied. Much later humans also developed from them. One group of dinosaurs also survived: the ancestors of **birds**. That is why researchers say that birds are descended from dinosaurs. So every blackbird is a distant relative of Tyrannosaurus.

gewusst: The Chicxulub crater is around 180 kilometres wide.
Dinosaurs have also been found in Switzerland: in Frick in the canton of Aargau many skeletons of Plateosaurus have been dug up.

teile.einleitung: A vibration is a quick trembling to and fro. We feel it with the skin, for example when the phone buzzes in a trouser pocket or a heavy lorry drives past.
wichtigste: A vibration is a quick oscillation, that is, a trembling to and fro.
In a phone a small motor produces the vibration.
When you hum, the vocal cords in the larynx oscillate.
A seismograph measures the shaking of earthquakes.
Deaf people can feel music through vibrations.
Spiders notice from the trembling of the web that an insect is caught.

abschnitte.text: In a **vibration** something moves very quickly to and fro. This is also called an **oscillation**. How often something oscillates per second is measured in **hertz**. In the skin there are special **touch corpuscles** that sense such fine shaking. That is why we feel vibrations even when we hear nothing.

In a phone a small **motor** turns very fast. It makes the device tremble, and you feel it on your skin. It is similar with the **electric toothbrush**: a motor moves the brush head very fast. When a heavy lorry drives close by, it even makes the **ground** oscillate. You feel this vibration with your feet.

Every note arises from an oscillation. If you pluck a **guitar string**, it swings to and fro and produces the note. With your fingers you feel a fine trembling. When you hum, the **vocal cords** in the larynx also oscillate. If you put your hand to your throat, you can feel it. Loud music makes the ground and the air oscillate, which is why **deaf** people can feel the bass with their whole body.

Many animals use vibrations to sense their surroundings. A **spider** often sits at the edge of its web. If a trapped insect struggles, it makes the threads oscillate. The spider feels this with its legs and knows at once where the prey is. Fish, too, feel fine movements in the water with their lateral line organ.

In an **earthquake** the ground shakes. A **seismograph** records even the smallest ground movements. In Switzerland the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures with many stations across the whole country. Most earthquakes in Switzerland are so weak that you do not feel them. The instruments register them all the same.

gewusst: Strong vibrations from tools such as pneumatic drills can in the long run strain hands and joints. That is why there are protective rules at work.
Elephants can sense through the ground vibrations that come from other elephants far away.

teile.einleitung: Cones are sensory cells in the retina of the eye. With them we see colours and sharp details in bright light.
wichtigste: **Cones** are light-sensitive cells in the **retina**.
They are responsible for **colour vision** in bright light.
People with normal colour vision have **three kinds of cone**.
A retina has around 6 million cones, far fewer than rods.
The cones are most densely packed in the **fovea**.
Colour vision is tested with the **Ishihara test**.

abschnitte.text: In the retina there are two kinds of light-sensing cells. The **rods** are very sensitive and help us to see at dusk, but they do not recognise colours. The **cones** need a lot of light. In return they tell colours apart and give a sharp picture. A retina contains about **6 million cones**, but well over 100 million rods.

There are cones for **short-wave**, **medium-wave** and **long-wave** light. Roughly speaking, they can be called blue, green and red cones. Each colour stimulates the three kinds to different degrees. From their signals the brain mixes all the colours we see. That is why a screen can show a great many colours with three basic colours.

In the middle of the retina lies the **fovea**. There are almost only densely packed cones there. This is where we see most sharply, for example when reading. At the edge of the retina there are far fewer cones. That is why colours at the edge of your field of vision are harder to recognise.

In some people one kind of cone works differently. The most common form is **red-green colour blindness**. The tendency for it lies on the **X chromosome**. Men have only one X chromosome, which is why they are affected more often. The **Ishihara test** finds this out: plates by the Japanese eye doctor Shinobu Ishihara show numbers made of coloured dots.

Dogs have only **two kinds of cone**. They see blue and yellow well, but hardly red and green. Many birds have **four kinds of cone**, one of them for ultraviolet light. Such creatures are called **tetrachromats**, because “tetra” means four in Greek.

gewusst: Birds can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to humans.
At dusk almost only the rods are working. That is why colours look pale in the evening.

teile.einleitung: Atrial fibrillation is a heart rhythm disorder in which the atria of the heart twitch chaotically instead of contracting in an orderly way. It is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder and affects mainly older people.
wichtigste: In atrial fibrillation the atria are excited in a disorderly way about 350 to 600 times a minute.
In the ECG the P waves are missing, and the intervals between the heartbeats are irregular.
The most dangerous result is a stroke caused by a blood clot.
The CHA2DS2-VASc score helps to estimate the risk of stroke.
An electrical cardioversion can restore the normal rhythm.
In catheter ablation the openings of the pulmonary veins are electrically isolated.

abschnitte.text: Normally the **sinus node** sets the rhythm of the heart. In **atrial fibrillation**, by contrast, many excitations circle through the atria in a disorderly way. They are excited about **350 to 600 times per minute**. An orderly contraction is then no longer possible, and the atria only twitch. The ventricles beat completely irregularly in the process, which is called **absolute arrhythmia**.

With an **ECG**, atrial fibrillation can be recognised well. Because the atria are not excited in an orderly way, the **P waves** are missing. The intervals between the ventricular beats, the **RR intervals**, are irregular. Many of those affected feel their heart skipping, racing or shortness of breath. Others notice nothing at all, and the fibrillation is found by chance.

In the fibrillating atria the blood flows slowly. Above all in the left **atrial appendage** it can clot. If such a **clot** comes loose, it can travel with the bloodstream to the brain and block an artery there. This leads to a **stroke**. To estimate the risk, the **CHA2DS2-VASc score** is used. It counts risk factors such as age, high blood pressure, diabetes and earlier strokes, and the higher it is, the more likely it is that blood thinning is needed.

In **electrical cardioversion**, under a short anaesthetic, an electric shock timed to the ECG is delivered. In it all the heart muscle cells are excited at the same time, and afterwards the sinus node often takes over again. Disturbing sources of excitation often sit at the **openings of the pulmonary veins**. In **pulmonary vein isolation**, a form of catheter ablation, these places are electrically cut off from the atrium by scarring. Medicines can also regulate the rhythm or the heart rate.

Atrial fibrillation is distinguished by its duration. **Paroxysmal** atrial fibrillation occurs in attacks and stops again by itself. It usually ends within 48 hours, at the latest after 7 days. If it lasts longer, it is called **persistent** atrial fibrillation. The risk of atrial fibrillation rises clearly with **age**.

gewusst: Many smartwatches can now detect an irregular pulse and so give a hint of atrial fibrillation.
The word “paroxysmal” comes from Greek and means “in attacks”.

teile.einleitung: With a brace, crooked teeth and a faulty bite are slowly corrected. Many children and teenagers in Switzerland wear one for a while.
wichtigste: The specialist field is called **orthodontics**.
In a fixed brace an **arch wire** connects the brackets.
A **removable brace** can be taken out by the wearer.
**Aligners** are transparent plastic trays.
Teeth move because the jawbone is broken down on the pressure side and built up on the tension side.
A **retainer** holds the teeth in place after treatment.
With a fixed brace, thorough brushing is particularly important.

abschnitte.text: **Orthodontics** is a specialist field of dentistry. It treats crooked teeth, gaps and faulty bites, in which the upper and lower teeth do not fit together properly. The specialists are called orthodontists. Treatment often begins at school age, while the jaws and teeth are still growing.

With a fixed brace, small plates called **brackets** are glued onto the teeth. A springy **arch wire** runs through all the brackets. It applies gentle pressure and slowly moves the teeth into the desired position. At regular intervals the wire is checked and adjusted.

A **removable brace** consists of a plastic plate with wires. You take it out for eating and brushing. But it only works if you wear it for long enough. **Aligners** are almost invisible plastic trays. They are replaced by new ones every few weeks, and each one moves the teeth a little further.

Teeth do not sit rigidly in the jaw. If you keep pressing lightly on a tooth, the **bone on the pressure side** is broken down. On the other side, the **tension side**, new bone forms. In this way the tooth moves very slowly through the jaw. That is why treatment often takes one to several years.

Food remains and plaque easily get stuck around brackets and wire. Without thorough brushing there is a risk of white **decay spots** and gum inflammation. After treatment the teeth often want to go back to their old position. A **retainer**, for example a thin wire behind the teeth or a tray, prevents this.

gewusst: Without a retainer, teeth can shift again even years after treatment.
The word bracket comes from English and means a support or holder.

teile.einleitung: The cytoskeleton is the inner framework of a cell. It gives the cell shape and support and helps with transporting substances and with movement. Unlike our bony skeleton, it is constantly being built up and broken down.
wichtigste: The cytoskeleton consists of microtubules, actin filaments and intermediate filaments.
Microtubules are hollow tubes made of the protein tubulin.
At about 25 nanometres, microtubules have the largest diameter.
The motor protein kinesin carries small sacs along the microtubules.
Keratin forms the intermediate filaments in skin cells.
In animal cells most microtubules start from the centrosome.

abschnitte.text: The cytoskeleton of animal cells consists of three kinds of fibre. **Microtubules** are about 25 nanometres thick, **intermediate filaments** about 10 nanometres and **actin filaments**, also called microfilaments, about 7 nanometres. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Each kind of fibre has its own tasks, and together they form a movable network throughout the whole cell.

Microtubules are **hollow tubes** made of the protein **tubulin**. They consist of pairs of alpha and beta tubulin. In animal cells most microtubules start from the **centrosome**, which contains two centrioles. Microtubules can grow quickly and then suddenly fall apart again. This switching is called **dynamic instability**. It allows the cell to rebuild its framework quickly, for example during cell division.

**Motor proteins** run along the microtubules as if on rails. **Kinesin** carries small sacs, called vesicles, usually towards the edge of the cell. **Dynein** runs in the opposite direction. Both use up energy in the form of **ATP** as they do so.

Intermediate filaments make cells tear-resistant. In skin cells they consist of **keratin**. Keratin also makes hair and nails tough. **Actin filaments** often lie just under the cell membrane. They help the cell to change its shape and to move. In muscle cells they work together with the protein myosin.

Some cells have fine hairs called **cilia**, or longer **flagella**. In cross-section they show a typical pattern: nine double tubes around two single microtubules in the middle. This is written as **9 × 2 + 2**. Dynein makes the double tubes slide against each other, and so the hairs beat. Cilia in the airways, for example, move mucus and dust upwards.

gewusst: Without a cytoskeleton many cells would simply collapse like a tent without poles.
Kinesin moves forward with small steps, a process that can be watched under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: Crying is a natural reaction of the body. We cry when we are sad or in pain, but also out of great joy.
wichtigste: Crying is normal for all people, whether children or adults.
Babies cry to show that something is wrong.
Great joy can also bring tears of joy.
When cutting onions, a substance irritates the eyes.
When crying hard, you breathe in bursts, and this is called sobbing.
“Crocodile tears” are false tears.

abschnitte.text: Tears are made in the **tear glands** above the eyes. A little tear fluid flows all the time and keeps the eye moist. When we cry, the glands make much more of it. Part of it flows through small channels into the **nose**. That is why your nose often runs too when you cry. After crying for a long time, the eyes are often **red and swollen**.

We cry when we are sad, in pain or disappointed. Very hard crying is called crying **bitterly**. You often breathe in bursts, and this is called **sobbing**. Great joy can also make you cry, for example when you see someone again: these are **tears of joy**. Crying is normal for **all people**, for girls and boys, children and adults.

**Babies** cannot talk yet. By crying they show that something is wrong. They cry when they are hungry, tired, cold or in pain. Over time parents learn to understand their baby's crying. So crying is also a way of communicating.

When **cutting onions**, a substance escapes from the onion into the air. It irritates the eyes, and they wash it away with tears. This has nothing to do with sadness. The saying **“to cry crocodile tears”** means that someone is only pretending to be sad. So they are false tears.

gewusst: Many people feel relieved and calmer after crying.
Tears contain salt, which is why they taste slightly salty.

teile.einleitung: Dental floss is a very thin thread used to clean the gaps between the teeth. The toothbrush hardly reaches there.
wichtigste: **Dental floss** cleans the gaps between the teeth.
It looks like a very thin thread.
It removes food remains and plaque from between the teeth.
Experts recommend cleaning the gaps **once a day**.
You guide it carefully back and forth between the teeth.
For larger gaps there are **interdental brushes**.

abschnitte.text: The toothbrush cleans the outer, inner and chewing surfaces. But something often stays stuck between the teeth. **Food remains** and **plaque**, in which bacteria live, collect there. Tooth decay can develop from this plaque, and the gums can become inflamed. With dental floss you get the remains out.

You take a piece of dental floss and wind the ends around your fingers. Then you guide the thread between two teeth with gentle **back-and-forth movements**. You place it against the side of the tooth and move it carefully up and down. This way the gums are not injured. For each gap you use a clean piece.

A **floss holder** is a small plastic frame in which the thread is stretched. With it, children can also use dental floss more easily. For larger gaps **interdental brushes** are suitable. They look like tiny bottle brushes and clean there about as well as dental floss. At the dentist's or the dental hygienist's you can be shown what suits you best.

The first time, the gums sometimes bleed slightly. This usually means that they are already a little **inflamed** there, because they have not been cleaned for a long time. With regular care the bleeding usually stops after a few days. If it bleeds for longer, you should ask at the dentist's.
A good time is **in the evening** when you brush your teeth. Then you take time for thorough care. This way no remains stay between the teeth overnight.

gewusst: Dental floss is mostly made of plastic today, but in the past it really was made of silk. That is where its German name “Zahnseide”, meaning “tooth silk”, comes from.
The gaps make up a large part of the tooth surface, which the brush does not reach well.

teile.einleitung: The hyoid bone is a small, curved bone at the front of the neck. It is special because it is not connected to any other bone by a joint.
wichtigste: The **hyoid bone** lies in the neck between the lower jaw and the larynx.
It has **no joint** with other bones.
It is **horseshoe-shaped** like a U.
It consists of a body and two **greater and two lesser horns**.
The **tongue** is attached to it by muscles.
It is important for **swallowing and speaking**.
In Latin it is called **os hyoideum**.

abschnitte.text: The hyoid bone lies at the front of the **neck**, between the **lower jaw** and the **larynx**. You can carefully feel it just above the Adam's apple. The technical term is **os hyoideum**. The Greek word recalls the shape of the letter upsilon, because the bone is U-shaped.

Almost all bones are connected to other bones by **joints**. The hyoid bone is not. It is held in place only by **muscles** and **ligaments** and so in a way hangs freely in the neck. This makes it the only human bone without a jointed connection to another bone.

The hyoid bone is curved like a **horseshoe**. At the front lies the **body**. Two **greater horns** and two **lesser horns** stick out backwards and upwards. Muscles and ligaments are attached to them. Its German name, “Zungenbein”, meaning “tongue bone”, comes from the fact that the **tongue** is anchored to this bone by its muscles.

Muscles of the **tongue**, the **floor of the mouth** and the **larynx** are attached to the hyoid bone. They work together when the mouth and throat move. When **swallowing**, muscles pull the hyoid bone and larynx upwards and forwards. This covers the windpipe so that no food gets into it. If you put your fingers on the front of your neck while swallowing, you can feel this movement. The hyoid bone also plays a part in **speaking**.

gewusst: The hyoid bone is one of the bones you can hardly see from outside, even though it lies directly under the skin of the neck.
Many mammals also have a hyoid bone, and in some it is made up of several parts.

teile.einleitung: The cell cycle is the sequence a cell goes through from one division to the next. It is strictly controlled so that cells divide only when everything is in order.
wichtigste: The cell cycle consists of **interphase** and **mitosis**.
Interphase includes the **G1, S and G2 phases**.
In the **S phase** the DNA is doubled.
Cells that no longer divide are in the **G0 phase**.
**Cyclins** and kinases control the sequence.
**p53** is called the “guardian of the genome”.
In many cells the **telomeres** get shorter with every division.

abschnitte.text: **Interphase** makes up most of the cycle. It usually lasts many hours. In the **G1 phase** the cell grows. In the **S phase**, the synthesis phase, all the DNA is doubled. In the **G2 phase** the cell prepares for division. The actual **mitosis** often takes only about an hour.

Many specialised cells, such as **nerve cells**, leave the cycle. They are then in the **G0 phase**. There they no longer divide, but they remain metabolically active and carry out their task. Some cells, for example liver cells, can re-enter the cycle when needed.

The sequence is controlled by proteins called **cyclins**. Their amount rises and falls during the cycle. They bind to **kinases** (CDK) and so allow the move into the next phase. At **checkpoints** the cell checks whether everything is right. The protein **p53** is called the “guardian of the genome”: if there is DNA damage, it stops the cycle until it is repaired, or it triggers programmed cell death. For discovering this control, Leland Hartwell, Tim Hunt and Paul Nurse received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2001.

**Tumour suppressor genes** slow down cell division or promote the repair of DNA. They act like brakes. If both copies of such a gene fail, the brake is missing and cells can divide uncontrollably. The gene for p53 is altered in many tumours.

In 1961 **Leonard Hayflick** showed that normal human cells in cell culture divide only about **40 to 60 times**. After that they stop. This limit is called the **Hayflick limit**. One reason is the **telomeres**, the protective caps at the ends of the chromosomes. In many body cells they get shorter with every division if the enzyme **telomerase** is missing.

gewusst: In 2009 the Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for discovering how telomeres and telomerase protect the chromosomes.
Cancer cells often switch on telomerase and so can divide far more often.

teile.einleitung: Anger is a strong feeling that everyone knows. It shows that something bothers us or seems unfair, and you can learn to deal with it well.
wichtigste: When you are angry, your muscles tense up.
Many people then clench their fists and grit their teeth.
Angry people often speak loudly.
Animals also show anger: dogs growl and cats hiss.
Exercise and a break help you to calm down again.
The German saying “Mir platzt der Kragen” means: I am getting very angry.

abschnitte.titel: What anger does in the body
abschnitte.text: When you feel **anger**, the body gets ready to act. The heart beats faster and the **muscles** tense up. Often the hands close into **fists**. The jaw muscles also become hard, which is why you **grit your teeth**. The voice often becomes **louder** and sharper.

Animals can also become angry or make threats. A **dog** growls and so gives a warning: don't come too close! A **cat** hisses loudly and shows its teeth. Often it also arches its back and fluffs up its fur. This makes it look bigger and more dangerous.

Anger is a normal feeling. The important thing is not to harm anyone. **Exercise** helps to release the tension in the body, for example **running** outside. After an argument a **break** often helps. It gives the body time to calm down. Afterwards you can calmly say what bothered you.

Language has many expressions for anger. Someone who says in German **“Mir platzt der Kragen”**, literally “my collar is bursting”, can no longer hold back their anger. People also say someone **“hits the roof”** or **“sees red”**. Such images show how strong anger can feel. Talking about feelings helps others to understand us.

gewusst: Breathing deeply and slowly can help to calm the body when you are angry.
Anger can also be useful: it shows us that something is not right for us.

teile.einleitung: CHEOPS is a space telescope that measures planets around other stars precisely. It is a mission of ESA in which Switzerland and the University of Bern play the leading role.
wichtigste: CHEOPS is an ESA mission, scientifically led by the University of Bern.
The telescope launched in December 2019 on a Soyuz rocket.
It studies known exoplanets and determines their size.
To do so it uses the transit method: the star briefly becomes slightly dimmer.
CHEOPS orbits at a height of about 700 km, passing over the poles.
On board are 2,748 reduced children's drawings on two titanium plates.

abschnitte.text: **CHEOPS** is a mission of the European Space Agency **ESA**. Switzerland is its most important partner. The **University of Bern** leads a consortium from eleven countries and is responsible for the science. The telescope was built in Switzerland and in other European countries. On 18 December 2019, CHEOPS launched on a **Soyuz rocket** from the European spaceport in French Guiana.

CHEOPS does not search for new planets, but measures **known exoplanets** very precisely. Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars other than the Sun. When such a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a little light, and the star becomes **slightly dimmer** for a short time. This method is called the **transit method**. The bigger the planet, the more light disappears. That is how its size can be calculated.

abschnitte.titel: A planet like a rugby ball
abschnitte.text: One well-known measurement concerns the planet **WASP-103b**. It orbits very close to its star. The star's strong **tidal forces** stretch it out lengthwise. According to the CHEOPS measurements, it is therefore not round, but shaped like a **rugby ball**. In 2023, CHEOPS also helped to detect a **ring** around the dwarf planet **Quaoar** at the edge of the Solar System, a ring that lies surprisingly far out.

CHEOPS flies around Earth at a height of about **700 km**, passing over the **poles**. The orbit is chosen so that the Sun is always at roughly the same angle to the satellite. This matters for very precise brightness measurements, because the conditions then hardly change. The telescope always looks away from the Sun, so that no sunlight disturbs it.

Children were able to submit drawings for CHEOPS. **2,748** of them were drawn by lot, greatly reduced in size and engraved on two **titanium plates**. These plates now fly with the satellite around Earth. In this way, many young people have become a small part of this space mission.

gewusst: CHEOPS stands for “CHaracterising ExOPlanet Satellite”.
Bern has a long tradition in space travel: even on the first Moon landing in 1969, the astronauts set up a solar wind sail from the University of Bern.

teile.einleitung: The human body is a fascinating system of trillions of cells, many organs and countless processes that work together perfectly. The heart pumps blood, the lungs take in oxygen and the brain controls everything. In this chapter you will learn how your body is built and how to keep it healthy.
wichtigste: The body consists of many trillions of cells.
In a human cell the genetic information DNA is stored mainly in the nucleus.
The heart pumps blood through the whole body.
An adult human has about 206 bones and over 600 muscles.
The skin is the largest human organ.
Several organs work together in organ systems, for example in digestion or breathing.
A healthy diet, exercise and sleep keep the body fit.

abschnitte.text: The body is built from tiny **cells**, which can only be seen under the microscope. In every **cell nucleus** the genetic information DNA is stored, a kind of blueprint for the whole person. Cells of the same kind together form a tissue, for example muscle tissue. Organs such as the heart, stomach or liver are made from different tissues. Several organs together form an organ system.

The **heart** is a hollow muscle the size of a fist in the chest. It pumps blood through a huge network of blood vessels to all the cells. In adults at rest it beats about 60 to 80 times a minute, which is around 100,000 beats a day. An adult has about 5 litres of blood. The blood brings oxygen and nutrients and takes waste away.

When we breathe in, the **lungs** take in oxygen, and when we breathe out they give off carbon dioxide. Breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm. In the **digestive system** food is broken up and broken down in the mouth, stomach and intestines. The nutrients get into the blood, and the rest is passed out of the body. The liver and kidneys clean poisons out of the blood.

The **skeleton** gives the body support and protects organs such as the brain, heart and lungs. An adult has about 206 bones, and a newborn baby even more, because some grow together later. Muscles move the bones at the joints. The largest muscle is the gluteus maximus in the buttocks, and the smallest sit in the ear.

The **brain** and the spinal cord form the central nervous system, the body's control centre. Through nerves it receives messages from the sense organs. With our eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin we see, hear, smell, taste and touch. Hormones act as messenger substances in the blood and control, for example, growth.

The body needs a balanced diet with vegetables, fruit, wholegrain foods and protein. Enough water, exercise in the fresh air and enough sleep are just as important. The **immune system** protects us from germs, and vaccinations help it. Looking after your teeth and washing your hands are also part of everyday health care.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body with a particular task, for example the heart.
The control centre of the cell, in which the DNA lies.
Genetic information, a kind of blueprint for the body.
Several organs that carry out a task together.
The body's defence system against germs.

gewusst: If all the blood vessels of an adult were laid end to end, they would be more than twice as long as the distance around the Earth.
The smallest human bone is the stirrup in the ear, and it is only about 3 millimetres long.
An adult's skin covers about 1.5 to 2 square metres.

teile.einleitung: The tooth fairy is a fairy-tale figure. When a milk tooth falls out, she fetches it during the night and leaves a little surprise behind.
wichtigste: The tooth fairy is a made-up figure from stories.
Children put their milk tooth under their pillow.
The tooth fairy comes during the night while the child is asleep.
She takes the tooth away and often leaves a coin behind.
In France and French-speaking Switzerland a little mouse brings the present.

abschnitte.text: The **tooth fairy** is a **fairy-tale figure**. Children look forward to her visit when a **milk tooth** falls out. This happens from about the age of six, when the permanent teeth grow in. The story of the tooth fairy makes saying goodbye to the tooth easier. Many families tell it to their children.

In the evening the child puts the milk tooth **under their pillow**. During the **night**, while the child is asleep, the tooth fairy comes. That is why nobody sees her. She collects the tooth. In return she leaves a **coin** or a small present behind.

It is not a fairy everywhere. In **France** and in **French-speaking Switzerland**, “la petite souris”, the **little mouse**, fetches the tooth. In **Spain** people tell of the little mouse **“Ratoncito Pérez”**. It too fetches the tooth and brings a present. So every region has its own story.
Some families keep the milk teeth as a memento. There are small **tooth boxes** for this. This way the tooth does not get lost. Sometimes people also write down when the tooth fell out.

gewusst: A child has 20 milk teeth, which fall out one after another.
Stories of a mouse that fetches milk teeth exist in many countries.

teile.einleitung: Vein valves are small valves in the veins. They make sure that the blood flows in only one direction, namely towards the heart. They are especially important in the legs.
wichtigste: Vein valves stop the blood in the veins from flowing back.
They are pocket-shaped folds of the innermost wall layer of the vein.
In the legs there are especially many vein valves.
Together with the leg muscles they form the muscle pump.
The large venae cavae have no valves.
If the valves close poorly, varicose veins can develop.

abschnitte.text: Vein valves are small **pockets** on the inner wall of the veins. When the blood flows towards the heart, they lie flat against the wall and let it through. If the blood wants to flow back, the pockets fill and close the vein. This way they act like **valves** that open in only one direction. They are folds of the **intima**, the innermost wall layer, and are covered with endothelium.

In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against **gravity**. That is why leg veins have especially many valves. When the leg muscles tense, they press on the deep veins. The valves make sure that the blood then flows only upwards. This mechanism is called the **muscle pump**. People who walk a lot therefore help the blood on its way to the heart.

Not all veins have valves. The upper and lower **vena cava**, which open directly into the heart, have none. There the blood is drawn in mainly by the **suction** of breathing and the heart. When you breathe in, a negative pressure arises in the chest that pulls the blood towards the heart. The heart itself also sucks in blood as it relaxes.

If the valves in the surface veins of the legs no longer close properly, the blood backs up. The veins widen and become twisted: **varicose veins** develop, medically **varices**. If the blood congestion lasts a long time, it is called **chronic venous insufficiency**. Then the legs swell, the skin changes colour and, in the worst case, an open leg ulcer develops. Compression stockings and exercise can help.

Vein valves played an important part in the history of medicine. The English doctor **William Harvey** published his teaching on the **circulation of the blood** in 1628. As an argument he used the vein valves: they let the blood flow only towards the heart. This did not fit the old idea that blood flows back and forth in the veins. So the valves helped to prove the closed circulation.

gewusst: Harvey had studied in Padua, where his teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the vein valves precisely.
With a simple experiment on the forearm, Harvey was able to show that blood in the veins cannot be pushed away from the heart.

teile.einleitung: A rotating star chart shows which stars and constellations you can see in the sky at a particular time. You set the date and time, and the right night sky appears in the window.
wichtigste: You set the date and the time against each other.
The edge of the oval window shows the horizon.
The star disc turns around the Pole Star.
A chart is only valid for one particular geographical latitude, for Switzerland about 47 degrees north.
In summer you have to subtract one hour because of summer time.
Planets are not drawn in, because they wander through the constellations.

abschnitte.text: A rotating star chart consists of two discs. At the bottom is the **star disc** with all the stars, and above it the **cover disc** with an oval window. The **dates** are written around the edge of the star disc, and the **times** around the edge of the cover disc. If you turn the time you want over today's date, the window shows the matching sky. The star disc turns around the **Pole Star**, which stands almost exactly at the celestial north pole. All the other stars seem to turn around it during the night.

The edge of the oval window shows the **horizon**. Only the stars inside the window are currently above the horizon and visible. Stars outside it have set at that time. Because the visible part of the sky depends on the **geographical latitude**, a chart is valid only for one particular latitude. The further north you live, the more stars stay above the horizon all the time, and the fewer southern stars you see. For Switzerland, a chart for about **47 degrees north** is suitable.

On a star chart, **east is on the left** when north is at the top. On a map it is the other way round. The reason: you look at a map from above, but at the sky from below. If you hold the star chart **above your head** and look up, the directions are right again. It is best to hold the edge with the direction you are facing downwards.

Many star charts are set to **standard time**, in Switzerland Central European Time (CET). In summer, however, **summer time** applies, which is one hour ahead. That is why in summer you have to **subtract one hour**. If the clock shows 11 pm, you set the chart to 10 pm.

At night, it is best to read the chart with **red light**. Weak red light hardly dazzles eyes that have got used to the dark. White light would spoil your **night vision** for a long time. **Planets** are not marked on the chart permanently, because they wander through the constellations over weeks and months. You look up their position in an astronomical **yearbook**.

gewusst: The eyes need about half an hour until they have got fully used to the dark.
A rotating star chart works without electricity and without the internet, year after year.

teile.einleitung: Ticks are small arachnids that suck blood. A tick bite is usually harmless but can pass on diseases. That is why protection is important.
wichtigste: Ticks wait in **long grass** and in bushes.
In Switzerland they are active mainly **from spring to autumn**.
Adult ticks have **eight legs**.
Ticks feed on **blood**.
They are removed with **tick tweezers** or ordinary tweezers.
A red ring that gets bigger is called **erythema migrans** and is a warning sign.

abschnitte.text: Ticks belong to the **arachnids**, not to the insects. Adult ticks have four pairs of legs, so **eight legs**. They feed on the **blood** of humans and animals. When they suck, they become much fatter. In Switzerland the **castor bean tick** is the most common kind of tick.

Ticks sit on **grasses**, in the undergrowth and in **bushes**, usually not very high above the ground. They let themselves be brushed off by people or animals walking past. They do not drop from trees. They are active when it is warm enough, so usually **from spring into autumn**.

In the woods **long trousers** and closed shoes protect you. Light-coloured clothes help you to spot ticks early. There are also products that you spray on your skin or clothes. After an outing you **check your body for ticks**. Ticks like to bite into warm spots, for example the backs of the knees, under the arms or along the hairline.

A tick should be removed as quickly as possible. With **tick tweezers** or ordinary tweezers you grip it close to the skin. Then you pull it out slowly and straight. Afterwards you disinfect the spot. You should not cover the tick with oil or glue.

Ticks can pass on diseases, in Switzerland mainly **Lyme disease** and **tick-borne encephalitis**, **TBE** for short. There is a vaccination against TBE, but not against Lyme disease. After a bite you watch the spot for **a few weeks**. If a red ring forms that gets bigger, or if you get a fever, you go to the doctor.

gewusst: Ticks do not have eyes like ours. They sense their victims by their breath and body heat, among other things.
A tick that has sucked itself full can weigh many times its own weight.

teile.einleitung: The vestibular organ is our organ of balance. It lies well protected in the inner ear and reports to the brain how we turn, tilt or accelerate the head.
wichtigste: The vestibular organ lies in the labyrinth of the inner ear, right next to the cochlea.
Each side has three semicircular canals, which detect turns in all directions.
The utricle and saccule report gravity and acceleration in a straight line.
The otoliths are tiny crystals of calcium carbonate.
The vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps your gaze steady when the head moves.
Robert Bárány received the Nobel Prize in 1914 for his research on the organ of balance.

abschnitte.titel: An organ in the inner ear
abschnitte.text: The organ of balance lies in the **labyrinth** of the inner ear, right next to the **cochlea**. Both are filled with a liquid, the **endolymph**. The vestibular organ consists of two parts: the three **semicircular canals** and two small sacs called the **utricle** and **saccule**. On each side of the head there is one such organ. Its signals run to the brain through a nerve.

Each inner ear has **three semicircular canals**, which stand roughly at right angles to each other. This way turns in all directions of space can be detected. When you turn your head, the endolymph, because of its inertia, lags behind a little. In doing so it bends fine **sensory hairs**, which inform the brain about the turn. If you spin round in a circle for a long time and then stop, the liquid flows on a little further, and you feel dizzy.

In the utricle and saccule lie the **macular organs**. They carry a membrane with tiny crystals, the **otoliths** or ear stones. These consist of **calcium carbonate** and are heavier than their surroundings. That is why the membrane shifts when you tilt your head or accelerate straight ahead. This is how you feel **gravity**, for example in a lift or when a train pulls away.

When the organ of balance reports a turn of the head, the eyes at once move just as fast in the opposite direction. This is the **vestibulo-ocular reflex**. This way the picture on the retina stays steady. If the eyes and the organ of balance report contradictory things, this can lead to **travel sickness**. If you read in a car, for example, the eyes report rest, but the organ of balance reports movement. This conflict of the senses can cause nausea and dizziness.

In the **caloric test** the doctor flushes warm and cold water into the ear canal. The change in temperature creates a flow of the endolymph in the lateral semicircular canal. The eye movements this sets off show whether the organ on each side works. A common disorder is **benign positional vertigo**. In it, loosened ear stones get into a semicircular canal and fake a turn. With targeted positioning manoeuvres they can be moved back.

gewusst: The Austrian ear doctor Robert Bárány received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1914 for his research on the vestibular apparatus.
The organ of balance also works in the dark and with your eyes closed: you still feel whether you are lying, standing or turning.

teile.einleitung: In constipation, bowel movements are rare, and the stools are hard. This is unpleasant but common. With the right diet and enough exercise you can often do a lot about it.
wichtigste: In constipation the stools are rare, hard and difficult to pass.
The technical term for it is obstipation.
Healthy is about three bowel movements a day to three a week.
Fibre and drinking enough help most.
Exercise stimulates the activity of the gut.
People who often suppress the urge weaken the signal over time.

abschnitte.text: In constipation **bowel movements** are rare, and the stools are often hard and difficult. This can cause **stomach ache** and a feeling of fullness. In technical language constipation is called **obstipation**. The word comes from the Latin “obstipare”, which means to stuff full. In adults it is usually called constipation when the bowels move less than three times a week.

**Fibre** is made up of parts of plants that the body cannot digest. It binds water and makes the stools softer and bulkier. A lot of fibre is found in **wholemeal bread**, vegetables, pulses and fruit. Animal foods such as meat or cheese contain almost none. For fibre to work well, the body also needs enough **liquid**, best of all water.

Physical **exercise** also gets the gut going. Running, cycling or swimming stimulate the activity of the gut. People who sit a lot are more likely to get constipation. It is also important to give in to the **urge to go**. People who often suppress it get the gut used to it, the signal becomes weaker, and the stools stay longer in the gut.

Medicines that encourage bowel movements are called **laxatives**. They make the stools softer or stimulate the gut. You should take them only for a short time and after medical advice. Often it is enough to change your diet. If you have severe stomach pain, blood in the stools or constipation that lasts a long time, you belong with the doctor.

gewusst: The large intestine takes water from the food pulp. The longer the stools stay there, the harder they become.
On journeys many people get constipation, because eating, drinking and the daily routine change.

teile.einleitung: Teeth are the hard tools in our mouth with which we bite off and break up food. A child has 20 milk teeth, and an adult later has up to 32 permanent teeth. They are protected by a hard white layer, the tooth enamel.
wichtigste: A child has 20 milk teeth.
From about the age of 6 the milk teeth are replaced by permanent teeth.
An adult has up to 32 teeth, including the four wisdom teeth.
The hard white layer on the teeth is called tooth enamel.
A lot of sugar is particularly harmful to the teeth.
Holes in the teeth are caused by the disease tooth decay.
You should brush your teeth at least twice a day.

abschnitte.text: Every tooth has a task. With the flat **incisors** at the front we bite things off. The pointed **canines** hold and tear the food. The broad **molars** at the back grind the food like millstones. All the teeth together are called the set of teeth.

The visible part is called the crown, and the part in the jaw is called the root. On the outside the tooth is protected by **enamel**, the hardest substance in the whole body. Underneath lies the yellowish **dentine**. Right inside is the pulp with nerves and blood vessels. That is why a hole hurts when it reaches the nerve.

The first milk teeth usually appear at the age of about six months. By around three years all 20 milk teeth are there. From about the age of 6 the **change of teeth** begins: the permanent teeth push up from below and the milk teeth become loose. The wisdom teeth come only in adulthood or not at all. Permanent teeth do not grow back, which is why you have to look after them well.

abschnitte.titel: Tooth decay, the enemy of teeth
abschnitte.text: Bacteria live in the mouth that make acid from **sugar**. This acid attacks the tooth enamel and can eat a hole into it. This disease is called **tooth decay**. Frequent snacking and sweet drinks greatly increase the risk. A dentist drills out the diseased tissue and fills the hole with a filling.

For decades Switzerland has had **school dental care**: specialists show children at school how to brush properly. Many municipalities offer regular check-ups with the school dentist. Since the 1950s there has been table salt with fluoride in Switzerland, which strengthens the teeth. As a result children in Switzerland today have much less tooth decay than in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: A child's first 20 teeth, which later fall out.
A hard white protective layer on the crown of the tooth.
A disease in which acid eats holes into the teeth.
A yellowish layer under the tooth enamel.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is harder than any bone in your body.
Sharks keep growing new teeth throughout their lives, and some use up thousands of them.
A person's teeth are so unique that people can be identified by them.

teile.einleitung: We feel warmth every day: in the sun, by the fire or under the duvet. Our body needs warmth and has to protect itself from the cold.
wichtigste: Wool keeps you warm because a lot of air is trapped between the fibres.
Dark clothes get warmer in the sun than light ones.
Rubbing produces heat from friction.
A campfire warms the skin with heat radiation.
The skin compares temperatures with its own.
On a tap, red stands for warm and blue for cold.

abschnitte.text: In winter we like to wear clothes made of **wool**. A lot of **air** is trapped between the wool fibres. This air holds in the body's warmth, because air conducts heat poorly. In bed a **hot-water bottle** warms the feet. And **emperor penguins** stand close together in the icy Antarctic winter so that they lose less heat.

A **black** T-shirt gets warmer in the sun than a white one. Dark colours absorb more sunlight than light ones. If you sit close to a **campfire**, you feel the warmth on your skin. The fire gives off **heat radiation**. It warms us even without us touching the fire.

When it is cold we rub our hands together. This produces **heat from friction**. The skin does not feel temperatures exactly like a thermometer. It compares them with its own. That is why after a **snowball fight**, lukewarm water feels hot on your cold hands.

In many old Swiss farmhouses there is a **tiled stove**. It stores the heat of the fire in its tiles. Long after the fire has gone out, it still gives the heat off to the **living room**. On a tap, **red** usually shows warm water and **blue** cold. This way you know which way to turn it.

gewusst: Emperor penguins take turns in the group so that it is not always the same ones standing on the outside in the cold.
The normal human body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: The neck of the tooth is the narrow area between the crown and the root. If it is exposed, it often becomes sensitive to cold.
wichtigste: The neck of the tooth lies where the crown meets the root.
This is where enamel and root cement meet.
Exposed tooth necks are often sensitive to pain.
Scrubbing too hard can push the gums back.
Tooth decay develops more easily at the neck of the tooth than on the crown.
Special toothpastes seal the fine channels in the dentine.

abschnitte.titel: Where the neck of the tooth is
abschnitte.text: A tooth has a **crown**, which you can see, and a **root** in the jaw. Between them lies the narrow **neck of the tooth**. In a healthy mouth it lies at the edge of the **gums**. On the outside the crown is covered with **enamel**, and the root with **root cement**. The boundary between the two runs exactly at the neck of the tooth.

At the neck of the tooth the protective enamel is missing. If it is exposed, the **dentine** shows through. Fine **channels** run through it and carry stimuli directly to the nerve. **Cold** in particular, for example when eating ice cream, but also sweet or sour things then cause a short, stabbing pain.

Anyone who scrubs with a lot of pressure and a **hard toothbrush** can push the gums back. **Periodontitis** also makes the gums shrink. Strong side-to-side scrubbing can even cause notches at the neck of the tooth. These are called **wedge-shaped defects**, because in cross-section they look like a wedge.

Root cement and dentine are **softer** than enamel and contain fewer minerals. That is why acids from bacteria attack them more quickly, and **tooth decay** develops more easily. Gentle brushing with a soft brush is important. Many **toothpastes for sensitive teeth** contain substances that seal the open channels. Then stimuli such as cold reach the nerve less strongly.

gewusst: The enamel of the crown often ends very thinly at the neck of the tooth.
More pressure when brushing does not make the teeth cleaner, but it does harm the neck of the tooth.

teile.einleitung: Chickenpox is a very catching childhood illness. Lots of itchy blisters on the skin are typical.
wichtigste: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus.
The virus belongs to the herpes virus family.
It is passed on through the air and spreads very easily.
You should not scratch the itchy blisters, otherwise scars can remain.
You usually get chickenpox only once in your life.
A vaccination protects against the illness.

abschnitte.text: Chickenpox is caused by the **varicella-zoster virus**. It belongs to the **herpes virus** family. The viruses fly through the **air** when people breathe and talk, even over several metres. That is also where the German name “Windpocken”, meaning “wind pox”, comes from: they spread as if carried by the wind. That is why chickenpox is very catching. Most people get it as a **child**.

First small **red spots** appear on the skin. These turn into **blisters**, which are filled with fluid and are very **itchy**. Often there is a fever as well. After a few days the blisters dry up and form **scabs**. These later fall off by themselves.

You should **not scratch the blisters**. Scratched blisters can become inflamed, and afterwards small **scars** sometimes remain. A **cooling lotion** from the chemist's soothes the skin. Short fingernails help you not to injure the skin. Warmth and scratchy wool often make the itching worse.

Anyone who has had chickenpox is usually protected afterwards. That is why you normally get it only **once in your life**. There is also a **vaccination** against chickenpox, which protects you from becoming ill. But after the illness the virus stays quietly in the body. Many years later it can cause **shingles**.

gewusst: The word “zoster” in the name of the virus stands for shingles, which the same virus can cause later.
With chickenpox you often find spots, blisters and scabs on the skin at the same time.

teile.einleitung: In July 1969 people set foot on the moon for the first time. The mission was called **Apollo 11** and came from the American space agency NASA. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed, while Michael Collins waited in orbit.
wichtigste: Apollo 11 landed on the moon on 20 July 1969.
Neil Armstrong was the first person on the moon, and Buzz Aldrin followed him.
Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the spacecraft Columbia.
Armstrong and Aldrin were outside for about two and a half hours.
The whole journey took about 8 days.
Several hundred million people watched live on television.

abschnitte.text: Three astronauts went on the flight: **Neil Armstrong**, **Buzz Aldrin** and **Michael Collins**. They launched on 16 July 1969 in Florida with the huge rocket **Saturn V**. The spacecraft consisted of two parts: the command ship **Columbia** and the lunar module **Eagle**. Collins stayed in Columbia and orbited the moon while the other two landed with Eagle.

On **20 July 1969** Eagle touched down in the “Sea of Tranquillity”, a flat, dark plain on the moon. A few hours later Armstrong climbed down the ladder. As he did so he said the famous words: “That's one small step for man, **one giant leap for mankind**.” Shortly afterwards Aldrin followed. **Several hundred million** people all over the world watched on television, including in Switzerland.

Armstrong and Aldrin were outside for about **two and a half hours**. They put up a **US flag**, collected moon rock and set up measuring instruments. These included a **mirror for laser light**. To this day researchers send laser beams from the Earth to this mirror and so measure the distance to the moon very precisely. One instrument came from Switzerland: a sail from the **University of Bern** caught particles of the solar wind.

Afterwards Eagle flew back to Columbia, and the three astronauts set off for home. On **24 July 1969** the capsule landed in the **Pacific Ocean**. The whole journey took about **8 days**. With this the USA had reached its goal of taking people to the moon and back before the end of the 1960s.

gewusst: The solar wind sail from the University of Bern was the first experiment to be set up on the moon, even before the flag.
The astronauts' footprints are probably still there, because on the moon there is no wind to blow them away.

teile.einleitung: **Apollo 13** was meant to land on the moon in 1970. But on the way an oxygen tank exploded. Instead of a landing, an exciting fight for survival began, which the crew and mission control won together.
wichtigste: Apollo 13 flew in April 1970.
On the way to the moon an oxygen tank exploded.
The crew reported: “Houston, we've had a problem.”
The commander was Jim Lovell.
The lunar module Aquarius served as a lifeboat.
The spacecraft flew around the moon and back to Earth.

abschnitte.text: The commander of Apollo 13 was **Jim Lovell**. With him flew **Fred Haise** and **Jack Swigert**. Actually **Ken Mattingly** was supposed to fly. But shortly before the launch it was learnt that he might have caught **German measles**. Because he might fall ill, he was not allowed to go, and Swigert stepped in. In the end Mattingly did not fall ill at all.

The launch in **April 1970** went well. But on the way to the moon an **oxygen tank** exploded in the service module. The spacecraft lost a lot of oxygen and power. The crew reported the breakdown with the words: “**Houston, we've had a problem**.” Houston is the city in the USA where NASA's mission control is. A moon landing was now impossible.

abschnitte.titel: The lunar module as a lifeboat
abschnitte.text: The three astronauts moved into the lunar module **Aquarius**. It had actually been built for only two people and a few days. Soon there was **too much carbon dioxide** in the cabin, which is the gas we breathe out. The filters from the command ship did not fit into the lunar module. So, following instructions from mission control, the astronauts made a fitting connection out of **sticky tape**, **cardboard** and plastic. It was cold, and water and power had to be carefully rationed.

Turning round was not possible. Instead **Apollo 13 flew around the moon** and let the moon's gravity fling it back towards the Earth. Shortly before arrival the astronauts climbed back into the command capsule and left the lunar module behind. The capsule landed safely in the **Pacific Ocean**. The mission is known as a “successful failure”, because all three were saved.

gewusst: On their way around the moon the crew of Apollo 13 travelled further from the Earth than any human being had done before.
The story of Apollo 13 was told in a well-known film in 1995.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin C is a nutrient vital for life that we have to take in with our food. The body needs it above all for a strong immune system and healthy connective tissue. Many people think of lemons, but red peppers and rose hips contain even more of it.
wichtigste: Chemically, vitamin C is called ascorbic acid.
The body needs it for a strong immune system and healthy connective tissue.
Humans cannot make vitamin C themselves and have to eat it.
A lot of vitamin C is found in peppers, citrus fruits, kiwis, berries and cabbage.
Vitamin C dissolves in water and is partly lost in long cooking.
A severe deficiency leads to the illness scurvy.
In 1933 the Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein developed a process to make vitamin C artificially.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs it for
abschnitte.text: Vitamin C helps the **defence cells** of the **immune system** to fight germs that cause illness. The body also needs it to make **collagen**. Collagen is a protein that makes skin, bones, teeth, gums and blood vessels firm and elastic. That is why wounds heal better with enough vitamin C. It also helps the gut to take up iron from plant food.

**Citrus fruits** such as oranges and lemons are well known. Even more vitamin C, however, is contained in red peppers, rose hips, sea buckthorn and blackcurrants. Kiwis, strawberries, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and potatoes also supply a lot of it. People who eat fruit and vegetables every day usually get enough.

Vitamin C is **water-soluble**, so it dissolves in the cooking water. Heat, light and air destroy it little by little. That is why raw or briefly steamed vegetables contain more vitamin C than those cooked for a long time. Freshly squeezed juice should be drunk quickly. The body gets rid of surplus vitamin C through the kidneys in the urine.

If vitamin C is missing for weeks, the illness **scurvy** develops. In it the gums bleed, teeth fall out and wounds heal badly. In the past many sailors on long sea voyages suffered from it, because they had no fresh fruit. The Scottish doctor **James Lind** showed in an experiment in 1747 that citrus fruits help against scurvy. Today scurvy is very rare in Switzerland.

The Hungarian researcher **Albert Szent-Györgyi** obtained vitamin C from peppers around 1930 and received the Nobel Prize in 1937. The Swiss chemist **Tadeus Reichstein** found a way in 1933 to make vitamin C artificially in large amounts. His process was used in industry for a long time. Today vitamin C is also added to foods so that they stay fresh longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name of vitamin C.
A protein that makes skin, bones and blood vessels stable.
An illness that arises from a severe lack of vitamin C.
A substance that dissolves in water.

gewusst: Most animals can make vitamin C themselves, but humans, apes and guinea pigs cannot.
Red peppers contain about twice as much vitamin C as a lemon.
On food packaging vitamin C is often given as E 300.

teile.einleitung: The gums surround the teeth and protect the jawbone. Healthy gums are pale pink and firm.
wichtigste: The technical term for the gums is gingiva.
Healthy gums are pale pink, firm and fit closely around the tooth.
Inflammation of the gums is called gingivitis.
Bleeding gums when brushing your teeth are typical of it.
The most common cause is a layer of bacteria along the gum line.
With good oral hygiene the inflammation usually heals again.

abschnitte.text: The **gums** surround the teeth like a tight collar. Dentists call them the **gingiva**, a word from Latin. Between the tooth and the edge of the gum there is a shallow groove, the **gingival groove**. With healthy gums it is only a few millimetres deep. Between two teeth the gum rises up as a small point, the **papilla**.

Healthy gums are **pale pink** and **firm**. They fit closely around the tooth and normally do not bleed when you brush. If they are red and swollen, on the other hand, this is a sign of **inflammation**. This is called **gingivitis**. It is the most common disease of the gums.

The most common cause of gingivitis is a **layer of bacteria** along the gum line. If this layer is not removed thoroughly, the gums react with an inflammation. A typical sign is **bleeding gums when brushing your teeth**. If the papillae shrink back because of an inflammation, dark gaps appear between the teeth.

A simple inflammation of the gums can be **reversed**. If the plaque is removed regularly, the gums usually become healthy again within a few days to weeks. This includes thorough tooth brushing and cleaning the **spaces between the teeth**. If an inflammation lasts a long time, it can go deeper. Then it is called **periodontitis**.

gewusst: Anyone who stops brushing because their gums bleed usually makes it worse, not better.
The gums are a mucous membrane, like the inside of the cheeks.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that is important above all for good eyesight. The body takes it in from animal foods or makes it from the orange pigment beta-carotene.
wichtigste: Chemically, vitamin A is called retinol.
Beta-carotene from carrots is a precursor of vitamin A.
Vitamin A is fat-soluble, so it is taken up better with a little fat.
A deficiency can lead to night blindness.
The liver stores vitamin A, which is why liver as a food is very rich in it.
Too much vitamin A from supplements can be harmful.
Golden Rice was developed, among other places, at ETH Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Vitamin A is chemically called **retinol**. The name recalls the **retina** of the eye. In the **rods** of the retina vitamin A is used to make **visual purple**, also called rhodopsin. It makes seeing in dim light possible. If vitamin A is missing, you see badly at dusk: this is called **night blindness**.
