The orange pigment in carrots is called **beta-carotene**. It is a **precursor** of vitamin A, which the body converts when needed. Beta-carotene is also found in pumpkin, apricots and peppers. Because vitamin A and its precursor are **fat-soluble**, it is best to prepare carrots with a little oil or butter. This way the gut can take them up much better.

The **liver** builds up large reserves of vitamin A. That is why liver as a food contains a great deal of it. Eggs, butter and dairy products also supply vitamin A. What the body does not need is not simply got rid of in the urine but **stored**. If you take very large amounts through supplements, the vitamin can build up and poison you. With normal food this hardly happens.

In poor countries **vitamin A deficiency** is still common today. To help, researchers developed **Golden Rice**. This genetically modified variety of rice makes a precursor of vitamin A in the grain and is therefore yellowish. It was developed by **Ingo Potrykus** of ETH Zurich and **Peter Beyer**. The use of genetically modified plants is still debated today.

gewusst: The liver of polar bears contains so much vitamin A that even a small amount can be poisonous for humans.
If you eat a great many carrots, the skin can turn slightly orange. This is harmless and goes away again.

teile.einleitung: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist. In 1895 he discovered the rays that now bear his name in German and with which you can look inside the body.
wichtigste: In 1895 in Würzburg Röntgen discovered X-rays.
In German-speaking countries they are now called Röntgen rays.
The first famous X-ray picture shows his wife's hand.
Röntgen studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today's ETH.
He did not patent his discovery.
In 2004 the element roentgenium was named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen** was born in Germany in 1845. He studied mechanical engineering at the **Polytechnic in Zurich**, today's **ETH**. After that he gained his doctorate at the **University of Zurich**. Later he became a professor of physics, among other places at the University of **Würzburg**. There he made his famous discovery.

On **8 November 1895** Röntgen was experimenting with a glass tube through which electric current flowed. He noticed unknown rays that even passed through paper and wood. He called them **X-rays**, because he did not know what they were. In German-speaking countries they are now called **Röntgen rays**. At the end of 1895 he took an X-ray of the hand of his wife **Anna Bertha**. On the picture you can see the bones and her ring.

X-rays pass through soft tissue more easily than through **bone**. That is why bones appear light on the picture. This shows, for example, broken bones or holes in the teeth. In large amounts, however, the rays can damage cells. A **lead apron** protects parts of the body that are not being examined, because lead blocks the rays well.

In 1901 Röntgen received the very first **Nobel Prize in Physics**. He did not **patent** his discovery, because it was meant to benefit everyone. That is why he hardly earned any money from it. In 2004 the artificially made chemical element with the atomic number 111 was named after him: **roentgenium**, with the symbol Rg.

gewusst: In 1901 Röntgen became the first person ever to receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.
In many languages, English for example, the rays are still called X-rays today.

teile.einleitung: Our body has a body clock that runs roughly on a 24-hour cycle. This circadian rhythm controls when we get tired, when our body temperature rises and when certain hormones are released.
wichtigste: “Circadian” means **about a day**.
Without time cues the body clock usually runs **a little longer than 24 hours**.
**Jürgen Aschoff** studied the body clock in a bunker in Andechs.
In the morning the body releases a lot of **cortisol**.
Core body temperature is lowest in the **early hours of the morning**.
In 2017 the Nobel Prize was awarded for research on clock genes in the **fruit fly**.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “circa” for about and “dies” for day. It refers to biological rhythms with a period of **around 24 hours**. Rhythms that repeat several times a day are called **ultradian**, for example the sleep cycles during the night. Rhythms that last longer than a day are called **infradian**. The science of biological rhythms is called **chronobiology**.

In most people the body clock runs a little **longer than 24 hours**. That is why it has to be reset every day. This is done by **time cues**, above all **daylight**. Mealtimes and exercise also help. If all time cues are missing, the rhythm runs **freely** with its own period and shifts a little each day compared with clock time.

From the 1960s the German researcher **Jürgen Aschoff** had volunteers live for weeks in an underground room in **Andechs** in Bavaria, without a clock and without daylight. In this way he was able to show how the body clock runs freely. Aschoff is considered one of the founders of chronobiology. Later **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash** and **Michael Young** studied the clock genes in the **fruit fly** Drosophila. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in **2017**.

Many body values follow the rhythm. The **cortisol level** rises in the second half of the night and reaches its peak shortly after waking up. Cortisol helps to provide energy for the day. In the evening the body makes the sleep hormone **melatonin** when it gets dark. **Core body temperature** is lowest in the early hours of the morning and highest in the late afternoon.

If you fly across several time zones, the body clock no longer fits the local time. This is called **jet lag**. After a **flight eastwards** adjusting is usually harder. Then you have to sleep earlier, so you have to put the body clock forward. Because it runs a little longer than 24 hours anyway, it is easier to shift it later than earlier.

gewusst: Plants have a body clock too. Some flowers open and close at fixed times of day.
The central body clock of humans sits in a tiny region of the brain, directly above the crossing of the optic nerves.

teile.einleitung: Scales measure how heavy something is. There are scales for people, for babies, for the kitchen and even very simple balance scales that compare two things with each other.
wichtigste: With bathroom scales you measure body weight in kilograms.
If nobody stands on the scales, they show 0 kg.
In the kitchen you weigh out ingredients with kitchen scales, usually in grams.
On balance scales the heavier side sinks down.
Babies are weighed at the paediatrician on baby scales.
If you want to compare your weight, you always weigh yourself at the same time of day.

abschnitte.text: With **bathroom scales** you measure body weight. They show how many **kilograms** you weigh. If nobody stands on them, nothing presses on the scales, and they show **zero**. A thermometer, by contrast, measures temperature, not weight. Many bathroom scales today are digital and show the weight as a number.

You can also calculate with scales. Nina weighs 25 kg, her **school bag** weighs 3 kg. If she stands on the scales with the school bag, they show 25 plus 3, so **28 kg**. You can also subtract: Mum weighs 68 kg with the baby and 62 kg without the baby. 68 minus 62 makes **6 kg**, so that is how heavy the baby is.

In the kitchen you need **kitchen scales**. With them you weigh out flour, sugar or butter for cooking and baking, usually in **grams**. At the paediatrician there are **baby scales**. They have a tray in which you lay the baby. They measure very precisely, even small differences, because with babies every gain matters.

**Balance scales** are a very old kind of scales. A beam rests in the middle, and a pan hangs from each end. If you put something on each side, the **heavier side** sinks down. If both are equally heavy, the beam stays **level**. With weights, goods could be weighed this way thousands of years ago.

Over the course of the day body weight changes a little. Eating and drinking make a small difference. If you want to compare your weight well, you therefore always weigh yourself at the **same time of day**, for example in the morning. It is also important to put the scales on a firm, level floor. On a soft carpet they often measure inaccurately.

gewusst: Until 2019 the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris, the international prototype kilogram. Today it is fixed by a constant of nature.
The scales are a symbol of justice. The figure of Justitia often holds a pair of scales in her hand.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin D is a special vitamin, because your body can make it itself in the skin with the help of sunlight. It makes sure that bones and teeth get enough calcium and grow strong. In winter, however, the sun in Switzerland often shines too weakly for this.
wichtigste: The body makes vitamin D in the skin with the help of sunlight.
For this it needs the sun's UV-B rays.
Vitamin D helps the body to take up calcium for bones and teeth.
Only a few foods such as oily fish and egg yolk contain a lot of vitamin D.
In children a severe deficiency leads to the bone disease rickets.
In winter the sunlight in Switzerland is hardly enough to make enough vitamin D.
That is why babies in Switzerland often get vitamin D drops.

abschnitte.text: In the skin there is a substance that arises from cholesterol. When the sun's **UV-B rays** hit it, a precursor of vitamin D is made from it. In the **liver** and in the **kidneys** this precursor is then converted into the active form. In summer it is often enough to hold your face, hands and arms out in the open for some time. You should still always avoid sunburn.

Vitamin D makes sure that the gut takes enough **calcium** from the food. Calcium is the most important building material for bones and teeth. Without vitamin D the bones stay soft. Vitamin D also supports the muscles and the immune system. Because it acts like a messenger substance, experts also count it among the hormones.

Only a few foods contain a lot of vitamin D. These include oily fish such as **herring**, salmon and mackerel, as well as egg yolk. Some mushrooms and cod liver oil also supply vitamin D. With food alone, however, you usually do not reach the requirement. The body makes the largest part itself with sunlight.

In Switzerland the sun stands so low from about October to March that hardly any UV-B rays reach the ground. The body then lives on the reserves that it stored in fat and muscle in summer. For **infants**, experts in Switzerland recommend vitamin D drops. Older people or people who are rarely outdoors also sometimes need supplements. You should, however, talk about this with a doctor.

If children lack vitamin D for a long time, **rickets** develops. In it the soft bones bend, for example the legs. In the past rickets was common in cities with a lot of smoke and little sun. In adults the softening of the bones is called osteomalacia. Too much vitamin D from tablets can, however, also do harm.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible rays of the sun with which the skin makes vitamin D.
A mineral that bones and teeth are mainly made of.
An illness in children in which the bones become soft.
An oil from fish liver that contains a lot of vitamin D.

gewusst: In the past many children had to swallow a spoonful of cod liver oil every day to prevent rickets.
Window glass also swallows a large part of the UV-B rays, so behind a pane you hardly make any vitamin D.
The body can store vitamin D from the summer for several weeks to months.

teile.einleitung: The calf is the thick muscle at the back of the lower leg, between the knee and the heel. It helps us when walking, jumping and cycling.
wichtigste: The calf lies at the back of the lower leg.
The calf muscle pulls the heel upwards, which is how we stand on tiptoe.
At the bottom the calf muscle turns into the strong Achilles tendon.
At the front of the lower leg the shinbone lies directly under the skin.
In a calf cramp the muscle suddenly contracts and hurts.
Gentle stretching usually helps against a cramp.

abschnitte.text: Feel your lower leg for a moment. At the front you can feel the hard **shinbone** directly under the skin. At the back is the soft, round **calf**. It consists mainly of one large muscle, the **calf muscle**. It has several parts that join together at the bottom into the **Achilles tendon**. This tendon is attached to the heel.

When the calf muscle contracts, it pulls the **heel** upwards through the Achilles tendon. This lets you stand on **tiptoe**. If you stand on your toes on one leg, the muscle carries your whole weight. It is then tightly tensed and feels hard. When walking, running and jumping, too, the calf pushes you off the ground with every step.

When **cycling**, the legs press down on the pedals again and again. The calf muscles work hard as they do so. That is why racing cyclists often have very strong calves. The calf is also trained when hiking in the mountains, playing football or dancing. A muscle that works regularly becomes stronger and gains stamina.

Sometimes the calf suddenly becomes very hard and hurts a lot. This is a **calf cramp**: the muscle contracts and does not let go. It can happen during sport or at night in bed. It usually helps to **pull your toes gently towards your body**. This stretches the calf, and the cramp soon eases again.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon is considered the strongest tendon in the human body.
Its name comes from the Greek legendary hero Achilles, who could only be wounded at his heel.

teile.einleitung: DART was a NASA mission that tested whether an asteroid can be deflected from its path by an impact. On 26 September 2022, the probe hit the small asteroid Dimorphos.
wichtigste: DART stands for “Double Asteroid Redirection Test”.
The probe hit the asteroid moon Dimorphos on 26 September 2022.
Dimorphos orbits the larger asteroid Didymos.
What was tested was the kinetic impactor, that is, a fast impact.
The orbital period of Dimorphos became about 33 minutes shorter.
The ESA mission Hera is meant to study the system closely at the end of 2026.

abschnitte.text: Asteroids are lumps of rock that orbit the Sun. If one were heading towards Earth, we would want to be able to deflect it. **DART**, the **Double Asteroid Redirection Test**, tested one method for this: the **kinetic impactor**. In it, a probe crashes into the asteroid at high speed and gives it a push. DART hit at about **6 kilometres per second**. It was the first test of its kind.

The target was a **double asteroid**. The larger body is called **Didymos**, its small moon **Dimorphos**. The system was **no danger** to Earth, which is why it was well suited to the experiment. On **26 September 2022**, DART struck Dimorphos. The small Italian satellite **LICIACube** was released shortly before. It flew past a few minutes after the impact and photographed the cloud of ejected material.

Before the impact, Dimorphos took about **11 hours and 55 minutes** for one orbit around Didymos. Afterwards it was about **33 minutes** less. A change of at least 73 seconds had been expected. This was measured mainly with **light curves** from telescopes on Earth: when Dimorphos passes in front of or behind Didymos, the brightness of the system changes. From these eclipses the orbital period can be determined precisely.

Why was the effect so large? At the impact, large amounts of **rock were thrown into space**. This material acted like an extra **recoil**, similar to that of a rocket. As a result, the push on Dimorphos was greatly boosted. For defending against asteroids, this is an important finding.

The European mission **Hera** is meant to study the Didymos system closely. It launched in **October 2024** and, according to plan, is due to reach Didymos and Dimorphos at the **end of 2026**. Hera will measure the crater, the mass and the structure of Dimorphos. That will help us understand more precisely how well the method worked.

gewusst: Didymos means “twin” in Greek.
DART was about as big as a small car, while Dimorphos is about as big as a football stadium.

teile.einleitung: When we are really cold, our teeth sometimes chatter. This is no accident: it is the body's way of trying to warm itself up. Chattering teeth are a sign that the body is losing too much heat.
wichtigste: In the cold the muscles shiver very quickly.
Working muscles produce heat.
When the jaw muscles shiver, the teeth knock together.
Shivering from cold happens by itself.
Often you get goose pimples at the same time.
Warm clothes and exercise help.

abschnitte.text: Our body always wants to stay at about the same temperature, around 37 degrees. If it gets too cold, the muscles start to **shiver** very quickly. The **jaw muscles** shiver too. They open and close the mouth with small, rapid movements. As they do, the teeth knock together and **chatter**.

When muscles work, **heat** is produced. You notice this when you run, too. When **shivering from cold**, many muscles work at the same time without you moving from the spot. The heat helps the body to keep its temperature. The body controls shivering **by itself**, and you can hardly stop it on purpose.

Often you get **goose pimples** at the same time. The fine hairs stand up and small bumps appear on the skin. With a **fever**, too, you can shiver hard, even though the body is actually warm. When the fever rises, you feel cold and shiver violently. This is called **the shivers** or chills. Here too the teeth can chatter.

You get cold particularly quickly when you stand **wet in the wind**, for example after swimming in a lake. Wet skin loses a lot of heat through **evaporation**. Then it helps to dry yourself and put on **warm clothes**. **Exercise** produces extra heat. A warm drink also does you good.

gewusst: Many animals also shiver in the cold to warm themselves up.
Bumblebees make their flight muscles shiver to warm up on cool mornings before they fly off.

teile.einleitung: The heart has two atria, a right one and a left one. They lie at the top of the heart, take in the blood from the veins and pass it on to the ventricles below.
wichtigste: The technical term for the atrium is atrium.
The right atrium passes its blood on to the right ventricle.
The atria have a thinner muscle wall than the ventricles.
With every heartbeat the atria contract first.
Each atrium has a small, ear-shaped pouch, the auricle.
Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder.

abschnitte.text: The heart consists of four chambers: two **atria** at the top and two **ventricles** at the bottom. In technical language the atrium is called **atrium**, the Latin word for entrance hall. The **right atrium** takes in blood low in oxygen from the body. The **left atrium** receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. Each atrium passes its blood on through a valve to the ventricle below.

The atria have a **thinner muscle wall** than the ventricles. They have to move the blood only a short way into the nearby ventricle. This needs little strength and so little muscle. The ventricles, by contrast, pump the blood to the lungs or into the whole body. On each atrium sits a small bulge that recalls an ear, the **auricle**.

In the right atrium lies the **sinus node**, the heart's natural pacemaker. The electrical excitation starts there, that is, at the top of the heart. That is why with every heartbeat the **atria** contract first. They press a little more blood into the ventricles and so top up their filling. Only after that do the ventricles contract.

While the ventricles contract and eject blood, the atria are **relaxed**. During this time new blood is already flowing into them from the veins. When the ventricle is relaxed again, the valve opens, and the blood flows downwards. This is how atria and ventricles work in turn. This is repeated with every heartbeat.

If the atria no longer contract in an orderly way but twitch irregularly, it is called **atrial fibrillation**. It is the most common lasting **heart rhythm disorder**. It occurs mainly in older people. Some of those affected feel their heart skipping, others notice nothing at all. A doctor can detect it with an **ECG** and treat it.

gewusst: The right atrium receives its blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae, the largest veins of the body.
The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is called the mitral valve, because it recalls the mitre, a bishop's hat.

teile.einleitung: Hiking is very popular in Switzerland. A dense network of well-marked paths leads through valleys and forests and over mountains.
wichtigste: Switzerland has around 65,000 kilometres of hiking trails.
Ordinary hiking trails are marked in yellow.
Mountain trails are marked white-red-white.
The signposts show roughly how long it takes to reach the destination.
Good walking boots, a rucksack and a packed lunch are part of it.
You take your rubbish back home with you.

abschnitte.text: The hiking trails of Switzerland are marked in the same way everywhere. Ordinary **hiking trails** can be recognised by **yellow signposts** and yellow diamonds. The signposts show the destinations and the **walking time** in hours and minutes. This makes it easy to plan how long you will be out. The whole network is around **65,000 kilometres** long.

**Mountain trails** are marked **white-red-white**. They are steeper, narrower and more difficult than ordinary hiking trails. Here you need to be sure-footed and have good footwear. For even more demanding paths in the high mountains there are **alpine trails**, which are marked white-blue-white. Before a mountain hike you check the weather, because it can change quickly.

In your **rucksack** you carry everything you need on the way and keep your hands free. This includes drinks, a rain jacket and **provisions**, that is food for the way such as bread, cheese and fruit. **Walking boots** have a thick sole with a tread and give good grip on stony paths. Sun cream and a hat protect you from the strong sun in the mountains.

Along many hiking trails there are **fireplaces**. Families like to **grill** sausages there, best of all a **cervelat** on a stick. Anyone who goes hiking shows respect for nature. You pack up your **rubbish** and throw it away at home, because it harms plants and animals. You also leave grazing animals and wild animals in peace.

gewusst: The signposts in Switzerland are looked after by the organisation Swiss Hiking Trails and the cantons.
Hiking is one of the most popular leisure activities in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Vital capacity is the largest amount of air that you can breathe out after breathing in as deeply as possible. It shows how much air the lungs can move.
wichtigste: You measure vital capacity by breathing in as much as possible and then breathing out as completely as possible.
In the doctor's surgery it is measured with a spirometer.
In healthy adults it is usually about 3 to 5 litres.
It is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve and expiratory reserve.
Even after the strongest breathing out, the residual volume stays in the lungs.
Vital capacity and residual volume together make up total capacity.

abschnitte.text: You breathe in **as deeply as possible** and then breathe out **as completely as possible**. The amount of air breathed out is the **vital capacity**. In healthy adults it is usually between about 3 and 5 litres. It depends, among other things, on **height**, age, sex and training. Taller people usually have a larger chest and so also larger lungs.

In a normal breath you move the **tidal volume**, about half a litre. Beyond that you can breathe in even deeper, which is the **inspiratory reserve**. After a normal breath out you can still press out more air, the **expiratory reserve**. Vital capacity is the sum of these three parts. With 0.5 litres, 3 litres and 1 litre that makes 4.5 litres altogether.

Even with maximum breathing out, about 1 to 1.5 litres of air stay in the lungs. This **residual volume** stops the lungs from collapsing. If you add vital capacity and residual volume together, you get the **total capacity**. With a vital capacity of 4.5 litres and 1.5 litres of residual air, the lungs therefore hold 6 litres. The residual air cannot be measured with a simple spirometer.

In the doctor's surgery vital capacity is measured with a **spirometer**. You blow hard into a mouthpiece, and the device measures how much air flows and how fast. This way you can tell whether the lungs are working well. At school you can simply **estimate** your own vital capacity. You breathe in deeply and blow through a tube into an upturned bottle filled with water, and the amount of water pushed out corresponds to the air breathed out.

In old age vital capacity usually **decreases**. Lungs and chest become less elastic, so you can move less air. Regular endurance sport keeps the breathing muscles strong. Smoking, by contrast, harms the lungs and can reduce vital capacity. In some lung diseases it is clearly smaller than normal.

gewusst: The spirometer for measuring vital capacity was introduced by the English doctor John Hutchinson in the 19th century. He also coined the term “vital capacity”.
Players of wind instruments train their breathing especially well.

teile.einleitung: The distances in the solar system are huge. In kilometres they give awkwardly long numbers. That is why astronomers use the **astronomical unit**, **AU** for short: the average distance between the Earth and the sun.
wichtigste: An astronomical unit is the average distance between the Earth and the sun.
Since 2012 it has been fixed at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres, around 150 million km.
Venus is around 0.7 AU from the sun, Jupiter around 5.2 AU.
Saturn is around 9.5 AU away, Uranus around 19 AU and Neptune around 30 AU.
Sunlight takes just over 8 minutes to travel one AU.
One light year equals around 63,000 AU.

abschnitte.titel: A measuring stick for the solar system
abschnitte.text: The Earth does not go around the sun in an exact circle but in a slightly oval orbit. That is why its distance varies a little. The **astronomical unit** corresponds roughly to the **average distance between the Earth and the sun**. Since **2012** it has been **fixed exactly** by the International Astronomical Union: **149,597,870,700 metres**. That is around **150 million kilometres**. So **2 AU** is around **300 million kilometres**.

With the AU the distances are easy to imagine. The Earth is exactly 1 AU away. **Venus** is around **0.7 AU** from the sun, and Mars around 1.5 AU. **Jupiter** orbits at around **5.2 AU**, **Saturn** at around **9.5 AU**. Further out come **Uranus** at around **19 AU** and **Neptune** at around **30 AU**. So Neptune is about 30 times as far from the sun as the Earth.

Light is very fast, but not infinitely fast. Sunlight takes just over **8 minutes** to travel one AU. So the light we see left the sun about 8 minutes ago. To reach **Uranus** at around 19 AU it takes 19 times as long, that is around **2 hours and 40 minutes**. To Neptune it is about 4 hours.

For distances to other stars the AU is too small. There the **light year** is used, that is the distance light travels in one year. One light year equals around **63,000 AU**. The nearest star after the sun is just over 4 light years away, which is over 250,000 AU.

gewusst: The space probe Voyager 1 is more than 160 AU from the sun and so is the most distant object ever built by humans.
In the past the AU was calculated from observations, for example when Venus passed in front of the sun.

teile.einleitung: **Amateur astronomy** means that people watch the sky in their free time, out of curiosity and for pleasure. Many have their own telescope, and others visit public observatories. Some even help science with valuable observations.
wichtigste: Amateur astronomers observe stars, planets and galaxies as a hobby.
In Switzerland the Swiss Astronomical Society is their umbrella organisation.
Public observatories offer guided tours for the public.
The eyes need around 20 to 30 minutes to get used to the dark.
The Bortle scale rates the darkness of the sky in nine levels.
Amateurs keep discovering new comets and supernovae.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are many astronomy clubs. Their umbrella organisation is the **Swiss Astronomical Society** (SAG). Many clubs run a **public observatory**. This is an observatory that offers guided tours to the public. A well-known one is the **Urania Observatory** in Zurich's old town. It stands on a high tower and has been open to the public since **1907**.

When you go outside from a bright room, at first you see only a few stars. The eyes need around **20 to 30 minutes** to get fully used to the dark. That is why amateur astronomers use a torch with **red light**, which dazzles the eyes less. A dark sky without many lights is very important. The **Bortle scale** rates in **nine levels** how dark the night sky is at a place.

Amateur astronomers keep discovering **new comets** and **supernovae**, that is exploding stars. Because there are so many of them, they can often watch the sky more closely than the few large observatories. Many measure the **brightness of variable stars** over years. Such long series of measurements are very valuable for professionals.

A **star party** is a meeting of amateur astronomers at a place with a dark sky, often in the mountains or in the countryside. There they set up their telescopes, observe together and swap tips. Often visitors are also allowed to look through the telescopes.

gewusst: Even with simple binoculars you can see Jupiter's moons and craters on the moon.
Many comets bear the names of the amateur astronomers who discovered them.

teile.einleitung: Dental care means everything we do to keep our teeth and gums healthy. The most important thing is to brush your teeth thoroughly at least twice a day. Anyone who looks after their teeth well can keep them for a lifetime.
wichtigste: You should brush your teeth at least twice a day.
Each brushing should take about two to three minutes.
Toothpaste with fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant.
Dental floss or small brushes clean the gaps between the teeth.
You change your toothbrush about every two to three months.
Less sugar and fewer sugary drinks protect against tooth decay.
Regular check-ups at the dentist spot problems early.

abschnitte.text: It is best to brush after breakfast and in the evening before going to bed. In Switzerland many children learn the **KAI method**, named after the German words for the surfaces: first the chewing surfaces, then the outer surfaces, then the inner surfaces. This way you do not miss any spot. You brush with gentle pressure and small movements from the gum towards the tooth. An egg timer or a timer helps you to brush for long enough.

**Fluoride** is a mineral that makes tooth enamel harder and more resistant to acid. That is why most toothpaste contains fluoride. For children there is special children's toothpaste with less fluoride. After brushing you spit out the foam but do not rinse too much, so that the fluoride can work.

The toothbrush does not reach every spot between the teeth. Food remains and **plaque** get stuck there. These spots can be cleaned with **dental floss** or small interdental brushes. Teenagers and adults in particular should do this every day. This also keeps the gums healthy.

Bacteria in the mouth make acid from sugar, which attacks the teeth. It is particularly harmful to keep snacking all day or sipping sweet drinks. Regular meals and water to quench your thirst are better. Sugar-free chewing gum stimulates **saliva**, which neutralises acid. In Switzerland the **little tooth man** with an umbrella marks sweets that do not harm the teeth.

You should have your teeth checked at least once a year. The dentist discovers small holes before they hurt. A **dental hygienist** removes hard tartar and polishes the teeth. If teeth are crooked, a brace can help. In many Swiss municipalities there is a school dentist for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mineral that strengthens tooth enamel.
A soft film of bacteria on the teeth.
A thin thread for cleaning the gaps between the teeth.
An order for brushing: chewing surfaces, outer surfaces, inner surfaces.

gewusst: Even in ancient Egypt people cleaned their teeth with powders and chewing sticks.
The first toothbrushes with bristles are said to have existed in ancient China.
The little tooth man with the umbrella is a Swiss symbol and was made famous by the campaign Aktion Zahnfreundlich.

teile.einleitung: VO2max is the largest amount of oxygen that a person can take in and use per minute at full effort. It is regarded as an important measure of endurance. It is measured in the laboratory or roughly estimated with running tests.
wichtigste: VO2max means maximal oxygen uptake.
The relative VO2max is given in ml per minute and kg of body weight.
Cross-country skiers reach especially high values.
In healthy people it is mainly the pumping power of the heart that limits VO2max.
With age VO2max gradually decreases.
It is measured directly with spiroergometry.

abschnitte.text: The V stands for volume, O2 for **oxygen** and max for **maximal**. VO2max states how much oxygen the body can take in per minute at the highest load. The muscles need oxygen to gain energy. The more oxygen they get, the longer and faster you can exert yourself. The **absolute VO2max** is given in litres per minute.

So that you can compare people of different weights, the oxygen uptake is divided by **body weight**. This gives the unit **ml/(min·kg)**, that is millilitres per minute and kilogram. An example: an athlete weighs 70 kg and has an absolute VO2max of 4.2 l/min. That is 4200 ml/min. 4200 divided by 70 gives **60 ml/(min·kg)**.

In healthy, trained people it is mainly the **cardiovascular system** that is limiting. The **cardiac output**, that is the amount of blood the heart pumps per minute, decides how much oxygen-rich blood reaches the muscles. According to the **Fick principle**: oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times the **arteriovenous oxygen difference**. This difference shows how much oxygen the tissues take from the blood.

The highest relative values are reached by endurance athletes, especially **cross-country skiers**. Cross-country skiing uses a great deal of muscle mass over a long time. Top athletes reach values about twice as high as in untrained people. From young adulthood onwards VO2max slowly **falls**, among other reasons because the highest heart rate decreases. Regular **endurance training** can slow this decline.

VO2max is measured directly with **spiroergometry**. In it you run or cycle on a machine ever faster and breathe into a mask. A device analyses the breathing gases and so measures the oxygen uptake. Simpler is the **Cooper test**: you run as far as possible in 12 minutes. From the distance VO2max can be roughly estimated. The test is also used in school sport.

gewusst: The Cooper test is named after the American doctor Kenneth Cooper, who developed it in the 1960s.
Sled dogs and horses have a much higher VO2max per kilogram than even the best human endurance athletes.

teile.einleitung: Most planets spin like a slightly tilted spinning top. **Uranus**, on the other hand, lies almost on its side: its axis of rotation is tilted by around **98°**. That is why it has very strange seasons.
wichtigste: The axial tilt is the angle by which the axis of rotation of a planet is tilted.
For Uranus it is around 98°, so it almost rolls along its orbit.
A Uranus year lasts about 84 Earth years, and one season around 21 years.
One pole is lit by the sun without a break for around 42 years.
Uranus was probably tipped over by a collision with a large body.
Its rings and large moons lie in its tilted equatorial plane.

abschnitte.text: Every planet turns around an imaginary line, the **axis of rotation**. The **axial tilt** shows how much this axis is tilted compared with the vertical to the plane of the orbit. For the Earth it is about **23.4°**. This tilt gives us summer and winter. For Uranus it is around **98°**, which is more than a right angle.

Uranus takes about **84 Earth years** to go once around the sun. Because it is tilted so much, during part of its orbit one pole points almost directly at the sun. This pole is then lit for around **42 years** without a break, while the other lies in darkness for 42 years. So one **season** lasts around **21 years**. When the space probe **Voyager 2** flew past in **1986**, the **south pole** was pointing almost exactly at the sun.

Nobody knows for certain. The most likely explanation is a **collision** with a very large body when the solar system was still young. This impact could have tipped the planet over. Some researchers also think of several smaller collisions. The **rings** and large **moons** of Uranus orbit in its tilted **equatorial plane**. So they were tilted along with it.

Every planet has its own axial tilt. Mars is tilted similarly to the Earth. **Venus** has a tilt of around **177°**. So it is practically upside down, and that is why, seen from above, it spins the opposite way to most planets. Jupiter, by contrast, stands almost upright.

gewusst: Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1781, the first planet to be found with a telescope.
To this day only one single space probe has visited Uranus: Voyager 2.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is long-sighted sees things close up blurrily, but often sees well in the distance. Glasses or contact lenses with converging lenses help.
wichtigste: Long-sighted people mainly see things close up blurrily.
Usually the eyeball is built a little too short.
The sharp image would only form behind the retina.
A converging lens corrects long-sightedness.
The technical term is hyperopia.
Children can often make up for slight long-sightedness themselves.

abschnitte.text: In a healthy eye the rays of light meet exactly on the **retina**. A sharp image forms there. In **long-sightedness** the **eyeball** is usually built a little too short. The rays of light would only meet **behind the retina**. That is why a blurred image forms on the retina, especially of things close up. The technical term is **hyperopia**: “hyper” means “over” in Greek.

Long-sighted people have difficulty above all with **reading** or with needlework. They often see well in the distance. When looking at things close up, the eye constantly has to work harder than necessary. This is tiring and can cause **headaches** and tired eyes. That is why it is important to have your eyes checked.

Many children are slightly long-sighted and hardly notice it. Their **lens** is very elastic and can curve strongly. In this way it makes up for the error itself. But this can be tiring. An eye doctor can tell during an examination whether glasses are needed.

Long-sightedness is corrected with a **converging lens**. It is thicker in the middle than at the edge. The lens increases the focusing power so that the image forms on the retina again. Such spectacle lenses act a little like a **magnifying glass**. That is why, if you look from outside at the eyes of a very long-sighted person, they look **enlarged**.

gewusst: With short-sightedness it is the other way round: diverging lenses help, and the eyes look smaller behind the glasses.
Spectacle lenses for long-sighted people have values with a plus, those for short-sighted people with a minus.

teile.einleitung: In the middle of the desert in Arizona in the USA there is a huge, round hole. It is the **Barringer Crater**, also called **Meteor Crater**. It was formed when an iron meteorite struck about 50,000 years ago.
wichtigste: The Barringer Crater lies in Arizona in the USA.
It is about 1 kilometre wide.
It is about 50,000 years old.
It was made by an iron meteorite.
It is named after Daniel Barringer.
Astronauts practised there for the journey to the moon.

abschnitte.text: The **Barringer Crater** lies in the desert of **Arizona** in the **USA**. It is about **1 kilometre** wide and around 170 metres deep. All around it a wall of rock rises up. In English it is also called **Meteor Crater**. It is one of the best-preserved impact craters on the Earth, because in the dry desert there is little rain that could wear it away.

About **50,000 years ago** a chunk from space struck here. It was an **iron meteorite**, probably a few dozen metres across. It raced towards the Earth at very high speed. On impact it was mostly destroyed, and huge amounts of rock flew away. Many small pieces of iron from the meteorite were found around the crater.

In the past researchers did not agree. Some thought the crater had been formed **by a volcano**, for example by a steam explosion. The mining businessman **Daniel Barringer**, on the other hand, was convinced that a meteorite had struck. For years he searched for a large lump of iron in the ground but found none. Later researchers were able to prove that he was right. That is why the crater is named **after Daniel Barringer**.

abschnitte.titel: A practice ground for the moon
abschnitte.text: The crater looks similar to the craters on the moon. That is why in the 1960s **astronauts** of the Apollo programme practised here for the journey to the moon. They learnt to recognise rock and to collect samples. Today visitors can look at the crater from the rim.

gewusst: The crater still belongs to the Barringer family today.
The meteorite left much less iron than Barringer had expected, because most of it vaporised on impact.

teile.einleitung: Toenails are hard plates on the tips of the toes. They protect the sensitive tips of the toes and keep growing throughout life.
wichtigste: A person normally has **ten toenails**.
The largest is usually the nail of the **big toe**.
Toenails **protect** the tips of the toes.
Nails cut too short and rounded can **grow in**.
After a knock a nail can turn **dark blue or black**.
If a nail falls off, a new one usually grows back.

abschnitte.text: Toenails are made of **keratin**, a tough horny substance. Hair and fingernails are made of it too. The nails are hard like little plates and **protect** the sensitive tips of the toes from above. Each foot has five toes with one nail each, ten altogether. The largest is usually the nail of the **big toe**.

A nail grows out of the **nail root**, which lies under the skin at the base of the nail. From there it slowly pushes forwards. Toenails grow much more slowly than fingernails. If a nail falls off after an injury, a new one usually grows back, as long as the nail root stays healthy. But this takes many months.

Toenails are best cut **straight** and not too short. If a nail is cut too short and rounded, it can grow into the skin at the side. This is called an **ingrown toenail**. It hurts and can become inflamed. After a bath the nails are a little softer and easier to cut.

Shoes should have **enough room** for the toes at the front. If they are too tight, they press on the nails. This can hurt and injure the nails. Children's feet in particular grow quickly, so you check regularly whether the shoes still fit.

If you stub your toe hard or something heavy falls on it, **blood can collect under the nail**. The nail then looks dark blue or black. The discolouration often grows out slowly with the nail. If it hurts a lot, you should ask a doctor.

gewusst: Nails feel no pain when you cut them, because they have no nerves.

teile.einleitung: The cell nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It contains the genetic information, the blueprint for everything the cell makes.
wichtigste: The **cell nucleus** controls the cell and contains the genetic information.
The genetic information is stored as **DNA**.
The mass of DNA and proteins is called **chromatin**.
Before division, **chromosomes** become visible.
Mature **red blood cells** have no nucleus.
**Robert Brown** described the cell nucleus around 1831.

abschnitte.text: The genetic information lies in the **cell nucleus**. From there the processes in the cell are controlled. The nucleus is surrounded by a **nuclear envelope** made of two membranes. Tiny **nuclear pores** let substances in and out. This is how copies of the genes get from the nucleus into the cytoplasm, where proteins are made according to this blueprint.

The genetic information is stored in **DNA**, deoxyribonucleic acid. This is a very long molecule. Its building blocks form the blueprint for the cell's **proteins**. When the cell is not dividing, the DNA lies loosely together with proteins. This mass is called **chromatin**. The name comes from the Greek “chroma” for colour, because it can be strongly stained with dyes.

When the cell prepares to divide, the DNA is tightly wound up and packed together. Then you can see it under the microscope as thread-like **chromosomes**. A human body cell has **46 chromosomes**. If you unrolled the DNA of a single cell, it would be about two metres long.

Not every cell keeps its nucleus. Human **red blood cells** lose it as they mature. This gives them more room for the red blood pigment **haemoglobin**, which carries oxygen. But without a nucleus they cannot divide. They live for about four months and are then replaced.

Around 1831 the Scottish botanist **Robert Brown** observed the cell nucleus in the cells of orchids. He called it “nucleus”, Latin for kernel. **Brownian motion**, the random jiggling of tiny particles in liquids, is also named after him.

gewusst: In the cell nucleus there is a dark area, the nucleolus. Building blocks for the ribosomes are made there.
The DNA of all the cells of one person laid end to end would be many billions of kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin B12 is a vitamin vital for life, needed for the blood and the nerves. The body needs only tiny amounts of it, but cannot make it itself.
wichtigste: In nature only bacteria and other micro-organisms make vitamin B12.
At the centre of the molecule sits a cobalt atom, which is why it is called cobalamin.
The daily requirement is given in micrograms.
For uptake in the gut you need the intrinsic factor from the stomach.
A deficiency can lead to anaemia and nerve damage.
The body has reserves for several years.

abschnitte.text: Neither plants nor animals can make vitamin B12 themselves. Only **micro-organisms** such as **bacteria** make it. Animals take it in through their feed or through bacteria in the digestive tract. Humans get it mainly from **animal foods** such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. People who eat a vegan diet therefore usually need a supplement with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 is the only vitamin with a **metal atom** at its centre, namely **cobalt**. That is where its chemical name **cobalamin** comes from. Like all B vitamins it is among the **water-soluble** vitamins. Even so it is an exception: the body can store larger reserves of it, above all in the liver. The daily requirement is only a few **micrograms**, that is millionths of a gram.

For the gut to be able to take up vitamin B12, a special substance from the **stomach** is needed. It is called the **intrinsic factor**. It binds the vitamin and makes its uptake in the **small intestine** possible. If this substance is missing, a deficiency results even though you eat enough vitamin B12. Then **injections into the muscle** are often given, which bypass the gut.

Vitamin B12 is needed to make **red blood cells** and for healthy **nerves**. A deficiency lasting a long time leads to **anaemia**, and you feel tired and weak. It can also damage the nerves permanently. Because the body has reserves for several years, a deficiency often shows only late. That is why, if it is suspected, the blood is tested.

gewusst: For the discovery that liver helps against a certain severe anaemia there was a Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1934. Later it was found that vitamin B12 was the active substance.
The chemist Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the structure of vitamin B12 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964 for it.

teile.einleitung: Digestion is the name for the way in which our body breaks down food and splits it into small building blocks. It begins in the mouth and leads through the gullet, stomach and gut. At the end the nutrients reach the blood, and the leftovers are got rid of.
wichtigste: Digestion begins in the mouth.
Saliva helps with eating: it makes the food slippery and begins to break it down.
Through the gullet the food reaches the stomach.
After the stomach comes the long organ, the gut.
Well-chewed food is digested more easily.
In the small intestine most nutrients reach the blood.
The digestion of a meal takes about one to three days altogether.

abschnitte.text: Digestion begins in the **mouth**. The teeth chop up the food, and the tongue shapes it into a mouthful. In the process it is mixed with **saliva**, which the salivary glands produce, about a litre a day. Saliva makes the food slippery and already begins to break down starch. People who chew well relieve the stomach, because well-chewed food is digested more easily.

When you swallow, the mouthful slides into the **gullet**. It is a muscular tube that is about 25 centimetres long in adults. With wavelike movements it pushes the food to the stomach. That is why you can even swallow standing on your head. A small lid, the **epiglottis**, stops the food from reaching the windpipe.

The **stomach** is a stretchy bag that can take in a whole meal. It kneads the food and mixes it with gastric juice. In this there is hydrochloric acid, which kills germs, and a substance that breaks down proteins. This produces a thin **chyme**. Depending on the meal, the food stays in the stomach for about two to four hours.

After the stomach comes the **gut**, which consists of the small intestine and the large intestine. In the small intestine, which is several metres long, the food is fully broken down with juices from the pancreas and bile. The nutrients pass through the gut wall into the blood. In the large intestine water is taken from the rest. What is left is got rid of as faeces.

For good digestion the body needs **dietary fibre**, also called roughage. It is found in wholemeal bread, vegetables, fruit and pulses. Drinking enough water and moving about also help the gut. In the gut live trillions of useful bacteria, the **gut flora**. They help with digesting and protect against germs that cause illness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Liquid in the mouth that makes food slippery.
Muscular tube that brings food from the mouth to the stomach.
Pulpy mass of food and digestive juices.
Plant fibres that stimulate the activity of the gut.

gewusst: The stomach makes a layer of mucus so that it does not digest itself.
The rumbling of the stomach arises when air and liquid are moved through the empty stomach and gut.
The gut of an adult is several metres long altogether.

teile.einleitung: A countdown is counting backwards to zero. We know it from rocket launches, but also from New Year's Eve or from games. At zero, what everyone has been waiting for happens.
wichtigste: In a countdown you count backwards, for example 3, 2, 1, 0.
The last number is always zero.
At a rocket launch, the rocket lifts off at zero.
“Countdown” is built from “count” and “down”.
The idea comes from the German film “Frau im Mond” (“Woman in the Moon”) of 1929.
If there is a problem, the countdown is stopped.

abschnitte.text: Normally you count forwards: 1, 2, 3. In a **countdown** you count **backwards**: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. So after 4 comes 3, and after 1 comes 0. The **zero** is always the very last number. Then the moment everyone has been waiting for has arrived. The word is English: “count” means to number and “down” means downwards.

At a rocket launch, the countdown shows exactly when it starts. Long before, a list of many tasks begins: filling tanks, checking equipment, watching the weather. In the last seconds, people count aloud together. At **zero the rocket lifts off**. That way everyone involved in the control centre knows at the same time what is happening.

Where does the countdown at a rocket launch come from? The idea comes from a **film**. In the German silent film **“Frau im Mond”** of **1929**, people counted backwards before the launch of a Moon rocket. The director wanted to increase the tension for the audience. Later, real space travel took over this idea.

If a **problem** is discovered before the launch, the countdown is **stopped**. Then experts check everything carefully. Sometimes it carries on after a short time, and sometimes the launch is put off to another day. Better to wait than to take a risk: that is the rule.

In Switzerland, too, there are countdowns with many people, especially on **New Year's Eve**. Shortly before **midnight**, many people count backwards together: ten, nine, eight and so on. At zero the **new year** begins, and people wish each other a happy new year. There are also countdowns in games, competitions or in calendars counting down to a birthday.

gewusst: An Advent calendar is really a countdown too: it counts the days until Christmas.
At a rocket launch, people often say “Liftoff” when the rocket leaves the ground.

teile.einleitung: A growth spurt is a time when you suddenly grow much faster than usual. The biggest spurt after the toddler years happens to teenagers, when growth increases strongly once again during puberty.
wichtigste: Teenagers have the clearest growth spurt, when growth speeds up during puberty.
On average girls reach the spurt about two years earlier than boys.
At the peak many grow about 8 to 10 centimetres a year.
Growth hormone particularly promotes growing taller.
The hands and feet usually grow first.
Calcium is particularly important for building bones.

abschnitte.text: In childhood you grow quite steadily, about 5 to 6 centimetres a year. With the **growth spurt** of adolescence things suddenly go much faster. At the **peak** many teenagers grow about **8 to 10 centimetres** a year. That is almost twice as fast as in the primary school years. After that, growth slows down quickly until it stops completely.

On average **girls** reach their growth spurt about **two years earlier** than boys. That is why girls aged 11 or 12 are often taller than boys of the same age. The boys catch up later. They usually grow a little more during the spurt and so on average end up taller. But when the spurt begins is different for every person.

The body does not grow everywhere at the same time. Usually the **hands and feet** get bigger first, then the arms and legs follow, and finally the **trunk**. Because the arms and legs get longer in a short time, your **sense of your own body** first has to get used to it. The brain needs some time to adjust the movements. That is why teenagers in a growth spurt sometimes seem a little clumsy.

For growth, new bones, muscles and organs have to be built. For this the body needs a lot of **energy** and **building materials**. That is why teenagers in a growth spurt are often especially hungry. The mineral **calcium**, a main building block of bones, is important. It is found, for example, in dairy products, mineral water and green vegetables.

An important driver of growing taller is **growth hormone**, also called **somatotropin**. It stimulates the **growth plates** of the bones. A particularly large amount of it is released during sleep. That is why enough sleep is important especially at this time. When the spurt is over, the growth plates gradually close.

gewusst: Because the feet grow first, teenagers in a growth spurt often need new shoes several times in a short period.
Some teenagers feel a pulling in their knees or heels when growing fast, because muscles and tendons have to catch up.

teile.einleitung: Cytokines are small proteins with which cells send each other messages. They play a large part in the immune system. They control inflammation, fever and the growth of cells.
wichtigste: Cytokines are messenger substances for communication between cells.
Interleukin-1 triggers fever.
Chemokines attract immune cells to a particular place.
Interleukin-10 slows down inflammation.
An excessive release is called a cytokine storm.
Some medicines catch the cytokine TNF-alpha.

abschnitte.text: Cytokines are **small proteins**. Cells release them to influence other cells. They act like messages: one cell tells another to grow, to divide or to fight germs. Cytokines include **interleukins**, interferons, chemokines and **tumour necrosis factor**, among others. The name interleukin means “between the leukocytes”, because they were first discovered as signals between white blood cells.

Some cytokines drive inflammation. **Interleukin-1** reaches the **hypothalamus** in the brain and raises the set point for body temperature there. This causes **fever**. Interleukin-6 and **TNF-alpha** also raise the temperature. Other cytokines such as **interleukin-10** reduce inflammation. They help to end an immune reaction once the work is done.

A special group is called **chemokines**. They form a gradient: close to the site of inflammation there is a lot of them, further away little. Immune cells follow this gradient and so find the place where they are needed. This directed movement is called **chemotaxis**.

Normally the release of cytokines is well controlled. But sometimes immune cells release huge amounts uncontrollably. This is called a **cytokine storm**. It can cause high fever, circulatory failure and damage to organs and is life-threatening.

In some diseases inflammation is too strong all the time. Medicines such as **infliximab** and **adalimumab** are antibodies that catch TNF-alpha. They are used, for example, for rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease and psoriasis. On the other hand, cytokines can also be given as medicines: the growth factor **G-CSF** stimulates the bone marrow after chemotherapy to make new white blood cells faster.

gewusst: The fact that you feel tired and weak with flu is also linked to cytokines that act on the brain.
Many cytokines work even in the tiniest amounts.

teile.einleitung: Claude Nicollier is the first Swiss person to have flown into space. He flew into space four times on the American space shuttle and, among other things, helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
wichtigste: Claude Nicollier was born in 1944 in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
His mother tongue is French.
Before he became an astronaut, he was a pilot in the Swiss Air Force.
He flew into space four times: in 1992, 1993, 1996 and 1999.
He made all his flights on NASA's space shuttle.
In 1999 he became the first Swiss person to make a spacewalk.

abschnitte.text: Claude Nicollier was born in **1944** in **Vevey** in the canton of Vaud. The town lies on **Lake Geneva** in western Switzerland. His mother tongue is therefore **French**. He studied **physics and astronomy** and was also a **pilot in the Swiss Air Force**. Later he became an astronaut of the European Space Agency ESA.

Nicollier made all his flights on the **space shuttle**. This was a spacecraft of the American space agency **NASA** that launched like a rocket and landed like an aeroplane. European astronauts were allowed to fly on it. Nicollier flew into space in **1992, 1993, 1996 and 1999**, that is, **four times**. On his first flight in the summer of 1992, he was **47 years** old.

The **Hubble Space Telescope** orbits Earth and takes pictures of the universe. On two missions, Nicollier helped to service the telescope. During the first repair in 1993, he operated the shuttle's large **robot arm**. With it he moved colleagues who were working outside on the telescope.

On his last flight in **1999**, Nicollier himself climbed out of the space shuttle. This made him the **first Swiss person** to make a **spacewalk**. Outside, he worked for several hours on the Hubble telescope and fitted new parts. After his flights he passed on his knowledge, among other things as a professor at **EPFL** in Lausanne.

gewusst: On his four flights, Nicollier spent more than 40 days in space in total.

teile.einleitung: The World Health Organization, WHO for short, is a specialised agency of the United Nations. It is based in Geneva and coordinates international health work.
wichtigste: The WHO is a specialised agency of the UN based in Geneva.
Its constitution came into force on 7 April 1948, and since then this day has been World Health Day.
The highest body is the World Health Assembly of all member states.
In 2026 the WHO is led by Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, who has been Director-General since 2017.
In 2020 the WHO declared the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic.
Since 1977 the WHO has published a model list of essential medicines.

abschnitte.text: The **WHO** is a legally independent **specialised agency** of the United Nations with its own member states. Its headquarters are in **Geneva**, in Switzerland. Its **constitution** came into force on **7 April 1948**. That is why **World Health Day** is marked every year on this day with a special theme. The WHO coordinates international cooperation in health care.

The highest body is the **World Health Assembly**. All member states are represented there. It meets every year in Geneva and decides the policy and budget of the WHO. The organisation is led by a Director-General. In 2026 this is the Ethiopian **Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus**, who has held the post since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022.

The WHO issues recommendations and guidelines for health. Since 1977 it has published the **Model List of Essential Medicines**. It names medicines that are important for the basic health care of every country and is revised about every two years. For antibiotics there is the **AWaRe** classification: Access, Watch and Reserve. It is meant to help use antibiotics in a targeted and sparing way.

The WHO watches diseases all over the world and gives warnings when there is danger. On **11 March 2020** it classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus as a **pandemic**. A great success was the fight against **smallpox**: in 1980 the WHO declared this disease wiped out. It also supports vaccination programmes against other diseases.

gewusst: According to the WHO constitution, health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease.
Smallpox is so far the only human disease that has been wiped out worldwide.

teile.einleitung: The Drake equation is a formula for estimating how many civilisations in our Milky Way could get in touch with us. It comes from the American radio astronomer Frank Drake.
wichtigste: Frank Drake presented the equation in 1961.
This happened at a conference at the Green Bank radio observatory.
N is the number of civilisations in the Milky Way able to communicate.
N is the product of several factors, for example R* and L.
Many factors are completely unknown, so the results vary greatly.
Its use lies in breaking the big question down into smaller questions.

abschnitte.text: In **1961**, a small conference took place at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory in **Green Bank** in the US state of West Virginia. The subject was the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. **Frank Drake** worked there as a radio astronomer. He wrote an equation on the board that served as the **agenda** for the discussion. That is how the **Drake equation** came about.

The result is called **N**: the number of civilisations in the Milky Way with which we could get in touch. N is the **product** of several factors. **R*** is the number of new stars per year in our galaxy, according to today's estimates a few per year. **fp** is the share of stars with planets, **ne** the number of habitable planets per system. Then come the shares on which life (**fl**), intelligence (**fi**) and technology for communication (**fc**) arise. **L** is the length of time during which a civilisation sends out detectable signals.

Let us assume: R* = 2, fp = 0.5, ne = 2, fl = 0.5, fi = 0.1, fc = 0.1 and L = 10,000 years. You **multiply** all the numbers: 2 · 0.5 · 2 · 0.5 gives 1. Then 1 · 0.1 · 0.1 gives 0.01. Finally 0.01 · 10,000 gives **100**. With these assumptions there would therefore be 100 civilisations. With other assumptions, something quite different comes out.

abschnitte.titel: What we know and what we do not
abschnitte.text: Thanks to the **search for exoplanets**, **fp** is now the best known: most stars have planets. The biological and social factors, however, are still **completely open**. Nobody knows how often life arises or how long civilisations last. That is why **L** is one of the most uncertain factors. Depending on the assumptions, the results vary over many **orders of magnitude**, from fewer than one to millions of civilisations.

The Drake equation does not give a reliable number. Its most important use is that it breaks the big question about alien civilisations down into **smaller questions**. It shows which questions research has to clear up: in astronomy, in biology and even in the history of societies. In this way it helps us to think about a difficult subject in an orderly way.

gewusst: As early as 1960, Frank Drake had listened for signals from two nearby stars with a radio telescope at Green Bank; the project was called “Ozma”.
To this day, no signal from an extraterrestrial civilisation has been reliably detected.

teile.einleitung: Werner Arber is a Swiss microbiologist from the canton of Aargau. He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1978 for discovering restriction enzymes.
wichtigste: Werner Arber was born in 1929 in Gränichen in the canton of Aargau.
He studied at ETH Zurich and later did research in Geneva and Basel.
In 1978 he received the Nobel Prize together with Daniel Nathans and Hamilton Smith.
He discovered restriction enzymes, which cut up foreign DNA.
His discovery became one of the foundations of genetic engineering.
In 2011 he became President of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences.

abschnitte.text: **Werner Arber** was born in 1929 in **Gränichen** in the canton of **Aargau**. He studied at **ETH Zurich** and then worked in **Geneva**. In 1971 he became professor of microbiology at the **Biozentrum** of the University of Basel. He did research there for many years. He is one of the best-known Swiss scientists.

Arber studied **bacteriophages**, which are viruses that attack bacteria. He showed that bacteria can cut up phage DNA that has got into them. For this they have special enzymes, the **restriction enzymes**. The bacteria protect their own DNA by **methylation**: they attach small methyl groups to the recognition sites. This way the enzyme does not recognise the bacterium's own DNA as a target.

Restriction enzymes do not cut DNA just anywhere. Each enzyme recognises a short, specific **sequence of bases**, which often reads the same on both strands. Such sequences are called **palindromic**. The enzyme cuts reliably there. This makes it possible to cut out pieces of DNA in a targeted way and put them together in new ways. This became an important foundation of **genetic engineering**.

In 1978 Arber received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**. He shared it with the Americans **Daniel Nathans** and **Hamilton Smith**. They had isolated and used restriction enzymes that Arber had predicted. In 2011 Arber became **President of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences** in the Vatican. He was the first Protestant in this post.

gewusst: Today restriction enzymes are used every day in laboratories all over the world.
Arber was a Protestant and yet he led the Pope's academy of sciences.

teile.einleitung: The spine consists of many single bones, the vertebrae. They carry the body, make it flexible and protect the spinal cord.
wichtigste: The bones of the spine are called vertebrae.
Humans have seven neck vertebrae, just like the giraffe.
The top vertebra is called the atlas and carries the head.
A canal containing the spinal cord runs through the vertebrae.
Springy intervertebral discs lie between the vertebrae.
Seen from the side, the spine has the shape of a double S.

abschnitte.text: The **spine** is not a single bone. It consists of many **vertebrae** stacked on top of each other. In the neck there are **seven neck vertebrae**, in the chest area twelve **thoracic vertebrae** and in the lower back five **lumbar vertebrae**. Below these come the **sacrum** and the **tailbone**. The lumbar vertebrae are the thickest because they carry the most.

The top neck vertebra is called the **atlas**. It is named after a giant from a Greek legend who holds up the sky. The atlas carries the head. Below it lies the second neck vertebra, around which the head can turn. The neck vertebrae make the neck flexible so that you can **nod** and **turn** your head.

In the middle of each vertebra there is a **hole**. Together these holes form a canal. In it lies the **spinal cord**, protected, which carries messages between the brain and the body. Between most vertebrae lies an **intervertebral disc**. It is like a small cushion and absorbs jolts. Seen from the side, the spine is curved like a **double S**, which gives it extra springiness.

Animals with a backbone are called **vertebrates**. They include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, including humans. Almost all mammals have **seven neck vertebrae**. This is true even of the **giraffe** with its long neck. In the giraffe each single neck vertebra is simply very long.

gewusst: A mouse and a giraffe have the same number of neck vertebrae, namely seven.
A giraffe's neck vertebra can be more than 20 centimetres long.

teile.einleitung: A burn happens when heat damages the skin, for example from a hot cooker plate, boiling water or fire. With the right first aid you can ease the pain and limit the damage.
wichtigste: Small burns are cooled with lukewarm to cool tap water, not with ice.
Home remedies such as butter or flour do not belong on a burn.
Usually three degrees are distinguished, and some classifications have a fourth.
Typical for the second degree are blisters, which you do not prick.
Clothing that has stuck on is left on the wound.
Burns over a large area are cooled only briefly, otherwise there is a danger of hypothermia.
If clothing is on fire, you roll the person on the ground or cover them with a fire blanket.

abschnitte.text: In a **first-degree** burn only the outer skin is affected. The skin is red and hurts, but usually heals without scars. In the **second degree** the dermis is also damaged, **blisters** form, and it hurts a lot. In the **third degree** the skin is destroyed deeply and can look white or black. Some classifications name a fourth degree as well, in which the tissue is charred.

A small burn is cooled at once with **lukewarm to cool tap water**. This eases the pain and limits the damage. **Ice** is not suitable, because it can damage the skin further. **Home remedies** such as butter, oil or flour are also wrong, because they encourage infections. Loose clothing, jewellery and watches are removed early, before the area swells.

A **burn blister** is not pricked. It protects the skin underneath from germs. If clothing sticks to the burnt skin, you do not tear it off but leave it stuck. This way the skin is not injured even more. After cooling, you cover the wound with a **sterile, non-fluffy dressing**, for example a burn dressing. Cotton wool is unsuitable, because fibres stay behind in the wound.

For burns over a large area you call the **emergency number 144** at once. Here long cooling is dangerous, because the whole body quickly cools down. This applies especially to children. That is why you cool only briefly and then cover the person up warmly. How large the burnt area is, you often estimate with your own **palm**: it corresponds to about one per cent of the body surface.

If a person's clothing is on fire, they must not run away. The draught when running fans the fire further. It is better to **roll** the person on the ground or to cover them with a **fire blanket**. This takes the oxygen away from the flames, and they are smothered. In a fire in Switzerland you call the fire brigade on the number **118**.

gewusst: Sunburn is also a burn, usually of the first degree, set off by the sun's UV radiation.
Burns from hot liquids are called scalds. They are among the most common accidents at home for small children.

teile.einleitung: Cell biology is the science of cells, the tiny building blocks of all living things. It studies how cells are built, how they work and how they divide. Almost all cells are so small that you can only see them under a microscope.
wichtigste: All living things consist of one or many cells.
Every cell is surrounded by a biomembrane made of a phospholipid bilayer.
The mitochondria are the main place of cellular respiration and of making ATP.
Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, but animal cells do not.
Prokaryotes such as bacteria have no cell nucleus, but eukaryotes do.
The passive movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane is called osmosis.
New cells always come from the division of cells that already exist.

abschnitte.text: In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at thin slices of cork under a simple microscope. He saw small chambers and called them cells. In 1838 and 1839 Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann stated that all plants and animals consist of cells. Rudolf Virchow added that every cell comes from another cell. These ideas form the **cell theory**.

A cell is like a small factory with different departments, the **organelles**. The **cell nucleus** contains the genetic information DNA and controls the cell. In the mitochondria energy is obtained in the form of ATP through cellular respiration. Ribosomes make proteins, and the cytoplasm fills the space in between. A human being consists of many trillions of such cells.

Every cell is surrounded by a thin covering, the **biomembrane**. It consists of a double layer of phospholipids, which are fat-like molecules. The membrane is selectively permeable, which means it lets only certain substances through. Water can pass through it, and this is called **osmosis**. That is why lettuce leaves shrivel in salt water and become crisp again in clear water.

In addition to the membrane, plant cells have a solid **cell wall** made of cellulose. They contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large vacuole with cell sap. Animal cells and human cells have neither a cell wall nor chloroplasts. That is why they are softer and can take on very different shapes, such as long nerve cells or round red blood cells.

Living things with a cell nucleus are called **eukaryotes**, and they include animals, plants and fungi. Bacteria are **prokaryotes**: they have no cell nucleus, and their DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes are usually much smaller and more simply built. They are among the oldest living things on Earth. In 1869 the Basel doctor Friedrich Miescher was the first to discover in cell nuclei the nucleic acid that we now call DNA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part inside a cell with a particular task.
The power station of the cell, in which cellular respiration takes place.
The movement of water through a membrane that does not let all substances through.
A living thing without a cell nucleus, for example a bacterium.
A tough substance of which the cell wall of plants is made.

gewusst: The yolk of a hen's egg is a single, huge cell.
The longest human nerve cells reach from the spinal cord to the toes and are about a metre long.
About as many bacterial cells live in the human body as there are body cells of our own.

teile.einleitung: A wobbly tooth is a milk tooth that has become loose and will soon fall out. It shows that a permanent tooth is already growing underneath. In many children the change of teeth begins at about the age of 6.
wichtigste: A wobbly tooth is usually a loose milk tooth.
It becomes loose because a permanent tooth pushes up from below.
The root of the milk tooth almost completely dissolves before it falls out.
Many children get their first wobbly tooth at about the age of 6.
The change of teeth takes several years, usually until about the age of 12.
New front teeth often have a slightly jagged edge.

abschnitte.text: Children first have **milk teeth**, 20 of them altogether. Under each milk tooth a **permanent tooth** is already growing in the jaw. It pushes up from below, and the **root** of the milk tooth slowly dissolves. As a result the milk tooth loses its hold and becomes loose. That is why a milk tooth that has fallen out is often just a small crown without a root.

In many children the **change of teeth** begins at about **6 years** old. Some get their first wobbly tooth a little earlier, others later. Usually the lower **front teeth** fall out first. After that the teeth fall out one by one, and new ones grow in. The whole change takes **several years**, usually until about the age of 12.

abschnitte.titel: Be patient with a wobbly tooth
abschnitte.text: If a wobbly tooth is still quite firm, it is best to wait. Over time it becomes **looser by itself** and falls out when it is loose enough. Pulling on it with force only hurts. But you may move it carefully with your tongue. When it falls out, it can bleed a little for a moment, but this stops quickly.

A **permanent tooth** takes the place of the milk tooth. It has to last a lifetime, which is why good tooth brushing is important. New **front teeth** often have a small, **jagged** edge. Over time it becomes smooth from biting. The permanent teeth are also bigger and often a little more yellowish than the milk teeth.

gewusst: Adults have up to 32 permanent teeth once all their wisdom teeth have grown.
In French-speaking Switzerland and in France, according to an old custom, the “petite souris”, a little mouse, brings a present for the tooth that has fallen out.

teile.einleitung: Cellular respiration is the power station of life: cells use oxygen to turn glucose into energy. It goes on all the time in almost all the cells of your body, even now while you are reading. Breathing with your lungs is there to supply the cells with oxygen.
wichtigste: In cellular respiration, cells use oxygen to turn glucose into energy.
It is also called aerobic respiration, because it needs oxygen.
Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste products.
The energy is stored in the molecule ATP.
The most important place for cellular respiration is the mitochondria.
Without oxygen, muscles can briefly obtain energy through lactic acid fermentation.
Cellular respiration is in a way the counterpart of photosynthesis in plants.

abschnitte.text: During digestion our food is broken down, for example into the sugar **glucose**. The blood brings glucose and oxygen to every cell. In the cell the glucose is broken down step by step. At the end **carbon dioxide** and water are produced. The cell stores the energy that is released in the molecule **ATP**.

**ATP** stands for adenosine triphosphate. You can imagine it as a small charged battery. The cell uses ATP to move muscles, to build substances or to pass on signals. From a single glucose molecule the cell obtains around 30 ATP. Part of the energy is released as heat and keeps our body warm.

Cellular respiration takes place in three stages. First the glucose is split in half in the cytoplasm, and this is called **glycolysis**.
