Then it continues in the **mitochondria**, in what is called the citric acid cycle. In the last step, the respiratory chain, oxygen is used up and most of the ATP is made. The citric acid cycle was researched by the biochemist Hans Krebs, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1953.

Breathing with the lungs and cellular respiration are closely linked. When we breathe in, the lungs take in oxygen, which the blood carries to the cells. The blood carries the carbon dioxide from cellular respiration back to the lungs, where we breathe it out. During sport the muscles need more energy, which is why we breathe faster and the heart beats more strongly.

During a sprint the muscles sometimes do not get enough oxygen. Then they obtain energy without oxygen through **lactic acid fermentation**. But this provides much less ATP. Yeasts use a similar fermentation and produce alcohol and carbon dioxide, which makes bread dough rise. In photosynthesis plants turn carbon dioxide and water back into glucose and oxygen.

begriffe.erklaerung: Grape sugar, the most important source of energy for cells.
A molecule in which the cell stores and passes on energy.
A part of the cell in which cellular respiration mainly takes place.
Taking place with oxygen.

gewusst: Every day your body makes and uses up about as much ATP as you weigh.
A large part of your body heat comes from cellular respiration.
Plants carry out cellular respiration too, not only photosynthesis.

teile.einleitung: With the **Artemis programme** NASA wants to take people to the moon again, for the first time since 1972. Later there are even meant to be bases there. Europe is taking part and supplies an important part of the spacecraft.
wichtigste: The main aim of Artemis is to take people to the moon again.
In Greek legend Artemis is the twin sister of Apollo.
The crew flies in the Orion spacecraft.
Europe supplies the service module of the Orion spacecraft.
In April 2026 four people flew around the moon on Artemis II.
The crew included an astronaut from Canada.

abschnitte.text: The first moon landing was achieved in 1969 with the **Apollo programme**. The new programme is called **Artemis**. In Greek legend Artemis is the **twin sister of Apollo** and the goddess of the moon. The name shows that Artemis follows on from Apollo. But this time women and people from other countries are also meant to go to the moon.

The astronauts fly in the **Orion** spacecraft. It launches on a large rocket called the **SLS**. Orion has a capsule for the crew and behind it a **service module**. This provides power, water, air and propulsion. The service module comes from **Europe** and is built on behalf of **ESA**. Switzerland is a member of ESA and so is also involved.

On **Artemis I** in 2022 Orion flew around the moon and back without people. In **April 2026**, with **Artemis II**, people flew around the moon again for the first time. On board were **4** astronauts: three from the USA and one from **Canada**. The crew set a record: they travelled **further from the Earth than any human being** before. A landing was not yet planned on this flight.

On later flights people are meant to land on the moon again. One goal is the area around the **moon's south pole**. There are craters there into which sunlight never falls, and **ice** is thought to be inside them. Water could later be used to make drinking water, air to breathe or even fuel. In the long term the moon is also meant to serve as a practice ground for journeys to **Mars**. When exactly the landings take place depends on the technology and on money.

gewusst: On Artemis II a person who is not from the USA flew to the moon for the first time.
On Artemis I there was a dummy on board, which used measuring instruments to test how much radiation people receive on the flight.

teile.einleitung: The chromosphere is a thin layer of the Sun's atmosphere directly above the shining surface. Normally it is outshone, but during a total solar eclipse it appears as a reddish fringe.
wichtigste: The chromosphere lies above the photosphere and is about 2,000 kilometres thick.
It glows reddish because of the hydrogen line H-alpha.
The temperature in it rises again after a minimum.
Spicules are narrow jets of gas that rise from it.
Above it come the transition region and then the corona.
The name comes from the Greek word “chroma” for colour.

abschnitte.text: The Sun has no solid surface. What we see as a shining disc is called the **photosphere**. Above it lies the **chromosphere**. It reaches up about **2,000 kilometres**. After that comes a thin boundary layer, the **transition region**, and finally the outermost layer, the **corona**. The name chromosphere comes from the Greek word **“chroma”** for colour, because during eclipses it appears as a coloured fringe around the Sun.

The chromosphere radiates especially strongly in one particular colour of hydrogen. This **H-alpha line** lies at 656 nanometres in the **red** part of the light. That is why the layer looks reddish during a total solar eclipse. Shortly before and after totality, when the Moon is just covering the photosphere, you see only the chromosphere for a few seconds. Its light then shows bright lines that suddenly flash up. This is called the **flash spectrum**.

You would expect it to get cooler further away from the Sun's interior. At the transition from the photosphere, the temperature indeed falls to a **minimum** of about 4,000 kelvin. After that, however, it **rises** again in the chromosphere to about 10,000 to 20,000 kelvin. In the **transition region**, only a few hundred kilometres thick, it then jumps to over a million kelvin. This layer is mainly observed in ultraviolet light.

Narrow, needle-shaped jets of gas shoot up from the chromosphere. They are called **spicules**. At about 20 kilometres per second they rise a few thousand kilometres and live only a few minutes. Bigger are the **prominences**: arcs of gas held above the chromosphere by **magnetic fields**. At the edge of the Sun they glow red, while in front of the solar disc they appear dark as **filaments**.

gewusst: With special H-alpha telescopes, the chromosphere can be observed even without an eclipse.
Exactly how the outer layers of the Sun become so hot is still not fully understood.
Never look at the Sun without a suitable protective filter, not even through a telescope.

teile.einleitung: In a sprain you twist your foot, and the ligaments at a joint are overstretched. It hurts, the joint swells, but the bone is not broken.
wichtigste: In a sprain the ligaments at the joint are injured.
The joint swells, hurts and is hard to move.
The ankle is the joint that is sprained most often.
First aid follows the RICE rule: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
You never put ice straight on the skin, but wrapped in a cloth.
Warming up well before sport helps to prevent sprains.

abschnitte.text: Joints are held together by **ligaments**. These are firm but slightly stretchy strands of connective tissue. If you twist your foot, the ligaments are suddenly **overstretched** a lot. This is called a sprain, in technical language a **distortion**. The bone stays whole. The **ankle** is hit most often, because when running and jumping you can easily turn your foot over.

After a sprain the joint **hurts** and becomes thick. Often you can hardly move it or put weight on it. Frequently the skin turns **blue** after a while. In the injury small blood vessels tear, and blood escapes into the tissue. This is how a **bruise** forms. If the pain is very strong or you cannot put your foot down at all, a doctor should check whether something is broken.

For sports injuries the **RICE rule** helps. **R** stands for rest: you stop playing at once. **I** stands for ice: cooling eases pain and swelling. **C** stands for compression, that is, a slightly pressing bandage. **E** stands for elevation: the injured part of the body is raised above the heart, so that it swells less.

You never put a cold pack or ice straight on the skin. The great cold could harm the skin. That is why you wrap the ice in a **cloth**. This way the joint is still cooled well. You cool with breaks and keep checking how the skin feels.

You do not carry on playing with a freshly sprained foot. The joint needs **rest**, otherwise the injury gets worse. A mild sprain usually heals within a few weeks. Before sport, a good **warm-up** helps: warmed-up muscles and ligaments are more elastic and hold the joint better. Suitable shoes also give the foot support.

gewusst: If a ligament tears completely in a serious injury, it is called a torn ligament.
The word “distortion” comes from Latin and means roughly “twisting”.

teile.einleitung: Dark matter is an invisible form of matter that gives off no light and reflects none. It can only be detected by its gravity, which affects stars and galaxies. According to current knowledge, there is about five times more dark matter in the universe than ordinary matter.
wichtigste: Dark matter is invisible and only makes itself noticed through its gravity.
It makes up about 27 per cent of the energy density of the universe.
The Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky suspected its existence in 1933 in the Coma galaxy cluster.
In the 1970s, Vera Rubin showed that spiral galaxies rotate too fast at their outer edges.
The gravitational lensing effect can be used to map where it is.
Possible dark matter particles are WIMPs and axions.
So far, no dark matter particle has been detected directly.

abschnitte.text: Dark matter is matter that cannot be seen because it does not give off, absorb or reflect light. But its **gravity** acts on stars, gas and galaxies. Without it, galaxies would fly apart. It is not the same as black holes or **dark energy**.

abschnitte.titel: Fritz Zwicky and the Coma Cluster
abschnitte.text: The Swiss astronomer **Fritz Zwicky** worked in California and studied the Coma galaxy cluster in 1933. He found that the galaxies in it were moving far too fast. The visible mass would never have been enough to hold them together. He concluded that a lot of invisible mass must be present and spoke of dark matter.

In the 1970s, the American **Vera Rubin** measured how fast stars in spiral galaxies orbit the centre. It was expected that outer stars would circle more slowly, just as the outer planets do around the Sun. But her **rotation curves** stayed flat far out, so the stars were moving just as fast. This is explained by a huge halo of dark matter around every galaxy.

Heavy masses bend light like a lens; this is called the **gravitational lensing effect**. It allows scientists to map where dark matter is in galaxy clusters. In the **Bullet Cluster**, two galaxy clusters have collided. There, most of the mass is separated in space from the hot gas, which is strong evidence for dark matter.

Researchers suspect that dark matter is made of unknown particles. Popular candidates are **WIMPs**, weakly interacting massive particles, and very light **axions**. Axions were originally proposed to solve a puzzle of particle physics, the strong CP problem. In deep underground laboratories, huge detectors wait for rare collisions, and scientists also search for it at CERN in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of galaxies held together by gravity.
A graph showing how fast stars at different distances orbit the centre of a galaxy.
A large mass that bends and distorts the light from objects behind it.
A suspected heavy particle that hardly reacts with ordinary matter.

gewusst: Dark matter particles are probably flying through your body right now without you noticing anything.
Fritz Zwicky also discovered many supernovae and, together with Walter Baade, coined the term supernova.
Our Milky Way sits inside a halo of dark matter that is much bigger than its visible disc.

teile.einleitung: Inside every tooth lies a soft, living tissue: the dental pulp. In German it is called “Zahnmark”, and in everyday language people often simply say the nerve of the tooth.
wichtigste: The **dental pulp** is the soft tissue inside the tooth.
In German it is called **“Zahnmark”**, meaning tooth marrow.
It contains connective tissue, nerves and blood vessels.
The pulp fills the pulp cavity in the crown and the root canals.
Inflammation of the pulp is called **pulpitis**.
In root canal treatment, diseased pulp is removed.

abschnitte.text: A tooth is built up in layers. On the outside lies the hard **enamel**, and underneath it the **dentine**. Right inside is the **pulp cavity** with the pulp. In every root the cavity continues as a narrow **root canal**. Nerves and vessels run through it to the tip of the root.

The pulp consists of connective tissue with **nerves** and **blood vessels**. The blood vessels supply the tooth with nutrients. The nerves report stimuli such as cold, heat or pain. At the edge of the pulp there are cells that can make new dentine throughout life. That is why the pulp cavity slowly gets smaller with age.

The ending “itis” means inflammation. So **pulpitis** is an inflammation of the pulp. Deep **tooth decay** is often the cause: it begins in the enamel, eats its way through the dentine and finally reaches the pulp. Pulpitis often causes severe, throbbing pain. Then you should go to the dentist quickly.

If the pulp is badly inflamed or has died, **root canal treatment** often helps. The dentist removes the diseased tissue from the root canals. Then the canals are cleaned and tightly filled. This way the tooth is saved, even though it is no longer alive inside.

After an accident, such as a fall onto the mouth, the pulp can die. Then breakdown products are deposited in the dentine. Over time the tooth looks **greyish** or brownish. Such a discolouration is a sign that you should have the tooth examined.

gewusst: The name pulp comes from the Latin pulpa and means flesh or the flesh of a fruit.
A tooth with dead pulp no longer feels cold, but it can still stay in the mouth for many years.

teile.einleitung: CaSSIS is a camera that takes colour and three-dimensional pictures of Mars from orbit. It was developed under the leadership of the University of Bern and flies on a European Mars probe.
wichtigste: CaSSIS stands for “Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System”.
The camera flies on the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, which reached Mars in 2016.
The development was led by the Physics Institute of the University of Bern.
With a rotation mechanism it takes stereo images.
It reaches about 4.6 metres per pixel and has four colour filters.
The stereo images are used to make height models of the Martian surface.

abschnitte.text: CaSSIS is the camera system of the **ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter**. This probe from ESA and Roscosmos launched in 2016 and reached Mars in the same year. Its main goal is to detect **trace gases** such as methane in the Martian atmosphere. Trace gases occur only in tiny amounts. Methane is exciting because it could point to geological or perhaps even biological processes. CaSSIS provides the pictures of the surface for this.

The development was led by the **Physics Institute of the University of Bern** under Nicolas Thomas. The University of Bern has long experience with measuring instruments for space. The name **CaSSIS** stands for “Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System”. It describes the two strengths of the camera: **colour images** and **stereo images**.

The telescope sits on a **rotation mechanism**. It first photographs an area at an angle looking forward. Seconds later, when the probe has flown on, it turns and photographs the same area at an angle looking back. This gives two images from different **viewing angles**, much as our two eyes see the world slightly differently.

From two images taken at different angles, **differences in height** can be calculated. This produces **digital height models**, that is, three-dimensional maps of craters, slopes and gullies. From its orbit about 400 kilometres up, CaSSIS reaches about **4.6 metres per pixel**. An image strip is about 9 kilometres wide. The focal length of the telescope is about 880 millimetres.

The image sensor is covered with **four colour filters**. They range from visible light to the **near infrared**, which our eyes can no longer see. Because different rocks and ice reflect light differently, they can be told apart in the colour images. This lets researchers see, for example, where fresh material has been uncovered.

gewusst: At 4.6 metres per pixel, you can make out boulders the size of a lorry in the images.
The name ExoMars means that the mission is looking for traces of life on Mars.

teile.einleitung: Growth means that a child becomes bigger and heavier over many years until it is grown up. Behind it lie cell division, hormones and special growth zones in the bones. Surprisingly, you grow most while you sleep.
wichtigste: New body cells arise during growth through cell division.
Long bones grow in length at the growth plates.
The growth hormone is made in the pituitary gland.
The body releases especially a lot of growth hormone during sleep.
A person grows fastest in the first year of life and in puberty.
After puberty the growth plates close and growth in height ends.
How tall someone becomes depends on genes, diet and health.

abschnitte.text: Every person begins as a single cell. Through **cell division** more and more cells arise from it. In the process a cell doubles its genetic information and divides into two daughter cells. A grown-up person finally consists of many trillions of cells. Even after growth, cells keep dividing, for example to renew skin or blood.

Long bones such as the thigh bone have, near their ends, a layer of cartilage, the **growth plate**. There new cartilage cells are constantly formed, which later turn into bone. This way the bone becomes longer bit by bit. On an X-ray you can see the growth plates in children as dark lines. Doctors can use them to estimate how much a child will still grow.

The **pituitary gland** is a gland the size of a pea at the bottom of the brain. It makes the **growth hormone**, which stimulates bones, muscles and organs to grow. An especially large amount of it is released at night in deep sleep. Enough sleep is therefore important for children and teenagers. In puberty the sex hormones also help.

A newborn baby is about 50 centimetres long. In the first year of life a baby grows by about 25 centimetres, as fast as never again later. After that it becomes calmer, and children then grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year. In **puberty** a growth spurt follows, in girls usually earlier than in boys. At about 16 to 18 years the growth plates close and growth in height is finished.

Body height is inherited to a large extent from the **genes** of the parents. A healthy diet with enough protein, calcium and vitamins is, however, also important. Exercise, sleep and the absence of serious illnesses also play a part. Because people today are better fed, they are on average clearly taller than 150 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A layer of cartilage in the bone in which the bone grows in length.
A small gland at the brain that makes the growth hormone, also called the hypophysis.
A process in which two new cells arise from one cell.
A time in which a person grows especially fast.

gewusst: In the morning you are about 1 to 2 centimetres taller than in the evening, because the discs between the vertebrae recover during the night.
A baby doubles its birth weight in about the first five months.
Nose and ears seem to go on growing in adulthood, because the cartilage tissue gives way with age.

teile.einleitung: Before anyone is allowed to fly into space, they have to practise for years. **Astronaut training** prepares them for work in weightlessness, for emergencies and for life in a cramped space. It involves water tanks, aeroplanes and even exercises in the snow.
wichtigste: Training to become an astronaut takes several years.
Spacewalks are practised in a huge water tank.
On a parabolic flight in an aeroplane you briefly experience weightlessness.
Besides English, astronauts often learn Russian.
In Europe the European Space Agency ESA trains astronauts.
Astronauts from Russia are called cosmonauts.

abschnitte.text: Work outside the space station is difficult and tiring. That is why astronauts practise these **spacewalks** in a **huge water tank**. In it there is a copy of parts of the space station. The astronauts wear a spacesuit that is weighted so that they neither sink nor rise. This makes the work feel similar to being in space. A training session can last many hours.

Real **weightlessness** on the Earth exists only for a short time. On a **parabolic flight** an aeroplane flies steeply upwards and then down again in an arc. During this arc the people in the aeroplane float for about 20 seconds. This is repeated many times one after another. In this way the astronauts get used to the feeling of floating.

In a **copy of the space station** the astronauts practise the **work and routines on board**, for example experiments, repairs or what to do in a fire. Because Russia is involved in the space station, many learn **Russian** as well as English. They also practise **surviving in forests, in the snow** or on water. This is because a capsule could also land **far away** from the planned place on its return.

In Europe **ESA**, the European Space Agency, chooses and trains its astronauts. An important training centre is in Cologne in Germany. The **training** lasts **several years**. The first Swiss person in space was **Claude Nicollier**, who flew several times on the space shuttle from 1992. In 2022 ESA once again chose a Swiss astronaut, **Marco Sieber**. By the way, astronauts from Russia are called **cosmonauts**, and those from China taikonauts.

gewusst: On a single parabolic flight the arc is often flown several dozen times.
On his flights Claude Nicollier helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope.

teile.einleitung: Heredity means that parents pass on features such as eye colour or blood group to their children. The information for this is in the genes on our DNA. The rules of heredity were discovered by the monk Gregor Mendel with peas, long before anyone knew what genes are.
wichtigste: Thanks to crossing experiments with peas, Gregor Mendel is regarded as the founder of the science of heredity.
Hereditary material lies as genes on the chromosomes.
Every gene occurs in two variants, one each from mother and father.
If you cross two parents who are both Aa, the dominant and recessive feature appear in a ratio of 3 to 1.
In the cross Aa times aa, 50 per cent of the offspring are purebred recessive.
If two alleles are fully expressed at the same time, it is called codominance.
Men are affected more often by X-linked recessive features, because they have only one X chromosome.

abschnitte.text: **Gregor Mendel** was an Augustinian monk in the monastery in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic. Between 1856 and 1863 he crossed thousands of **pea plants** and counted their features exactly, such as flower colour and seed shape. In 1866 he published his results, but hardly anyone took notice. Only around 1900 were his rules rediscovered by other researchers. Today he is regarded as the founder of **genetics**.

The hereditary information is stored in the **DNA**, which lies in the chromosomes of every cell. Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from the mother and 23 from the father. A section of DNA for a feature is called a **gene**. Of every gene we have two variants, the **alleles**. If both are the same, you are purebred, for example AA or aa. If they are different, you are mixed, that is Aa.

A **dominant** allele prevails over a **recessive** one, and it is written with capital letters. A child with Aa therefore shows the dominant feature. If you cross two parents who are both Aa, AA, Aa, Aa and aa result. So three quarters show the dominant and one quarter the recessive feature, the ratio is 3 to 1. In Aa times aa, 50 per cent of the offspring are purebred recessive.

If you look at two features at the same time, it is called a **dihybrid cross**. In the second filial generation, the F2, the features then split in the ratio 9 to 3 to 3 to 1. Sometimes two alleles are fully expressed at the same time, which is called **codominance**. An example is blood group AB, in which both features A and B are visible. In incomplete dominance, by contrast, a mixed form results, for example pink flowers from red and white ones.

Whether someone becomes a woman or a man is decided by the **sex chromosomes**: women usually have two X chromosomes, men one X and one Y. If a recessive feature lies on the X chromosome, men already show it when they have it once. That is why men are affected much more often by **red-green colour blindness** than women. Haemophilia is also inherited this way. Many features such as height, however, depend on many genes and also on the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA that contains the information for a feature.
One of several variants of a gene.
A hereditary factor that prevails over another.
A hereditary factor that becomes visible only when it is present twice.
Two alleles are fully expressed at the same time.

gewusst: Mendel worked with peas because they grow quickly and have clearly distinguishable features.
Identical twins have almost exactly the same hereditary information.
In Europe about one man in twelve is affected by red-green colour blindness, but fewer than one woman in a hundred.

teile.einleitung: At the dentist's your teeth are checked and looked after. Regular visits help to discover tooth decay early and keep the teeth healthy.
wichtigste: Children go for a dental check-up about once a year.
With a small mirror the dentist can also see behind the teeth.
An X-ray shows hidden holes.
Tooth decay is removed with a small drill, after the spot has been numbed.
The dental hygienist cleans the teeth thoroughly.
The orthodontist straightens crooked teeth with a brace.

abschnitte.text: For children a **dental check-up** about **once a year** is usual. This way **tooth decay** is found early, before it gets big. The dentist looks into the mouth with a small round **mirror** on a handle. With it they can also see the inner sides of the teeth. On an **X-ray** they can also spot hidden holes between the teeth. In many Swiss municipalities there is also a **school dentist** for this.

If a tooth has a hole, the diseased part has to go. So that it does not hurt, the dentist **numbs** the spot with an **injection**. Then they grind away the decay with a small **drill** that spins very fast. Finally they fill the hole with a **filling**. This seals the tooth again.

Various specialists work in a dental practice. The **dental hygienist** removes plaque and **tartar** particularly thoroughly. She also shows you how to brush properly. The **orthodontist** is a dentist who specialises in the position of the teeth. She straightens crooked teeth with a **brace**.

If a **permanent tooth** is knocked out in an accident, every minute counts. Hold the tooth by the crown, not by the root. It should stay **moist**, for example in **milk**. Then go **straight to the dentist**. If you are quick, there is a good chance that the tooth will grow back in.

gewusst: Chemists sell special tooth rescue boxes for knocked-out teeth.
In Switzerland many cantons have school dental care, so that all children are checked regularly.

teile.einleitung: Many children know this: in the evening or at night their legs suddenly hurt. This is called growing pains. They are unpleasant but usually harmless and go away by themselves.
wichtigste: Growing pains usually occur in the legs.
They typically come in the evening or at night.
They mainly affect children between about 3 and 12 years old.
Gentle massage and warmth often help.
Growing pains are usually harmless.
With swelling, redness or fever you go to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Growing pains are usually felt in the **legs**. The **calves**, the thighs or the backs of the knees are typical. Often both legs hurt. The pains usually come in the **evening** or at **night**. Sometimes a child wakes up because of them, but by the morning everything is usually fine again.

Growing pains occur in **children**, mainly between about **3 and 12 years old**. They are not known in babies or in older people. They often come in phases: for a few weeks they come often, and then not for a long time. Many children get them after a day with a lot of running and playing.

Despite their name, it is not certain that the pains really come from **growing**. The exact **cause** has still not been fully explained. One idea is that the muscles are tired from playing during the day. The important thing is: growing pains are **usually harmless** and stop by themselves.

**Gentle massage** of the legs often helps against growing pains. **Warmth**, for example a warm cushion, also soothes the muscles. Often **comfort** and closeness simply help too. But if the leg is **swollen** or red, if the child limps or has a **fever**, it is probably not growing pains. Then a doctor should take a look.

gewusst: Growing pains almost never occur during the day while playing, but usually only when resting.
A typical feature is that the pain is not in a joint but in the muscles in between.

teile.einleitung: Eyelashes are the short hairs on the edge of the eyelids. They protect the eye from dust like a little fence.
wichtigste: Eyelashes grow on the upper and the lower eyelid.
At the top they are usually longer and there are more of them.
They keep dust and small particles away from the eye.
If something touches the eyelashes, the eye closes at once.
If an eyelash falls out, a new one grows back.
Camels have particularly long eyelashes against the desert sand.

abschnitte.titel: A fence in front of the eye
abschnitte.text: **Eyelashes** are short, curved hairs on the edge of the **eyelids**. They grow at the top and bottom. On the upper lid they are usually **longer** and there are more of them. At the bottom they are shorter. Like a little fence, they keep **dust** and small particles away from the eye.

The eyelashes are very **sensitive**. If something touches them, the eye closes at once. This quick protection is called the **blink reflex**. We also close and open our eyelids often at other times, and this is called **blinking**. This keeps the eye moist, and the eyelashes help to wipe.

Eyelashes are hairs and fall out from time to time, like other hairs. Afterwards a **new eyelash** grows back in the same place. A single eyelash lives only a few months. That is why you sometimes find an eyelash on your cheek. Some children then make a wish and blow it away.

Many animals have eyelashes too. The **camel** is particularly well known for them. Its long, thick eyelashes protect its eyes from the sand in the desert. Some adults colour their eyelashes with **mascara**. This makes them look darker and longer.

gewusst: Camels even have two rows of eyelashes on each lid.
Eyelashes grow much more slowly and get much less long than the hair on your head.

teile.einleitung: In medicine, ventilation means the airing of the lungs. It refers to how much air is breathed in and out per minute and how much of it really reaches the air sacs of the lungs.
wichtigste: The minute volume is the tidal volume times the breathing rate.
Part of the air stays in the dead space of the airways and does not reach the air sacs.
Alveolar ventilation is the amount of air that reaches the alveoli per minute.
Hyperventilation leads to respiratory alkalosis, hypoventilation to respiratory acidosis.
The ventilation-perfusion ratio of the whole lung is about 0.8 at rest.
In artificial ventilation, PEEP keeps the air sacs open at the end of breathing out.

abschnitte.text: With every breath an adult at rest moves about half a litre of air. This is the **tidal volume**. The number of breaths per minute is called the **breathing rate**. If you multiply the two, you get the **minute volume**. With 0.5 litres and 12 breaths per minute that is 6 litres per minute. During sport this value rises sharply.

Not all the air breathed in takes part in gas exchange. Part of it stays in the nose, windpipe and bronchi, in the so-called **dead space**. In adults that is about 150 millilitres per breath. The air that really reaches the **alveoli** per minute is called **alveolar ventilation**. With a tidal volume of 500 millilitres and 14 breaths that is 350 times 14, so 4.9 litres per minute.

abschnitte.titel: Breathing too much or too little
abschnitte.text: If you breathe too fast and too deeply, it is called **hyperventilation**. Too much CO2 is breathed out, and the pH value of the blood rises: **respiratory alkalosis** develops. If you breathe too little, it is called **hypoventilation**. Then CO2 builds up in the blood, which is called hypercapnia. More carbonic acid forms, the pH value falls, and **respiratory acidosis** results.

For good gas exchange, ventilation and blood flow must match. The **ventilation-perfusion ratio** for the whole lung is about 0.8 at rest. In a standing person it is highest in the **apex of the lung**, because little blood flows there because of gravity. If areas receive blood but no air, it is called a **shunt**. This blood takes up no oxygen and mixes into the arterial blood low in oxygen.

If a person cannot breathe enough by themselves, a **ventilator** helps. It blows air into the lungs under positive pressure. Important here is the **PEEP**, the “positive end-expiratory pressure”. This is a residual pressure that stays at the end of breathing out. It keeps the alveoli open and so improves the uptake of oxygen.

gewusst: When you hyperventilate, your fingers can tingle and your hands can cramp, because the acid-base balance shifts.
During strong physical effort the minute volume can rise to many times the resting value.

teile.einleitung: Toes are the movable parts at the front of the foot. Every person normally has ten of them. They help with walking, standing and keeping your balance.
wichtigste: Each foot has **five toes**, ten altogether.
The **big toe** is the thickest and strongest.
The **little toe** sits right on the outside of the foot.
Toes help with **balance**.
Toenails are best cut **straight**.
The **ostrich** is the only bird with just two toes on each foot.

abschnitte.text: Each foot has five toes. The **big toe** consists of two bones, and the other toes usually of three. These bones are called **phalanges**. Joints connect them, which is why you can bend and straighten your toes. At the tip of each toe sits a protective toenail.

When you stand, your toes press lightly against the ground. In this way they help you to keep your **balance** and not fall over. When walking and running, you push off at the end with your **big toe**. It carries a lot of weight as you do so. The **little toe** on the very outside easily gets stubbed on table legs, which can hurt a lot.

Toenails are best cut **straight**. Then they do not grow into the skin so easily. After a bath the nails are softer and easier to cut. Shoes should have enough room at the front so that the toes are not squashed. Walking barefoot on soft ground strengthens the muscles in the foot.

In **ballet** there is dancing on pointe. Dancers stand on the tips of their toes in special **pointe shoes**. This needs a lot of training and strong feet. In sprinting, too, runners often touch the ground only with the front of the foot.

Many animals have toes too. Most **chickens** have four toes on each foot, and some breeds have five. The **ostrich** is the only bird with just **two toes** on each foot. This helps it to run fast. Horses even walk on just one single toe, whose nail has become the hoof.

gewusst: A horse's hoof is really a very large, hard toenail.
Some people who have no arms learn to paint or write with their toes.

teile.einleitung: Cells multiply by dividing. One mother cell produces two daughter cells with exactly the same genetic information.
wichtigste: The division of the nucleus in body cells is called **mitosis**.
One mother cell produces **two daughter cells**.
The daughter cells are **genetically identical**.
Before division the DNA is **doubled**, and this is called replication.
Between two divisions lies **interphase**.
The body needs cell division for **growth** and for replacing old cells.
If cells divide uncontrollably, **cancer** can develop.

abschnitte.text: Through cell division children **grow** and **wounds heal**. Dead cells are also constantly replaced, for example in the **skin** or the intestine. Blood cells are also continually being made. Bacteria and other single-celled organisms reproduce by dividing. So without cell division there would be no life as we know it.

A cell spends most of its time in **interphase**. During this time it grows and carries out its tasks. Before it divides, it has to **double its DNA**. This copying process is called **replication**. Afterwards each chromosome consists of two identical halves.

In **mitosis** the nucleus divides. First the chromosomes become compact and visible. Then they line up in the middle of the cell. Fine fibres pull the two halves of each chromosome to opposite sides. A new nucleus forms around each half. After that the **cytoplasm** also divides, and two **daughter cells** are produced. Each receives a complete copy of all the chromosomes.

With each division the number of cells doubles. If a bacterial cell divides every **20 minutes**, there are 6 divisions in 2 hours. So one cell becomes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and finally **64 cells**. That is why bacteria can multiply greatly in a short time when it is warm and there is enough food.

Normally cell division is strictly controlled. Cells divide only when it is necessary. If this control fails, cells divide uncontrollably. **Tumours** can develop. Malignant tumours are called **cancer**. Many cancer medicines work by slowing down cell division.

gewusst: In the skin a great many old cells are replaced by new ones every day. Dead skin cells make up part of house dust.
Some cells, such as most nerve cells in the brain, hardly divide at all in adults.

teile.einleitung: Every cell is surrounded by a wafer-thin covering, the cell membrane. It separates the inside from the surroundings and decides which substances get in and out.
wichtigste: The **cell membrane** forms the boundary of the cell and controls the exchange of substances.
It is **semi-permeable**, that is selectively permeable.
Small particles such as oxygen pass straight through.
**Membrane proteins** form channels and pumps.
**Diffusion** is movement from high to low concentration.
**Active transport** needs energy.

abschnitte.text: The cell membrane consists mainly of a **double layer** of fat-like molecules, the **phospholipids**. Their water-loving heads point outwards and inwards, and their water-repelling tails point towards each other. Many **membrane proteins** sit in this fatty layer. The membrane can be imagined as a moving mosaic in which the pieces can move sideways.

The membrane does not let everything through. It is called **semi-permeable** or selectively permeable. Very small, fat-soluble particles such as **oxygen** and **carbon dioxide** simply slip through the fatty layer. Water also gets through, often via special channels. Large or charged particles such as sugar and salts need **membrane proteins**, which act like gates.

Particles are constantly moving at random. As a result they move from places of **high** to places of **low concentration** until they are evenly spread out. This is called **diffusion**, as with a drop of ink in water. When water moves through a semi-permeable membrane, this is called **osmosis**. If you put a red blood cell into pure water, water flows in. The cell swells and can burst.

Sometimes a cell has to pump substances against the concentration gradient. This is called **active transport**. For this it needs energy. An important example is the **sodium-potassium pump**. It pumps sodium out of the cell and potassium in. This is very important, for example, for nerve cells.

gewusst: The cell membrane is only about one hundred-thousandth of a millimetre thick.
The Dane Jens Christian Skou received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1997 for discovering the sodium-potassium pump.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the “Znüni” is the small snack in the middle of the morning. Many children eat it at school during the long morning break.
wichtigste: **Znüni** means “at nine”, and it is eaten at about nine o'clock.
Before the Znüni comes breakfast, the **“Zmorge”**.
At school it is usually eaten during the **morning break**.
A Znüni gives **energy** for the morning.
Fruit and vegetables such as **mandarins** or **carrots** are a good choice.
Crisps are not a good Znüni, because they have a lot of **fat and salt**.

abschnitte.text: The word Znüni comes from Swiss German and means something like **“at nine”**. It is eaten at about **nine o'clock** in the morning. Other Swiss German names for meals are formed in a similar way: in the morning there is **“Zmorge”**, breakfast, at midday “Zmittag”, lunch, in the afternoon **“Zvieri”**, the afternoon snack, and in the evening “Znacht”, supper.

It is a long time from breakfast to lunch. A small Znüni gives **energy** for the morning. This helps you to **concentrate** better at school. But the Znüni should be small so that you are still hungry at lunchtime. Something to drink is part of it too, best of all water or unsweetened tea.

**Fruit** and **vegetables** are very suitable. A **mandarin** can be peeled without a knife and divided into segments. **Carrots** can be eaten raw and are good for nibbling, as are cucumbers or peppers. A piece of wholemeal bread, some cheese or nuts also fill you up. **Crisps**, on the other hand, are not a good Znüni. They contain a lot of fat and salt but few vitamins, and they do not keep you full for long.

At school the Znüni is usually eaten during the **long break** in the morning. You can take it with you in a **Znüni box**. Inside it the food stays clean and does not get squashed. The box can be used again and again, which saves rubbish. Some schools also have their own rules or weeks for a healthy Znüni.

gewusst: Many adults in Switzerland also take a Znüni break at work in the morning.
Raw potatoes are not eaten as a Znüni, because potatoes have to be cooked.

teile.einleitung: Didier Queloz is a Swiss astronomer from Geneva. Together with Michel Mayor he found, in 1995, the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star, and for this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
wichtigste: Didier Queloz was born in 1966.
In 1995 he was a doctoral student of Michel Mayor at the University of Geneva.
At the end of 1994 he was the first to notice the signal from the star 51 Pegasi.
In 2019, Mayor and Queloz received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He is a professor at the University of Cambridge and, since 2021, at ETH Zurich.
At ETH he heads a centre for the origin and spread of life.

abschnitte.text: Didier Queloz was born in **1966**. In the early 1990s he wrote his **doctoral thesis** under **Michel Mayor** at the University of **Geneva**. He helped with the software that analysed the light spectra of stars. For this he used **cross-correlation**: the measured spectrum is compared with a template made of many spectral lines. The point of best match shows tiny shifts very precisely.

When a planet orbits a star, it pulls the star slightly back and forth. As a result, the lines in the starlight shift ever so slightly. At the end of **1994**, Queloz noticed a regular wobble in the star **51 Pegasi** while Mayor was abroad. At first he believed it was a **measurement error**. But the signal stayed. In 1995 the two announced the discovery of **51 Pegasi b**, the first planet around an ordinary Sun-like star.

In **2019**, Mayor and Queloz received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. The Nobel Committee honoured the discovery of an **exoplanet** around a Sun-like star. This find began the systematic search for planets around other stars. Today thousands of them are known. When he received the prize, Queloz was a good twenty years younger than his teacher.

In the year **2000**, Queloz was the first to detect the **Rossiter-McLaughlin effect** in an exoplanet. When a planet passes in front of a rotating star, it first covers the side that is moving towards us, then the side that is moving away. This distorts the measurement in a typical way. That tells us how the orbit is tilted relative to the star's rotation.

Queloz is a professor at the **Cavendish Laboratory** of the **University of Cambridge** in England. In **2021** he also became a professor at **ETH Zurich**. There he heads a centre that researches the **origin and spread of life**. It combines astronomy, chemistry and biology. Queloz commutes between Switzerland and England.

gewusst: 51 Pegasi b is a giant gas planet that orbits its star in only about four days.

teile.einleitung: Cycling is fun, keeps you fit and gets you to your destination quickly. To be safe on the road, you need a well-equipped bike and must know the most important traffic rules.
wichtigste: A well-fitting cycle helmet protects the head in a fall.
You brake with the brake levers on the handlebars.
Before turning you stretch out your arm in the direction in which you want to go.
In Switzerland traffic keeps to the right: cyclists ride at the right edge of the road.
In the dark the bike needs a white light at the front and a red one at the back.
With the bell you draw other people's attention to yourself.
Many schoolchildren in Switzerland take the cycling test in primary school.

abschnitte.text: A bike has two wheels, a frame, handlebars and a saddle. With the **pedals** you drive the rear wheel through the chain. On the handlebars are the **brake levers**: when you pull them, the brakes press on the wheels or brake discs. The **bell** also belongs on the handlebars. With it you warn pedestrians, for example, so that they hear you.

The **cycle helmet** protects the head if you fall. It must fit well, must not wobble and must be firmly fastened. When it gets dark, the bike needs **lights**: white at the front and red at the back. Reflectors and bright clothes help drivers to see you early. Before a ride it is worth taking a quick look at the brakes, lights and tyres.

In Switzerland **traffic keeps to the right**, so you ride at the right edge of the road. If you want to turn, you show this with an **outstretched arm**. This way the others know what you are planning. Beforehand you look behind to see whether the road is clear. Traffic lights, road signs and cycle paths apply to cyclists just as they do to everyone else.

In many cantons children take the **cycling test** in primary school. Beforehand they practise with their teacher or with the traffic police. In the test they ride a route in real traffic. In doing so they show that they know the traffic rules and apply them correctly. Many children are proud when they have passed the test.

When cycling, mainly the **leg muscles** work, that is the muscles in the thighs and calves. With every push on the pedals they get stronger. Heart and lungs are also trained, because the body needs more oxygen. Cycling is easy on the joints, because the body weight rests on the saddle. People who ride regularly stay fit and are out in the fresh air.

gewusst: The word “Velo”, the Swiss word for a bicycle, comes from the French “vélocipède”, which means “fast foot”.
The forerunner of the bicycle was the running machine of Karl Drais from the year 1817. It still had no pedals, and you pushed yourself along with your feet on the ground.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the “Zvieri” is the small snack in the afternoon. After school it satisfies the first hunger until supper.
wichtigste: **Zvieri** means “at four”, and it is eaten at about four o'clock in the afternoon.
A classic Swiss Zvieri is **bread with a piece of chocolate**.
Healthy options are, for example, **yoghurt with fruit** or vegetable sticks.
**Cheese** provides a lot of protein.
The Zvieri should be rather **small**.
After the Zvieri comes supper, the **“Znacht”**.

abschnitte.text: The word Zvieri is Swiss German and means **“at four”**. It is eaten at about **four o'clock** in the afternoon. So there are about four hours between **“Zmittag”**, lunch at 12 o'clock, and the Zvieri at 4 pm. Then in the evening comes supper, in Swiss German **“Znacht”**. In the morning, in the same way, there is the Znüni.

A piece of **bread with some chocolate** is a typical Zvieri in Switzerland. Many adults still remember it from their own childhood. Rösti, fondue and raclette, on the other hand, are main meals and not a Zvieri. An apple, a piece of cheese or a glass of milk are also popular.

**Yoghurt with fruit** gives energy and vitamins. **Vegetable sticks** such as cucumber, carrot or pepper are crunchy and healthy. With a **quark dip** they taste even better. A piece of **cheese** provides a lot of **protein**, because cheese is made from milk. Jelly babies, sweets and lemonade, on the other hand, have a lot of sugar and hardly any other nutrients.

The Zvieri satisfies your hunger in the afternoon, for example after school or before training. But it should be rather **small**. That way you still have an **appetite** at supper. Anyone who eats too much in the afternoon often does not feel like eating properly in the evening.

gewusst: The Zvieri is so well known in Switzerland that companies and clubs also invite people to a “Zvieri” when they offer something to eat in the afternoon.
The word is pronounced a little differently depending on the region, but it means the same thing everywhere.
